Une fois que les données sont réalistes, elles sont partagées avec les branches, la PIROI et la FICR. La SN travaille avec le cluster FICR de l’OI à Madagascar qui lui, compile et rapporte à Nairobi.
Il n’y a pas de canevas standard pour le reporting. Les rapports prennent du temps parfois parce qu’ils ne sont pas acceptés par les partenaires et doivent être répétés. Il n’y a pas non plus d’analyse sur les restrictions qui affectent le PMER en cas d’épidémie. Les rumeurs reliées à l’épidémie sont collectées par les volontaires et envoyées au siège à travers un outil pour les gérer.

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_responses.epi_considerations: Les lacunes financières qui pourraient survenir durant les épidémies ne sont pas analysées.
component_responses.notes:
Les procédures financières existantes éclaircissent surtout l’utilisation du budget de projets et l’utilisation des fonds journaliers. Il n’existe pas de procédures financières d’urgence avec activation spécifique (début et fin). Les signatures qu’il faut collecter en urgences sont celles de la Gouvernance, donc du président, trésorier, etc, mais pas le SG. Ceci retarde l’intervention de la SN en urgence.  
Les procédures de transparence sont incluses dans les procédures financières et logistiques. Elles expliquent comment faire les choses en fonction du montant d’argent utilisé. (Exemple : les grandes sommes sont envoyées par transfert bancaire).  
Le personnel administratif, financier et les directeurs des opérations connaissent les accords (MOU) liés aux urgences.
Les lacunes financières qui pourraient survenir durant les épidémies ne sont pas analysées.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_responses.epi_considerations: Pas de plan pour assurer la continuité pour les interventions en épidémie.
component_responses.notes:
Le staff et les volontaires utilisent leurs téléphones, SIM et comptes personnels pour les communications. Ils ne transportent pas les contacts critiques sur leurs téléphones à tous moments.
Il existe une matrice de réaction rapide disponible en cas d’inondation pour assurer les interactions et la communication entre tous les secteurs d’intervention. Mais ce n’est utilisé que si le plan est déclenché. Les fiches ne sont pas considérées comme un protocole de notification d’urgence ou des procédures générales. 
La SN est active sur Facebook pour le grand public et sur WhatsApp en interne. Le site internet n’est pas géré par une personne et ne peut pas être mis à jour régulièrement.
Les radio VHF et HF avec le personnel et dans les véhicules n’existent plus, mais les fréquences sont encore officiellement libérées pour le CRCo. Depuis que le CICR est parti, la maintenance/ l’entretien n’est pas pris en charge et le personnel n’est pas formé sur les procédures d’utilisation. Les téléphones satellites n’existent pas non plus avec le personnel clé. 
Vu le contexte, le fait de ne pas avoir un réseau de communication de secours risque l’arrêt de l’intervention de la SN car les réseaux de communication peuvent tomber en panne au passage d’un cyclone. 
Des groupes électrogènes existent au siège et dans les branches. Le carburant est rechargé au besoin, sans réserve. La SN a des privilèges en cas de pénurie. 
Le siège a l’internet et les branches vont recevoir le budget pour une année de connexion. Il y a un seul point focal IT au siège qui n’a pas le temps de faire l’entretien de tous les équipements et de suivre le site. S’il y a un problème dans les branches, ils font appel à des prestataires vu le contexte des îles. 
La SN n’a de plan pour assurer la continuité pour les interventions en épidémie.

component_responses.epi_considerations:
Gestion de la Logistique :
- Les articles de secours pour les épidémies ne sont pas choisis en consultation avec l’Organisation mondiale de la Santé et avec le ministère de la santé.
- La SN n’est pas prête à gérer l’impact d’un confinement (perturbation de la chaîne d’approvisionnement, personnel/volontaires limités).
-Non

Gestion de la chaîne de distribution : localement pas de processus de gestion de la chaîne d’approvisionnement adaptés aux épidémies.

Approvisionnement : pas de processus. La SN achète chez OCOPHARMA si besoin.

Gestion de la flotte et du transport :
- Il y a un protocole écrit pour désinfecter. Les équipes qui vont sur le terrain doivent le faire. 
- les chauffeurs ne sont pas formés sur le contrôle des épidémies. 

Entrepôts et gestion des stocks : pas de procédures ou RH dédiées. Les médecins ou vaccins qui doivent rester au froid sont pris de chez OCOPHARMA et la SN les utilisent immédiatement.
component_responses.notes:
GESTION LOGISTIQUE
Il existe un responsable logistique au siège, des logisticiens formés dans les trois branches et des volontaires en logistique pouvant soutenir l’équipe existante en cas d’intervention d’urgence.
Le manuel logistique liste le rôle du responsable logistique entre autres. Les membres clés du personnel ne connaissent pas les services logistiques de la FICR. 
La SN n'a pas fait une analyse des options optimales pour la chaîne de distribution en termes de coûts, de rapidité et de fiabilité, surtout que c’est rarement la SN qui achète. D'habitude c'est la PIROI et la FICR qui le font.
Dans les 3 entrepôts il y a des stocks qui répondent aux normes. Un réapprovisionnement est nécessaire car ça n’a pas été fait après la dernière utilisation du matériel. Lorsque les articles de secours se rapportent aux épidémies, ils ne sont pas choisis en consultation avec l'Organisation Mondiale de la Santé et avec le Ministère de la Santé.
Les Stocks sont dans les entrepôts centraux des îles. Ils ne sont pas stockés dans les zones à risque. La SN a juste stocké des tantes dans 4 comités locaux pour ne pas devoir repartir à l'entrepôt central en cas de besoin. 
La SN n'est pas prête à gérer l'impact d'un confinement s'il en était le cas (perturbation de la chaîne d'approvisionnement, personnel/volontaires limités).

GESTION DE LA CHAINE DE DISTRIBUTION
En urgence, la SN est exemptée des douanes. Hors situation de crises, par exemple pour la préparation et l’anticipation, c'est difficile de recevoir du matériel et d'enlever les douanes. 
Les stocks et équipements adhèrent aux normes du Mouvement et sont coordonnés avec l'UNICEF et la PIROI.
Il n’existe pas de procédure rapide documentée pour les branches, pour commander davantage d’articles de secours et/ou d’équipement pour les actions précoces et les interventions immédiates.
Pas de procédures pour accepter (ou refuser), stocker, éliminer et signaler les dons en nature. Lorsque ça se passe, c'est informel.
La SN n'achète pas de l'extérieur, juste localement. En cas de besoin, ce sont la FICR et la PIROI qui s'occupent des achats internationaux. Localement, il n'y a pas de processus de gestion de la chaîne d'approvisionnement adaptés aux épidémies.

APPROVISIONNEMENT
La SN dispose d’un personnel formé à l’approvisionnement. Des procédures d'achat existent mais le document doit être révisé et mis à jour pour remplacer le terme "Directeur Administratif et Financier" (qui est barré) par le terme "Le comptable".  Les niveaux d'autorisation existent, les formulaires sont dans les kits Log et Finance (qui n’ont pas été fournis aux facilitateurs). Les procédures informent sur les dérogations en cas d'urgence. Le département de logistique utilise les procédures et les formats. 
La SN dispose d’une liste actualisée du peu de fournisseurs de biens et de services avec lesquels elle travaille (pour les articles médicaux, c'est chez OCOPHARMA), mais pas de liste noire qui évite de retravailler avec des fournisseurs qui n’ont pas accompli selon les accords. Il n’existe pas d'accords (cadre/généraux) signés au préalable avec des fournisseurs pour pouvoir accéder immédiatement aux marchandises.
La SN n'analyse pas la durabilité des produits et la réduction des emballages.

GESTION DE LA FLOTTE ET DU TRANSPORT
Il n’existe pas de PF pour la flotte (le point focal logistique ne l'est pas). 
La SN dispose de cinq voiture 4x4 (3 voitures au niveau siège national, 1 à Mohéli et 1 à Ngazidja) et une ambulance au niveau du siège mais ceci n’est pas suffisant pour les actions et interventions entreprises par le CRCo (A Anjouan, il y a une voiture CRF mais n'est pas utilisée par la SN). 
Les véhicules sont assurés, ont les ceintures mais pas d'extincteur ou de kits premier secours. La politique anti-arme existe sur papiers et des autocollants la traduisent dans les voitures mais il n'est pas clair si elle est mise en pratique de façon systématique. La SN fait appel à des mécaniciens agréés pour la maintenance.
Un journal de bord a été préparé par le point focal logistique à travers le projet avec la CR Japonaise. Le journal a été expliqué aux chauffeurs car sur papier, les procédures disent que ce sont eux qui doivent conduire mais en réalité, d’autres personnes prennent les voitures, mais elles ne sont pas informées de l’obligation d’utilisation du journal de bord.
Selon les procédures logistiques, le signalement des accidents est à la charge des chauffeurs, en utilisant un format mentionné dans le règlement intérieur mais non vérifié par les facilitateurs. Au niveau des branches, les SG gèrent ceci. Toutefois, ceci ne se fait pas en pratique.
Les personnes qui conduisent ont un permis de conduire pour les voitures. Les chauffeurs ont été formés 2 fois mais ne sont pas testés régulièrement. Les autres personnes qui conduisent n'ont pas de procédures spécifiques pour conduire les voitures du Croissant Rouge.
Les chauffeurs de la SN ne sont pas formés aux Premiers Secours, la conduite de défense, l'Accès plus sûr et le contrôle des épidémies. Un protocole est écrit pour la désinfection. Les équipes terrain en sont responsables. Il n’existe pas de procédures d’urgence concernant les heures de travail des chauffeurs en urgence y compris les horaires non-standards et les compensations. Ceci existe dans le manuel financier mais pour le fonctionnement normal.
Il n’existe pas de listes avec les références des compagnies de locations pour les voitures et les chauffeurs.

ENTREPOTS ET GESTION DES STOCKS
La SN dispose d’un manuel de gestion de l’entreposage et du stockage approuvé, comprenant des formulaires et des modèles normalisés, mais il ne couvre pas les considérations de stockage de kits médicaux durant les épidémies. Le personnel et les volontaires concernés sont formés sur les procédures et l'utilisation des formulaires.
La SN dispose de 3 entrepôts sécurisés, ils peuvent être accédés 24/7 et sont assez larges pour contenir les quantités d'équipement et de marchandise de secours pour le nombre de foyers que la SN envisage de soutenir selon leur plan d'intervention (1000 aux Grandes Comores, 150 à Anjouan et 150 à Mohéli).
Les entrepôts centraux des 3 îles sont utilisés pour le stockage, il n'existe pas d'autres locaux dans les comités, à proximité des communautés à haut risque pour un accès plus rapide.

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_responses.epi_considerations:
- formations du personnel clé et des intervenants sur la prévention et le contrôle des épidémies se fait uniquement au niveau des volontaires mobilisables (qui font partie des équipes d’intervention BDRT et NDRT).
- Il y a des mesures de protection pour l’utilisation des EPI qui sont distribués au moment d’intervenir.
- La SN vérifie les lois du travail locales pour déterminer si des compétences spécialisées sont nécessaires pour effectuer des tâches particulières pendant les épidémies en lien avec le ministère de la santé.
- pas de police d’assurance pour les épidémies. 
-Pas de dispositifs de santé mentale et de soutien psychosocial sont disponibles pour les équipes d’intervention
component_responses.notes:
Il existe un PF RH mais pas de PF volontariat. Les volontaires admis reçoivent des cartes de volontaire, qui sont renouvelées annuellement. Les volontaires actifs reçoivent aussi des gilets. Il n’y a pas de parcours d'apprentissage dont les volontaires prennent connaissance dès leur admission au CRCo. Pas de formation de base non plus sur le Mouvement et les attentes. En urgence, les volontaires spontanés ne sont pas informés sur un minimum de notions (Principes fondamentaux, réactions inacceptables, etc.) et donc des incidents peuvent survenir et sont un risque sur l’image du CRCo. Pas d'analyse spécifique sur l’accès sécurisé. Pas de formations sur la protection, l'abus et le genre. En Janvier 2024, les volontaires ont reçu pour la première fois une formation sur la sureté et la sécurité mais il n'existe pas de procédures pour que les bureaux régionaux prennent les décisions de façon autonome sur la sécurité de leurs équipes. Les mesures de protection (même en cas d’épidémies) se limitent aux EPI. Il n’existe pas de PF pour suivre cela non plus.
Des termes de référence sont préparés pour la mobilisation des volontaires durant les réponses d’urgence car c’est généralement une exigence reliée aux fonds. Il n’existe pas de signe d’institutionnalisation de cette procédure au cas où la SN agit hors lignes budgétaires. 
Les volontaires sont couverts par l’assurance de la FICR (qui ne couvrent pas les épidémies). Le code de conduite n’est pas connu ni signé par le staff et les volontaires. Les dépenses des volontaires ne sont remboursées que s’il y a un DREF qui se déclenche.
Il n’existe pas de base de données effective, digitale, pour gérer les volontaires sur base de leurs formations. Toutefois, des annexes existent dans le plan de contingence «Inondations» et notamment une cartographie des BDRT dans les 3 branches.
Dans les branches, les bases de données sont faites en forme de registre sur papier et de listes reliées aux formations. Même si les listes se capitalisent aussi sur Excel, les données utilisées en réalité sont sur papier. Les capacités en IT dans les branches doivent être renforcées.
Il y a deux ans, un projet avec la CR Française avait proposé de renseigner une base de données numérique, mais le PF n'avait pas le temps de suivre le travail qui s’est arrêté. Un nouveau point focal a été nommé en vue de suivre le renseignement et l’activation de l’usage de la base de données.
Pour les interventions, la SN appelle tous les volontaires disponibles à se mobiliser. Ceci permet d’avoir des capacités multisectorielles mais vu que de nombreux volontaires sont motivés, leur gestion devient difficile et des frustrations se créent lorsque les coordinateurs demandent à quelques volontaires de quitter les lieux (exemple 300 sur place alors que le besoin est de 20 volontaires).
Des procédures existent pour activer, déployer et gérer les BDRT et NDRT mais pas de procédures ni de fonds propres permettent d’augmenter (recrutement, rétention) ou de diminuer le personnel pendant les urgences.
Pas de stratégie formelle de rotation et de rétention du personnel durant les interventions. Des notions sont inclues dans le règlement intérieur mais ne sont pas spécifiques aux urgences.

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_responses.epi_considerations:
Des messages clés sur les risques sont élaborés/adaptés et partagés régulièrement avec le personnel et les volontaires pour diffusion publique pendant les épidémies.

La SN ne dispose pas d’un système de rétroaction communautaire pour les épidémies.
component_responses.notes:
Il y avait 3 points focaux pour la communication au niveau du siège mais deux sont en congé maternité, donc le point focal IT s’en occupe tout seul. Au niveau des branches, il n’y a pas encore de points focaux pour la communication. Le porte-parole officiel en urgence est le SG.
La SN informe sur la réponse à travers les médias locaux mais pas souvent dans les réseaux sociaux. Elle n’informe pas non plus sur les besoins non satisfaits parce que ceci peut créer des problèmes avec les autorités. Le site internet de la SN n’est pas mis à jour de façon à inclure les nouvelles régulières et le lien pour les donations n’y fonctionne pas.
La SN coordonne sa communication externe avec le Mouvement. Les messages d’urgence sont préparés au cas par cas et doivent être validés au niveau du ministère. Il n’existe pas de modèles standards et de messages généraux validés par type d’aléa. 
Le point focal IT lit les médias pour détecter les rumeurs et les commentaires négatifs et intervient, surtout si les volontaires ont mis des messages inappropriés. Il n’existe pas de politique et de directives pour l’utilisation des réseaux sociaux.

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_responses.notes: The auxiliary role and mandate of the DPRK RCS are defined in the Red Cross Law as “an independent health and relief organization founded in compliance with the voluntary wish of the citizens”. It further mentions that the “Red Cross Society shall conduct its activities in conformity with the relevant state laws and regulations, its own statute, the Fundamental Principles of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement and the Geneva Conventions to which the Democratic People`s Republic of Korea is a party and their Additional Protocol”. •	The mandate is reflected in policies, strategies and plans (e.g. DM Policy, Contingency Plans, RM Strategy). •	The Fundamental Principles are reflected in some, but not all policies, strategies and plans (e.g. not in drought or flood CP). It was noted there is need to ensure the Fundamental Principles are reflected in all operational documents. •	There is need for further dissemination of the mandate and Fundamental Principles among volunteers. •	The Red Cross Law states that the NS shall “disseminate the Fundamental Principles of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement and humanitarian laws and regulations”. The NS has a seat in the commission to promote dissemination of IHL. It was acknowledged that more understating of IHL is required amongst technical staff who also need skills of dissemination of IHL.

component_details.title: DRM Strategy
component_details.description: An outline of the overall goal that the NS seeks to achieve in its disaster and crisis response operations. The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

component_responses.notes: ●	The NS does not have a specific DRM strategy. However, elements normally found in DRM strategy are captured in their contingency plans, for example context analysis, target population and definition of sectors. Additionally, the overall DM objective is reflected in the DM policy. ●	Indicators to measure whether the NS is meeting operational objectives are missing from relevant operational documents (e.g. contingency and response plans). ●	Although there is no separate DRM strategy the elements usually found in a DRM strategy are captured in other documents (e.g. CPs) and are well known by staff and volunteers. ●	Staff from the different technical sectors and support services were included in the development of the CPs which are revised every 3 years.

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_responses.notes: ●	NS has a DM policy (developed in 2016) which reflects the services it would provide through different thematic sectors. ●	It is aligned with Sphere standards and is reflected in different operational documents (e.g. DM policy annexed in CPs). ●	The DM policy will be updated every 4 years with the adoption of a new strategy. ●	The DM policy includes guiding principles for decision-making and mentions collaboration with Government and international stakeholders.

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: ●	The Government has a National law on “Disaster Prevention, Relief and Recovery”, developed in 2015 and revised 2017 (revision supported by IFRC in 2016 by IFRC APRO IDRL Focal Point). ●	The focal department for IDRL is the DM department and the focal department for IHL is International Cooperation department. ●	There is no specific International Disaster Response Law (or use of Model Act), however: ○	The RC Law outlines that the “State shall grant preferential treatment such as exemption from custom duties to the goods and funds contributed by foreign corporate bodies and individuals and international Red Cross organizations in reference to the Red Cross work”. ○	There is no mention of expedited visa processing for HR, but this would be expected. To date, no international delegates have been brought in to support an emergency using such legal facility. ●	To date the NS has not yet seen a need to advocate for the development of IDRL with the DPRK Government. ●	The NS has documents that reflect exemptions that the NS can benefit from during a disaster (e.g. RC Law, IFRC status agreement, MoUs). ●	Although not directly linked to this component it is worth noting that in the context of DPRK there are implications of international sanctions that impact the NS’s capacity to carry out humanitarian activities in peacetime and during emergencies. The NS is working with the British Red Cross on international humanitarian diplomacy efforts related to these sanctions .

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_responses.notes: ●	Community engagement is described by DPRK RCS as an essential element of their preparedness, planning and response work. In practice, the NS gives examples of mechanisms for community engagement (e.g. focus group discussions, PASSA, VCA, CBHFA). Furthermore, with the Government authorities and the NS, community representatives are engaged through the Non-Standing Anti-Calamity Committees. ●	There is no specific focal point for CEA, but it was stated that this responsibility is mainstreamed into different positions and responsible personnel are trained in CEA as per NS training curriculum, which is in line with the IFRC guidelines. The IFRC also conducted a CEA training in 2017. ●	Within the NS 2016-2020 Strategic Plan it states to “Ensure Community Engagement and Accountability in all activities by RC staff and volunteers”. ●	There is no separate CEA plan but for the NS, CEA is a cross-cutting issue that must be reflected/incorporated in all programmes and positions. CEA is not seen as a separate area, but elements of CEA are incorporated into operational documents. For example, the contingency plan makes reference to incorporating suggestions from beneficiaries, the NS states there is a collection box for feedback and a column in reporting book for volunteer leaders to report to branches. ●	The NS adheres to Sphere standards; the handbook has been translated, printed and distributed to branches. ●	The NS states they provide protection services such as child-friendly spaces. ●	NS has their own Gender policy. ●	The NS has no plans or procedures, but in practice activities are designed to minimise harmful impacts of responses. For example, procurement is done locally to support local economy and there are some examples of using solar power to replace coal for heating. ●	There is currently no specific policy on protection for sexual exploitation and abuse. ●	Some staff are informed about the IFRC minimum standards for PGI through trainings. PGI is identified in the NS 2016-2020 Strategy but is not reflected in IFRC EPoA for Floods and Landslides (2018) and Heatwave (2018). Overall the NS states that where possible they follow PGI minimum standards, but they note there is still room for enhancement.

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: ●	DPRK RCS does not have a business continuity plan. ●	Procedures exist to repurpose funds from domestic sources, but not international sources.

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_responses.notes: ●	DPRK RCS has standard operation procedures for NDRT within their contingency plans which describe various action categories (e.g. activation of NDRT/PDRTs), activities, timeframes, and responsible parties. ●	Roles and responsibilities of NDRTs are defined in the CPs. ●	The NS has up-to-date and approved SOPs to respond to disasters and crises at branch level. ●	The NS SOPs do not contain procedures to scale alert levels up and down, but in practice the NS follows the alert level determined and communicated by the Government. ●	The NS does not have a decision-making flowchart, but a section referred to as “Coordination and Information Flow” is included in NS CPs and provincial CPs.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_responses.notes: ●	DPRK RCS has a standard response plan annexed in their contingency plans. ●	In addition to those “seriously affected”, the response plan takes into consideration “women, children, elderly, disabled” in the identification, selection and registration of people affected. ●	Noted there is a section of the contingency plans that describes that the CP (including the Response Plan) will be reviewed and updated after every response operation or reviewed at least once in five years, or as needed. ●	Response plan include mid- and long-term response activities, but NS does not have separate recovery plan.

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: ●	DPRK RCS and SCEDM co-chair the national pre-disaster meeting annually. ●	DPRK RCS and IFRC have a signed SOPs in preparation for emergencies (signed first time in 2019); additionally, the NS and IFRC have coordination meetings twice a year. ●	Noted that the NS does not have agreements with domestic or international suppliers, but the NS and IFRC have identified domestic suppliers and IFRC has agreements with international suppliers. ●	The NS does not have agreements with Social Protection systems to facilitate access to pre-existing databases of the vulnerable, but the NS noted that there would be no issue in receiving the information from SCEDM. ●	RC Law include expedited import of humanitarian aid, but no agreements are in place for visas for incoming personnel (see component 4. DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination).

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: ●	In DPRK RCS the emergencies coordinator is responsible for monitoring ongoing risks and coordinates with branches, State Hydrometeorological Administration and State Committee for Emergency and DM (SCEDM). ●	The NS are able to collect and analyse data on emerging trends related more to natural disasters. ●	The NS does not have multi-hazard maps but does have CPs for specific hazards that are updated regularly. A multi-hazard risk analysis map is available from the Government. ●	The NS carry out VCAs (which includes collection of disaggregate information) in communities where they have long-term programming. The NS is part of the Anti-Calamity Committee that also carry out VCA and the NS can have access to this information. ●	Given the context, the NS does not experience gaps or barriers to its acceptance, security and access. ●	EW systems are in place whereby the Government defines the thresholds for activation. The thresholds are hazard and geographically determined/specific. Many of these thresholds are captured in the NS CPs for example in drought, floods and influenza. ●	The NS states that an analysis of potential connectors and dividers is not applicable in the context of DPRK. ●	The NS does not do any cross-border coordination or risk monitoring.

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_responses.notes: ●	DPRK RCS has Contingency Plans for flooding, droughts and influenza (draft), updated regularly following pre-disaster meetings and/or after emergency operations. It was noted that there is a need to develop CPs for typhoon, earthquake and volcano scenarios. ●	3 Provincial Branches (South and North Hamgyong and South Phyongan provinces) have CPs based on their level of risk identified by the Government’s national multi-hazard mapping/analysis.  ●	The NS CPs include the triggers set by Government. ●	Noted that there is a need to develop CPs for other hazard-prone areas.

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_responses.notes: ●	DPRK RCS chose not to review this component as they felt the benchmarks were not applicable in the current context of DPRK.

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_responses.notes: ●	DPRK RCS focal point for disaster preparedness is the emergency coordinator within the DM department. ●	Preparedness plans exist within the NS’s contingency plans; plans include specific outputs, activities and which department/office that is responsible (e.g. DM, WASH, Health, Logistics, OD, NS Governing Board, HoCO IFRC). ●	Gaps are identified in the NS’s contingency plans as it relates to stock (e.g. DPRK RCS relief stock gap analysis). ●	Preparedness plans in CPs are reviewed and updated regularly. ●	The NS are not always able to implement preparedness plans due to lack of funding. ●	There is no policy or practice to allocate emergency or development budgets for preparedness activities. ●	There are some examples of how lessons learnt from operations have informed preparedness work (e.g. Drought Operations in 2018 and 2019).

•	The main responders during food insecurity are the Government and WFP. DPRK RCS monitors and analyses the food security levels in the country. •	The NS does not currently have technical staff or delivery mechanisms for food assistance. •	Historically the NS have experience providing food assistance and in the future are keen to increase coordination and possible collaboration with Government and WFP to explore options of providing food assistance in the future.

•	The Ministry of Public Security has an expressed interest (found in the stakeholder analysis section of the NS 2016-2020 Strategic Plan), for support in search and rescue by the DPRK RCS. The NS has engaged in search and rescue (e.g. Typhoon Lingling operation in 2019). •	Spanish RC provided training on mountain search and rescue in 2019.

●	DPRK RCS conducts VCAs in communities to identify disaster risks and the capacity of communities to respond. Based on the VCAs a community disaster preparedness plan is developed and implemented with communities. ●	The NS conducts regular awareness raising and public education through their RC youth team.  ●	The NS also conducts trainings on Community Based Early Warning and Evacuation (CBEWE) and organise simulation exercises with communities, however the trainings, systems and materials need to be improved. ●	CDRTs are trained and equipped to handle local responses in partnership with relevant local actors, however more training and equipment is required.  ●	CDRTs have an up-to-date response and contingency plan aligned with relevant local plans and resources that needs to be updated. ●	The NS ensures community assessment, planning and response are done in an inclusive, gender and diverse way.

component_details.title: Mapping of NS capacities
component_details.description: A list of the NS capacities including HR (staff, response teams and volunteers) and equipment that are available for disaster/crisis response. Teams could include branch and national response teams. This should be defined by technical speciality where relevant.

component_responses.notes: ●	Within DPRK RCS focal points exist for the different NS-specific areas of intervention to provide technical guidance, however it is acknowledged there is a need to maintain up-to-date technical skills. ●	Logistics Department has a database of materials and equipment; monthly stocking report is shared with IFRC. Gaps related to equipment and materials have been identified but are not addressed fully due to funding constraints. ●	Mechanisms are in place to share resources amongst branches but sharing with sister NSs is not practiced. ●	Currently NS capacities and resources are not mapped against the different IFRC levels of response (Green - Yellow - Red).

●	DPRK RCS’ multi-sectoral response needs are identified for different epidemic scenarios, but the scenarios do not include cross-border/multi-country outbreaks. ●	The draft NS CP for influenza includes procedures on data collection and feedback mechanisms to ensure community engagement in prevention and response interventions. ●	The NS has procedures for two-way communication with communities that help to track and address rumours. ●	Safety protocols for infection prevention and control within epidemics (e.g. social distance, use of PPE kits) are reflected in the CP for influenza, but the details need to be reinforced. ●	The NS is not part of the public authorities' safe and dignified management of dead bodies and identification system in infectious disease outbreaks. ●	The NS does not have appropriate personal protection equipment in place. ●	The role of NS in health in emergency is defined in NSDRR (Government) and reflected in CP for influenza, but there are insufficient materials to mobilise volunteers. ●	The NS’s role in the case of isolation and quarantine is reflected in the draft CP for influenza. However, the CP needs to be finalised and have more of a focus on the provision of Psychological First Aid (PFA) and messaging and awareness raising on the importance of isolation.

component_details.title: Early Action Mechanisms
component_details.description: Designed to translate warnings into anticipatory actions to help reduce the impact of specific disaster or crisis events. They focus on consolidating available forecasting information and putting procedures in place to ensure that a NS can act ahead of any disaster/crisis. Forecast-based financing is included within the scope of this area.

component_responses.notes: ●	DPRK RCS’s early warning and early action system include weather information shared by State Hydrometeorological Administration (SHMA) and includes disease surveillance. ●	NS does not have FbF protocols, but IFRC APRO have provided an orientation session (2019) with the NS and plan to carry out a feasibility study. ●	NS does not have a clear methodology to decide when and where early action should be taken but instead follows the early warning and early action direction provided by the Government. ●	Noted that DPRK RCS with support from IFRC used the Imminent DREF in 2018 and 2019, however currently there are no formal procedures in place when to request it. ●	NS is a member of the National Non-Standing Anti-Calamity Committee and follows its direction on early action based on weather forecasts. ●	Based on the context, the NS does not use new technologies for sending alert messages through mobile phones, but rather relies on the Government system.

component_details.title: Cash Based Intervention (CBI)
component_details.description: An effective and flexible way, including all forms of cash and voucher-based assistance, to support people affected by emergencies, maintaining their dignity and choice, while fostering local economies. Cash should also be mainstreamed into other sectors (including Relief, shelter, livelihoods) and services (Logistics, Finance, etc.)

component_details.title: Emergency Needs Assessment
component_details.description: Assess the extent and impact of the damage caused by the disaster/crisis and the degree of vulnerability of the affected population. The first step in any emergency response, such an assessment will identify the needs that require external intervention and the gaps to be filled. It is a vital component of the programme-planning process.

component_responses.notes: ●	DPRK RCS has standard templates for data collection. ●	NS collects disaggregated information according to gender, age groups and disability. ●	NDRT members are trained on the usage of these templates.

component_details.title: Affected population selection
component_details.description: Identification and selection of target Affected population for interventions, using a pre-defined set of criteria based on need and vulnerability. This includes consideration of specific vulnerabilities such as disability, age and gender.

component_responses.notes: ●	DPRK RCS has identified selection criteria in NS contingency plans and strategy (e.g. women, children under 5, orphans, elderly, disabled). ●	Currently there are no established procedures on data protection. There has never been a request to the NS from the Government to share information on affected populations as the Government has access to this information directly from local-level authorities and communities. ●	The NS states that there are procedures that explain how and when information should be shared (e.g. to verify affected population list with local authorities through SCEDM).

component_details.title: Emergency Operations Centre (EOC)
component_details.description: A central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions at a strategic level in an emergency situation. The common functions are to collect and analyze data; facilitate decision making that protects life and livelihoods; and disseminate those decisions to all concerned agencies and individuals. Generally located at the headquarter level of an organization.

component_responses.notes: •	DPRK RCS’s assigned focal point for its EOC (referred to as the emergency operations room) is the emergency coordinator within the DM department. ●	There are no specific SOP for the EOC or activation of EOC. ●	Roles and responsibilities of NDRT members are identified in CPs, but only for NS staff, not for volunteers. ●	The Emergency Operations Room does not have sufficient space and equipment. ●	EOC staff manage regular updated information but there is no facility to access real time information; information is reported using standardized situation reports (noted in IM Component that it needs to be improved). ●	The EOC has a back-up generator. Satellite phones and VHF radios are not available in country. The NS has not experienced situation of water shortage, so not clear what backups may be needed. Given the context, NS does not have designated emergency frequencies. ●	There is no plan for a backup EOC.

component_details.title: Information Management (IM)
component_details.description: Ability to manage information including requesting, receiving, analyzing and disseminating as per its procedures and partner requirements (IFRC and public authorities in particular). There should be a clear digital/paper trail that documents what, when and how the NS has acted and provides key information for the development of Emergency Plan of Actions. Includes IM between levels, between departments and Situational Reports, mapping, visualisation of data, GO platform (IFRC).

component_responses.notes: ●	DPRK RCS key staff and branches are familiar with various IM templates for assessment and reporting. ●	The NS at NHQ and permanent office have necessary equipment for compiling and sharing information (e.g. laptops, printers, projectors). ●	Upon request by the NS, the Central Bureau of Statistics and SCEDM can share information. ●	The NS is using the standardised reporting template, but it needs to improve. ●	All decisions and information are documented and filed at NHQ.

component_details.title: Testing and Learning
component_details.description: Drills and Simulations allow the organization to test, identify and learn from the results of these type of exercises and incorporate learning into future preparedness and response planning.

component_responses.notes: ●	DPRK RCS conducts annual simulations and/or drills together with the public authorities (i.e. SCEDM). NS is planning to take part in national level simulations. Some branches do this jointly with local governmental bodies like SCEDM. ●	After simulations and emergency operations, the NS organises real-time evaluations to capture lesson learned which are also discussed during national Pre-Disaster Meetings. Lessons learnt from the branches are shared with NHQ. ●	It was noted that elements of Safer Access (e.g. access, perception, acceptance and security) are not applicable in the context of DPRK. The NS expressed there have been no issues related to access, perception and acceptance. ●	The NS does not conduct cross-border simulations.

component_details.title: Activation of regional and international support
component_details.description: Procedures for requesting and accepting regional and international support in operations, including triggering coordination mechanisms for funding, materials and human resources deployments.

component_responses.notes: ●	DPRK RCS key staff are familiar with available IFRC/ICRC support (e.g. DREF, EA, Surge), but newly recruited staff need to receive training. ●	The NS has SOPs and organises regular coordination meetings with IFRC. ●	Procedures to request and incorporate regional and global support into NS response system are captured in NS-IFRC SOP. The CAS document refers to the “roles and responsibilities of the IFRC and DPRK Red Cross are further clarified by an operational MOU, the latest of which is valid for 2017-2018. DPRK Red Cross has and continues to support sister National Societies via its International Department with deployments of personnel and resources including delegates and RDRT personnel.” ●	The NS inform IFRC within 24 hours of an emergency and are familiar with IFRC emergency funding mechanisms and procedures for developing an DREF/EPoA/EA. ●	In time of emergency NS request bilateral assistance in accordance with established coordination frameworks and has MoUs and agreements signed with Partner National Societies (Iranian-, Spanish-, Turkish-, Italian- and Chinese RC). ●	The NS has an assigned focal point from the NS International Cooperation Department to act as a counterpart to regional/international responders. ●	Although not directly linked to the acceptance of RDRTs in this component, it is worth noting that two individuals have participated in a regional RDRT training but are not yet members of the roster. ●	The NS has received an orientation of the concept of FbF and FbA by DREF (July 2019).

component_details.title: CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL, RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR (CBRN) EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS

component_responses.notes: ●	To date DPRK RCS has not been engaged in CBRN, however the NS is interested to explore this area of work in the future.

●	In the context of DPRK the NS does not engage in livelihood activities during emergencies. ●	Many of the benchmarks in this component are captured in NS documents but in the context of DPRK there has not been a need to apply this service. Livelihoods is captured in strategic and operational documents (e.g. NS Strategic Plan 2016-2020, DPRK RCS Disaster Response Plan, Drought Contingency Plan, Flood Contingency Plan and DM policy).

•	DPRK RCS are familiar with and follow the PASSA Guidelines and have staff and volunteers trained on PASSA. •	Shelter items are pre-positioned in the seven NS warehouses in the high-risk areas of the country. •	The NS have agreed standard NFI kits prepositioned in the warehouses and SOP developed between the NS and IFRC. •	The NS has identified suppliers of shelter items and the IFRC have a framework for the procurement of shelter items like tarpaulins, water purification tablets and jerry cans. This can be done either internationally or in the country. The NS is involved in the selection process of suppliers. •	The relevant NS volunteers are trained in the use of prepositioned shelter materials to construct basic shelters through PASSA and emergency shelter setup training.

component_details.title: MANAGEMENT OF DEAD BODIES TO FACILITATE THEIR IDENTIFICATION

component_responses.notes: •	DPRK RCS chose not to review this component as they felt the benchmarks were not applicable in the current context of DPRK.

●	The main provider of RFL services domestically is the Ministry of Public Security. In this context the role of the DPRK RCS is to collect data on the missing people in the field and share with the Ministry of Public Security. ●	In time of a disaster the DM department of the NS would be responsible to provide the RFL services of the NS as above described. ●	In the context of DPRK the NS do not engage in RFL in collaboration with ICRC.

●	Although the Government NSDRR does not articulate the formal role of NS in recovery, but the NS sees recovery as important as reflected in the NS 2016-202 Strategic Plan, DM policy and in CPs (as early recovery). These documents need to be updated. ●	The RC Law does not specify the mandate of the NS in recovery. ●	It is also noted in Component 12. Response and Recovery Planning, that the NS does not have a separate recovery plan. ●	NS key staff are familiar with key recovery principles through NDRT training. ●	The NS engages in joint needs assessment and planning with public authorities and agencies like UNDP and UNICEF (e.g. 2016, 2018 and 2019) ●	The NS has collaborated with IFRC to meet recovery needs as described in the “Floods evaluation report 2018”.

component_details.title: NS-specific areas of intervention
component_details.description: Sector-specific or services provided by the NS in case of emergencies, it is in line with the NS mandate and legislation in country. It includes Community Based DP/DRR, Evacuation, Health in Emergencies, Epidemic and Pandemic, First aid, WASH, Food security and Livelihoods, Search and rRescue, Shelter, Management of dead bodies, RFL, Transition to recovery, and CBRN preparedness.

component_responses.notes: •	Evacuation is part of the DPRK RCS response strategy and is identified in different scenarios that are captured in the CPs. •	NS volunteer networks are part of the mechanism for the evacuation of communities in high-risk areas, providing assistance to elderly, children and disables populations.

•	First Aid is part of DPRK RCS's response strategy and is reflected in the NS DM policy and CPs. •	The NS includes First Aid training as part of its CBDRR strategy and DM policy.  •	The NS has trained First Aid staff and volunteers, but many are not adequately equipped and there is a need for continued First Aid training and refresher courses for staff and volunteers (adult and youth).

•	DPRK RCS has a WASH strategy. Elements of WASH are included in the NS contingency plans for floods and droughts. •	The NS has trained staff and volunteers, equipment and items at HQ and branch levels for emergency WASH response, especially provision of safe water. However, the NS has limited skills and equipment for mass sanitation, vector control and drought. •	The NS has six mobile water treatment units and other WASH-related items such as family hygiene kits, water purification tablets (WPT), jerry cans, hygiene promotion Information and Education and Communication (IEC) materials. •	WASH technical support in emergencies is available in the NS through RCRC Movement partners. The NS also has an MOU with relevant Government bodies such as the Ministry of Urban Management. •	The NS is engaged and coordinates with other organisations and networks in the national sectoral working group meetings/WASH cluster meetings.

●	All DPRK RCS volunteers receive basic first aid training. ●	Linked to the community risk reduction planning the community health volunteers develop community health contingency plans. ●	CBHFA volunteer training includes a session on proper reporting of suspected health events. ●	CBHFA volunteers are actively engaged in simulation planning, implementation and evaluation to ensure community awareness and involvement that include information on referral linkages with health facilities.

component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_responses.notes: ●	DPRK RCS manages information flow between communities and branches and between branches and headquarters through volunteer leaders that are members of community-level Anti-Calamity Committees. ●	Information provided by communities is considered in decisions taken at branches and headquarters. ●	The NS Branches attend, together with local authorities, quarterly communication and coordination meetings with CDRTs (Community Disaster Response Teams). ●	The NS support community-level response systems, where resources allow, but it was noted that this support is not sufficient to meet the full needs and there is requirement for more materials as well as trainings.

component_details.title: Cooperation with private sector
component_details.description: Mechanism that allows cooperation with private sector that often plays a strong role in response, particularly if there is impact on their staff and businesses. There is often a willingness to donate goods and services. Advance agreements help to expedite response actions.

component_details.title: Coordination with External Agencies and NGOs
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and collaboration with Non-Governmental Organization (NGO), both local and international NGOs, civil society organizations (CSOs) and United Nations agencies in country.

component_responses.notes: ●	DPRK RCS participates in the regular national Non-Standing Anti-Calamity Committee meetings which also includes Civil Society Organisations. The NS also participates on an ad hoc basis in the UN Humanitarian Coordination Team to which the IFRC is an official member. ●	The NS attend the cluster working groups in Shelter, DRR, WASH and Health cluster. The NS participates in the DRR cluster working group, co-chaired by the IFRC and with good representation by national actors. ●	The NS is familiar with the IFRC shelter cluster lead role but for the moment the shelter cluster is dormant as there are no other actors active in the country.

component_details.title: Civil Military Relations
component_details.description: Dialogue and interaction with military actors, essential to protect and promote humanitarian principles, avoid competition, minimize inconsistency and, when appropriate, pursue common goals.

component_details.title: Coordination with Movement
component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_responses.notes: ●	DPRK RCS has a mechanism for coordination and cooperation with ICRC and IFRC but this does not incorporate all of the specific elements of the SMCC (e.g. Movement Coordination Agreement, Movement Security Agreements, Joint NS-IFRC-ICRC Operational Plan, Joint Contingency Plans). ●	In-country coordination between IFRC/ICRC/NS ensured through weekly and quarterly coordination meetings. ●	Exchanges of information and coordination with neighbouring NS are organised and coordinated through IFRC (e.g. the GO – platform, information bulletin and operation reports). ●	IFRC support the NS in establishing a framework for receiving international assistance in times of emergency.

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_responses.notes: ●	DPRK RCS is a formal member of the national Non-Standing Anti-Calamity Committee responsible for humanitarian coordination. ●	The NS is a recognised DRR partner by the Government and has a clear role as stipulated in the Government “National Strategy for Disaster Risk Reduction 2019-2030” (NSDRR) and are familiar with the national authorities’ capacity to respond in a disaster through the participation by both partners in the annual  pre-disaster meetings. ●	The use of the emblem is regulated in the RC Law and respected by the Authorities. The NS express there has not been any cases where the public authorities has attempted to take control over NS assets and resources. ●	The different thematic areas of the NS have an established coordination mechanism with respective local and national authorities.

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_responses.notes: •	DPRK RCS responders are deployed and receive equipment according to ToRs. However, some PPE items still need to be included and provided. •	NDRT roles and responsibilities are captured in the CPs. •	The NS has learning paths for responders who attend both local and international workshops and trainings. These trainings are provided for both HQ staff and volunteers and needs to be continued. The NS also utilise national job training opportunities. •	Responders are trained in quality and accountability standards, but refresher training is required. •	Responders have official ID cards and RC visibility items (e.g. vest, caps, t-shirts). •	All citizens of DPRK are covered by public insurance. During an emergency IFRC also includes insurance for staff and volunteers as per IFRC requirements. •	Procedures to activate, deploy and manage branch and national response teams can be found in the CPs. •	Volunteer leaders in each community have a list of volunteers that are shared up to county-level. There is no consolidated database of all volunteers above this level. The information on volunteers includes names, contact details and trainings, but the detail and quality of information retained depends on the specific county branches and individual volunteer leaders. •	The NS incorporates response volunteers from relevant sectors such as health and WASH. •	The NS does not have expedited procedures to incorporate spontaneous volunteers. •	The NS has HR procedures to scale-up and down operations and for appreciation of volunteers during emergencies. •	The NS has no formal personnel rotation and retention strategy for responses, but it is reflected in the volunteer policy. •	Analysis is conducted in scenarios that entail safety and/or security concerns. •	Some staff and volunteers are trained in Psychological First Aid (PFA) and self-care and support to team, but more trainings need to be rolled out. •	Harassment in a workplace was not identified as an issue in the DPRK culture. •	The NS has a policy to cover volunteer expenses during an emergency (e.g. accommodation, transportation, communications and meals are covered).

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_responses.notes: ●	DPRK RCS has received an orientation/training on the Safer Access Framework by ICRC in 2018 but has not developed an action plan. ●	The NS has internal safety regulations and its staff and volunteers adheres to the Government safety policy and regulations. ●	A safety and security focal point at HQ sits within the OD Department and reports to the SG (who overall is accountable for safety and security for the NS). ●	The NS states that safety and security knowledge is shared with all staff and volunteer. This would require behavioural change and it is not clear whether the procedures are followed in practice.

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_responses.notes: ●	DPRK RCS has specific communications focal points at HQ (i.e. Director of Communications) and branches (i.e. Head of Branches). ●	There is no pre-identified official spokesperson, but staff would be appointed in an emergency. To date there has not been a need for such a role. For external media the IFRC represent the Movement and the NS. ●	The NS does not communicate before and during a disaster. After a disaster, the NS uses public media to report on the activities provided to affected people. ●	Communicating through Social Media is not applicable in DPRK. However, through the IFRC the NS indirectly uses international social media platforms with guidance from the IFRC communications department. ●	Key messages are developed both for a domestic and international audience with support from IFRC. ●	It was stated that the NS would not require a capacity to track negative media in the country as negative media criticising the NS does not occur. ●	Joint messages are developed between the NS and IFRC, for example, during the influenza response the Health Director would communicate with the IFRC for key messaging.

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_responses.notes: ●	DPRK RCS PMER staff provide technical support to the DM department who are responsible for the development, monitoring and reporting of Emergency PoAs. ●	The NS follows standard templates but there is a need to develop indicators to measure impact (linked to Component 2. DRM Strategy). ●	In general, lessons learned workshops are completed after every response. At the pre-disaster meetings the NS also discuss learning from previous responses, and develops a lessons learned report with recommendations which are shared with all departments in the NS. It was noted that it would be helpful to systematically meet with IFRC and share reports after the lessons learned exercise. ●	Although templates are followed and reports submitted on a timely basis, it was noted that the reporting template and reporting skills should be improved.

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_responses.notes: ●	DPRK RCS uses a Government financial system provided by the Ministry of Finance. ●	It was noted in the Logistics sub-component on Procurement that the NS does not have different levels for sign-off for specific amounts and everything is signed off by the SG. The NS internal system and regulations for procurement is the same for peacetime and emergencies. However, in emergencies processes can be expedited and if necessary (when staff are absent) go directly to the SG who has ultimate sign off for everything who can provide approval by phone. In the absence of the SG the Deputy SG can sign off in peacetime and emergencies. ●	The NS has procedures and carry out regular auditing. ●	The NS has system and procedures in compliance with the national financial regulation and NS financial regulation.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_responses.notes: •	DPRK RCS key staff are equipped with functioning mobile phones, SIM cards/load cards are readily available, however there is no system to ensure recharging is possible while in the field. •	The NS key personnel carry contact lists at all times with critical numbers saved as standard on all mobile phones. •	The Contingency Plans of the NS includes an approved Emergency Notification Protocol followed by all staff and volunteers. •	Portable generators are available at HQ however they are not available at all branches. •	The NS has trained IT focal points able to support technical issues and equipment and provide maintenance. •	Noted that many of the benchmarks in this component are not applicable in the context of DPRK.

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_responses.notes: •	DPRK RCS key staff are familiar with resource mobilisation options for humanitarian operations, for example the internal NS emergency fund, DREF and EA (call for support). •	The NS mobilises its resources for preparedness activities from international funding linked to longer-term programme support. The NS is also aware that some DREF funds can be used for preparedness.  •	The NS has an RM strategy, but it needs to be improved to include more workable and diverse RM options. •	In the context of DPRK the benchmark on ‘agreements and mechanisms for collaboration and fundraising with the private sector’ is not applicable.   •	Branches in highly vulnerable areas receive seed funding from HQ to start programmes. Once the programme has started branches are able to then mobilise resources from communities. •	The NS has an internal national emergency fund that is resourced from Government subsidies and membership fees. The criteria for accessing these emergency funds are defined by the Government. •	A resource mobilisation focal point for emergencies exists in both the communication and RM departments. •	The NS have agreements with national stakeholders. •	The NS communicates changes and reports on outcomes of resources provided. •	Within DPRK individuals can make donations to the NS bank account, however this is not common. Online donations are not possible in DPRK. •	Internationally individuals can donate via the IFRC. •	In addition to the IFRC emergency items catalogue the NS has a list of acceptable relief items, including more locally appropriate items (e.g. culturally appropriate clothing). •	The NS has a donor tracking table managed by the logistics department which records different donors and their specific allocations.

•	DPRK RCS has a dedicated logistics department that manages procurement, stock management, warehousing, transport and fleet. •	All staff involved in logistics have defined roles in their job descriptions and have received training to carry out their tasks, but training for new staff is needed. NS has volunteers trained in logistics who can act in a surge capacity during an emergency response, however more regular training is required. •	Key staff are familiar with IFRC logistics services to support NS emergency operations, but training on logistics and finance in emergencies is needed. •	The NS carries out a supplier evaluation on an annual basis (at the end of the year) to decide who to buy stock from the following year. They evaluate the suppliers that they have used and assess, cost, reliability, quality and speed of delivery. •	Pre-positioned relief items meet standards and reflect at-risk and/or affected population needs, however there are gaps in emergency household items (EHI) that needs to be filled. •	Relief items for new hazards also need to be considered. •	Pre-positioned relief items are strategically placed in 7 warehouses located in high-risk areas.

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_responses.notes:
The auxiliary role of LRC and its mandate, act of parliament and DM act are well established and shared with public authorities. 
LRC mandate is mentioned in key documents such as policies and strategies but its dissemination to staff and volunteers is not well monitored. 
The NS role is clarified for ….

component_details.title: DRM Strategy
component_details.description: An outline of the overall goal that the NS seeks to achieve in its disaster and crisis response operations. The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

component_responses.notes: LRC has a response plan and a draft DM policy, but they have not yet elaborated a DRM strategy.

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_responses.notes: LRC started to develop a DM policy but the document is still at draft stage and not yet complete. In particular it does not include the aspect of inclusivity yet.

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.notes:
Laos Government is in charge of IDRL.
LRC has trained IHL, but no focal point during emergencies.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_responses.notes:
•	LRC is working on the PSEA and Child Safeguarding policy.
•	There is no CEA system in place.
No focal point to participate in IASC working group.
LRC is developing SGBV reporting system that includes feedback and complaints mechanisms.
Although LRC considers Sphere (WASH/DM) in response, will need to disseminate PGI information in emergencies.  This is the core humanitarian standard. Need to be translated also.
Although LRC response caters for child protection and child safe spaces and PSS; child safeguarding policy need to be developed.
LRC follows IFRC minimum standards on PGI but need to be disseminated further.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_responses.notes:
LRC doesn’t have their own Early warning system (EWS), they follow Government system both EWS and monitoring hazards.
The VCA update is based on project and funding, similar to risk assessment at community level.

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_responses.notes: LRC doesn’t have contingency Plan, neither analysis of scenarios for multi-sectoral

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_responses.notes: LRC, DM department is responsible for risk analysis, however, there is no mapping of potential risk available yet (confirm with LRC)

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_responses.notes:
LRC has trained focal point for disaster preparedness.
LRC doesn’t have resource mobilization strategy, neither Policies and procedures to allocate emergency or development budgets for preparedness capacity strengthening.

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: LRC doesn’t have business continuity plan in place.

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_responses.notes: LRC doesn’t have SOPs for all specific areas of intervention and support services to respond to disasters and crises.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_responses.notes:
A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process are not yet in place.
LRC is working on DREF’s plan.

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes:
LRC doesn’t have pre-agreement with any supplier, nor with public authorities. 
LRC participated in pre-disaster meetings with Government, but not with IFRC or its partner.
No capacity mapping in place

component_details.title: Affected population selection
component_details.description: Identification and selection of target Affected population for interventions, using a pre-defined set of criteria based on need and vulnerability. This includes consideration of specific vulnerabilities such as disability, age and gender.

component_responses.notes:
•	Meetings held with community leaders / community members. Beneficiary selection criteria included, including mainstreaming PGI.
Data collected is shared with donors. LRC needs to take all possible steps in protection of data collected from affected population with regards to storage, purpose of sharing, approvals, etc.
Main staff are trained but staff skill levels and knowledge need to be improved.
Data collection training for emergency and response teams to be urgently conducted.
LRC cross checks affected population lists and validates sensitive data, checks for inclusivity, and considers sensitive population information.
Recommend create beneficiary selection record document when making agreement with community leaders

component_details.title: Emergency Operations Centre (EOC)
component_details.description: A central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions at a strategic level in an emergency situation. The common functions are to collect and analyze data; facilitate decision making that protects life and livelihoods; and disseminate those decisions to all concerned agencies and individuals. Generally located at the headquarter level of an organization.

component_responses.notes:
LRC has a focal point for EOC operations.  However, fully functional EOC does not exist.  Highly recommend a formal EOC be invested in, followed by establishing a formal Emergency Operations Team.
Although there is a centralized Lao Government EOC that accommodates LRC, the need for a LRC EOC is essential to coordinate its response activities, mobilizing of resources, etc. It’s a different set-up to the broader Lao Government EOC.
