WAREHOUSE AND STOCK MANAGEMENT: NS need to have a conducive storage facilities and most importantly in strategic high-risk areas. Key staff need to be informed of warehouse  procedures so as to able to report.

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_responses.notes: More traininQuality and Accountability,gs for different interventions showld be conduced (EVCA,BDRT, PSS,SGBV, Safe access,etc) for diversified action team. Crisis modifier and equipments should be in place and Activation of different SOP.

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_responses.notes: The NS has a good communications structure but need to enhance Communications in Emergencies (CiE) and recognize the importance and potential risks if CiE protocols are not standardized. This includes identifying and training key spokespersons for the NS as well as ensuring staff and volunteers take care in communicating, even as individuals, in social media.

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_responses.notes: More training for resouce mobilization eg DREF and preparedness programs to volunteersand staff  at branch level. Development of resources mobilization strategy for collaboration and fundraising and National emergency fund to be in place. Pre disaster agreement should be in place.

component_details.title: DRM Strategy
component_details.description: An outline of the overall goal that the NS seeks to achieve in its disaster and crisis response operations. The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

component_responses.notes: The DRM strategy is currently under revision. It should be a time bound plan to achieve the vision set out DRM policy. Once it's finalised it should be translated and disseminated within the organisation and to partners. Advocacy material should be produced and tailored made based on the target audience (leaflets, infographics, etc...)

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_responses.notes: The DRM policy should contain a vision, principles and protocols to guide decision making. It should contain DRM position within the organisation, vis-à-vis other sctors and services and its role with other actors.

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: The status of the Red Cross should be clarified wth the Government (RC is not an NGO). Advocacy on IDRL and IHL with Movement's support should be strengthened.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_responses.notes: The NS has recognised the need to further address quality and accountability. This can be achieved through documentation, institutionalisation and standardisation of Q&A guidelines and practices.

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_responses.notes: There is a RC law and it's currently being updated. Dissemination and greater advocacy should be an area of focus. There should be dedication in terms of time and resources for dissemination within the NS in addition to the local authorities and Government.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: "Early warning system and early action but also thresholds would be better placed in the DRM strategy and SoPs, rather than in the DRM Policy. Disaggregation of data by age, gender, disability, income and other context-specific diversity and cultural factors can support the planning and response process."

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_responses.notes: Every department should be accountable for actions that might lead to operational and reputational risks. Mecanisms has to be put in place and formalised regarding prevention, identification, and resolution of issues.

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_responses.notes: Preparendess is project related rather than strategic and institutionalised. A budget allocation from core funding should be made for disaster preparedness.

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: The NS does not have a strategy for business continuity including repurposing existing donor funds if required.

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_responses.notes: The NS is currently developing SoPs. Procedures should follow from the DRM strategy and make reference to the contingency and scenario plans.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_responses.notes: Currently not in existence. The recovery planning is the transition from response to long term programming.

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: Meetings organized by Government and authorities seems to be ad hoc or not organized. The NS has precedent of having pre-disaster agreements with partners. This should be further explored and revived.

component_details.title: Early Action Mechanisms
component_details.description: Designed to translate warnings into anticipatory actions to help reduce the impact of specific disaster or crisis events. They focus on consolidating available forecasting information and putting procedures in place to ensure that a NS can act ahead of any disaster/crisis. Forecast-based financing is included within the scope of this area.

component_responses.notes: In the absence of an ealy warning system it's not possible to carry out early action, which is a barrier to timely and effective response.

component_details.title: Cash Based Intervention (CBI)
component_details.description: An effective and flexible way, including all forms of cash and voucher-based assistance, to support people affected by emergencies, maintaining their dignity and choice, while fostering local economies. Cash should also be mainstreamed into other sectors (including Relief, shelter, livelihoods) and services (Logistics, Finance, etc.)

component_responses.notes: NS has recently started using CBI. Work in this area is currently being done to strengthen, institutionalise and disseminate it within the organisation.

component_details.title: Emergency Needs Assessment
component_details.description: Assess the extent and impact of the damage caused by the disaster/crisis and the degree of vulnerability of the affected population. The first step in any emergency response, such an assessment will identify the needs that require external intervention and the gaps to be filled. It is a vital component of the programme-planning process.

component_responses.notes: Existing capacity throughout the NS should be strengthened, leveraging on existing mechanisms and tools. This is crucial for volunteers, branches and sub- branches and should be related to information management.

component_details.title: Affected population selection
component_details.description: Identification and selection of target Affected population for interventions, using a pre-defined set of criteria based on need and vulnerability. This includes consideration of specific vulnerabilities such as disability, age and gender.

component_responses.notes: Relevant community based approach for identification and selection of beneficiaries is to be clarified and the possibility of allignement with the National system that is already in place should be considered.

component_details.title: Emergency Operations Centre (EOC)
component_details.description: A central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions at a strategic level in an emergency situation. The common functions are to collect and analyze data; facilitate decision making that protects life and livelihoods; and disseminate those decisions to all concerned agencies and individuals. Generally located at the headquarter level of an organization.

component_responses.notes: The EOC as a function is not formalised. It is not formally operational 24/7 during a response.

component_details.title: Information Management (IM)
component_details.description: Ability to manage information including requesting, receiving, analyzing and disseminating as per its procedures and partner requirements (IFRC and public authorities in particular). There should be a clear digital/paper trail that documents what, when and how the NS has acted and provides key information for the development of Emergency Plan of Actions. Includes IM between levels, between departments and Situational Reports, mapping, visualisation of data, GO platform (IFRC).

component_responses.notes: The quipement, standardised tools and mechanisms for sharing and storing information is not in place.

component_details.title: Testing and Learning
component_details.description: Drills and Simulations allow the organization to test, identify and learn from the results of these type of exercises and incorporate learning into future preparedness and response planning.

component_responses.notes: NS takes part in externally organised simulations however doesn't organise its own simulations and drills. Evaluation and review meetings are carried out after responses, however lessons learnt cannot be translated into action due to the absence of SoPs and response plans.

component_details.title: Activation of regional and international support
component_details.description: Procedures for requesting and accepting regional and international support in operations, including triggering coordination mechanisms for funding, materials and human resources deployments.

component_responses.notes: There is a good collaboration with Movement partners for requesting and managing international support. There is a need to go beyong Movement partners' support.

component_details.title: CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL, RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR (CBRN) EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS

component_responses.notes: The NS is exposed to some chemical hazards. Therefore this is an area where it needs to strengthen its capacity to protect its staff and volunteers.

component_details.title: MANAGEMENT OF DEAD BODIES TO FACILITATE THEIR IDENTIFICATION

component_responses.notes: NS lacks programmatic funding to transition responses into recovery

component_details.title: NS-specific areas of intervention
component_details.description: Sector-specific or services provided by the NS in case of emergencies, it is in line with the NS mandate and legislation in country. It includes Community Based DP/DRR, Evacuation, Health in Emergencies, Epidemic and Pandemic, First aid, WASH, Food security and Livelihoods, Search and rRescue, Shelter, Management of dead bodies, RFL, Transition to recovery, and CBRN preparedness.

component_responses.notes: CBHFA is not being done.

component_details.title: Mapping of NS capacities
component_details.description: A list of the NS capacities including HR (staff, response teams and volunteers) and equipment that are available for disaster/crisis response. Teams could include branch and national response teams. This should be defined by technical speciality where relevant.

component_responses.notes: There is knowledge to a certain extent of the NS's capacity. There is little documentation on this capacity which makes it difficult to verify them and use the updated information for planning and prioritisation.

component_details.title: Coordination with External Agencies and NGOs
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and collaboration with Non-Governmental Organization (NGO), both local and international NGOs, civil society organizations (CSOs) and United Nations agencies in country.

component_responses.notes: There are working groups in place of the cluster system, which the NS participates in when invited.

component_responses.notes: There is a discrepency between the HQ and field level on principles of collaborations with military bodies. However, there is a general understanding of the potential reputational risks.

component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_responses.notes: The NS has active coordination with Movement partners.

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities

component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_responses.notes: NS has a relatively low number of trained CDRTs as they are programme and project dependent.

component_details.title: MANAGEMENT OF DEAD BODIES TO FACILITATE THEIR IDENTIFICATION
NS-specific areas of intervention
component_details.description: Sector-specific or services provided by the NS in case of emergencies, it is in line with the NS mandate and legislation in country. It includes Community Based DP/DRR, Evacuation, Health in Emergencies, Epidemic and Pandemic, First aid, WASH, Food security and Livelihoods, Search and rRescue, Shelter, Management of dead bodies, RFL, Transition to recovery, and CBRN preparedness.

component_responses.notes: Adequate
To be integrated into the strategies currently under development
Falls outside of the scope of the URCS mandate
At the initial development stage
Uncodified
Needs to be properly integrated into the response mechanisms
At the initial development stage

component_details.title: Mapping of NS capacities
component_details.description: A list of the NS capacities including HR (staff, response teams and volunteers) and equipment that are available for disaster/crisis response. Teams could include branch and national response teams. This should be defined by technical speciality where relevant.

component_responses.notes: Levels of response to be developed

component_details.title: Early Action Mechanisms
component_details.description: Designed to translate warnings into anticipatory actions to help reduce the impact of specific disaster or crisis events. They focus on consolidating available forecasting information and putting procedures in place to ensure that a NS can act ahead of any disaster/crisis. Forecast-based financing is included within the scope of this area.

component_details.title: Cash Based Intervention (CBI)
component_details.description: An effective and flexible way, including all forms of cash and voucher-based assistance, to support people affected by emergencies, maintaining their dignity and choice, while fostering local economies. Cash should also be mainstreamed into other sectors (including Relief, shelter, livelihoods) and services (Logistics, Finance, etc.)

component_responses.notes: Needs improvement institutionally

component_details.title: Emergency Needs Assessment
component_details.description: Assess the extent and impact of the damage caused by the disaster/crisis and the degree of vulnerability of the affected population. The first step in any emergency response, such an assessment will identify the needs that require external intervention and the gaps to be filled. It is a vital component of the programme-planning process.

component_responses.notes: Further codification needed

component_details.title: Affected population selection
component_details.description: Identification and selection of target Affected population for interventions, using a pre-defined set of criteria based on need and vulnerability. This includes consideration of specific vulnerabilities such as disability, age and gender.

component_responses.notes: No major difficulties expected

component_details.title: Emergency Operations Centre (EOC)
component_details.description: A central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions at a strategic level in an emergency situation. The common functions are to collect and analyze data; facilitate decision making that protects life and livelihoods; and disseminate those decisions to all concerned agencies and individuals. Generally located at the headquarter level of an organization.

component_responses.notes: Revision and review are necessary

component_details.title: Information Management (IM)
component_details.description: Ability to manage information including requesting, receiving, analyzing and disseminating as per its procedures and partner requirements (IFRC and public authorities in particular). There should be a clear digital/paper trail that documents what, when and how the NS has acted and provides key information for the development of Emergency Plan of Actions. Includes IM between levels, between departments and Situational Reports, mapping, visualisation of data, GO platform (IFRC).

component_responses.notes: Some documents and tools exist, some needs to be revisied

component_details.title: Testing and Learning
component_details.description: Drills and Simulations allow the organization to test, identify and learn from the results of these type of exercises and incorporate learning into future preparedness and response planning.

component_responses.notes: general situation with trainings is good, but EPI is weak

component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_responses.notes: Strengthening communication within and without the NS

component_details.title: Cooperation with private sector
component_details.description: Mechanism that allows cooperation with private sector that often plays a strong role in response, particularly if there is impact on their staff and businesses. There is often a willingness to donate goods and services. Advance agreements help to expedite response actions.

component_responses.notes: Codification, enforcement, development

component_details.title: Coordination with External Agencies and NGOs
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and collaboration with Non-Governmental Organization (NGO), both local and international NGOs, civil society organizations (CSOs) and United Nations agencies in country.

component_responses.notes: To be improved

component_details.title: Civil Military Relations
component_details.description: Dialogue and interaction with military actors, essential to protect and promote humanitarian principles, avoid competition, minimize inconsistency and, when appropriate, pursue common goals.

component_responses.notes: Maintained and strengthened

component_details.title: Coordination with Movement
component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_responses.notes: URCS is able to share the achievements

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_responses.notes: Maintained and strengthened

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_responses.notes: Systemic decisions are to be made and properly implemented regarding further development of the spheres in question

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_responses.notes: Training of the staff and volunteers and development of the clear rules to be undertaken; need for a specialized full-time employed security officer for NS

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_responses.notes: Emergency communication needs to be improved; otherwise good job!

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_responses.notes: Integral frameworks to be designed

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_responses.notes: There is no such thing as too excellent to improve; necessary to maintain the existing level of skills and knowledge and constantly monitor the most recent developments

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_responses.notes: Modernization of the system  desperately needed

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_responses.notes: Initial development stage; lots of efforts needed

Potential could be strengthened even more //There is an effective system in place, functioning according to the procedures curently in effect//Regulations exist and are generally adhered to; no major difficulties //Sufficient number of vehicles at URCS' disposal managed accrding to he national legislation//Warehouses are properly equipped and staffed

component_details.title: DRM Strategy
component_details.description: An outline of the overall goal that the NS seeks to achieve in its disaster and crisis response operations. The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

component_responses.notes: •	BRCS National Response Plan & Strategy (NRPS) is a comprehensive document. It hasn’t been presented to the BRCS Board pending additional work on specific sections of the document to finalise the current version. •	Key sections on internal and external capacity and resources need to be completed in the NRPS. The elaboration of these sections is an opportunity to include key information related to current BRCS capacity following the transition and scaling down of Hurricane Dorian programming and handover from IFRC and other Movement partners.  •	NRPS informed the development of EOC and related SOPs (in progress), is a key document for all BRCS staff involved in preparedness and response ahead of the 2022 hurricane season (June to November).  •	HiE is not a priority for the NS going forward and focus remains on hydrometeorological emergencies and related impacts.  •	Consideration of Public Health in Emergencies risk and interventions to better articulate response to epidemics and pandemics is identified in the hazard identification section of the NRPS.

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_responses.notes: •	BRCS DRM Policy finalized in January 2021 as Version 1.0 •	DRM Policy clearly references Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement institutional frameworks and guidance across the entire DRM continuum from preparedness, anticipatory actions, response, recovery, risk reduction and community health to resilience.  •	Collaboration between health and DRM is referred to in strengthening community resilience through Community-based Disaster Risk Reduction (CBDRR) as well as Community-based Health and First Aid (CBHFA) initiatives.  •	Refer to the DRM policy in the preparation of response plans, procedures (SOPs) and continue to disseminate the policy among staff and volunteers.

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: •	BRCS President and DG are the leads on IDRL, both received training from IFRC, but there is no clear plan or follow-up following Hurricane Dorian. •	Unclear whether an existing Executive Board member continues to serve with BRCS who is the current focal point for IDRL and IHL.  •	IHL and HD are contained in the BRCS mandate and there is a dialogue with the GoB at the level of BRCS leadership. However, BRCS has no direct role with the GoB on IDRL and works through NEMA. •	There is no mention of IDRL in BRCS Strategic Plan, it is referred to in DRM Policy as guidance but was not implemented in the Hurricane Dorian Operations with IFRC.  •	No specific IDRL document or plan referred to in IFRC Operational Update No. 7 (Dec 2021).

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_responses.notes: •	BRCS has mechanisms in place to ensure affected populations are involved in response, and to ensure that their needs are being met.  •	BRCS implemented training activities in both CEA and PGI, however many of the staff trained has left, the focal point has multiple roles and cannot effectively carry on these tasks.  •	The CEA plan and SOPs are not yet finalized and the PGI Policy is incomplete.  •	The CoC, Anti-Harassment Policy and the PSEA Policy are integrated into the HR Policy and Manual and approved by the Executive Board. The Policies have been disseminated to the staff. While staff sign the HR policy at entry into the BRCS, and upon revision, there is no provision that the staff have to sign the HR Policy regularly so that they reaffirm various commitments e.g., once a year. •	BRCS's Code of Conduct (CoC) for staff and for volunteers (2 separate codes) does not have a firm commitment to Zero Tolerance for Any Violence. The BRCS CoC for volunteers has not been updated with PSEA.  •	The Minimum Standards for PGI in Emergencies have been integrated into various policies but require more learning and development among staff so they are implemented in programs and operations.  •	NS currently does not have the capacity to develop and use PGI analysis to adapt protection policies in a highly infectious disease environment, which will be critical for epidemic response.

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_responses.notes: •	BRCS Strategy 2030 was approved by the Board in 2021, and disseminated internally with staff and volunteers, and externally with the recent change in Government of Bahamas following the national election with new Ministers and leadership in key Departments and relevant Ministries.  •	BRCS auxiliary role remains consistent with the BRCS Act 1975. •	The development of BRCS DRM Policy 2021 and draft of National Response Plan & Strategy strengthens BRCS's role and responsibilities in coordination with the Ministry of Disaster Preparedness, Management and Reconstruction and NEMA.  •	There is a need to further clarify key functions of BRCS (mandate) within the National Response Plan specific with NEMA.  •	There is an ongoing discussion between BRCS and NEMA based on experience with Hurricane Dorian, National Response Plan & Strategy, program review and structure/capacity.  •	BRCS is working on new areas of programming including food security, migration, climate change adaptation, pandemic response (promotion of vaccination) aligned with key global challenges identified in IFRC S2030.   •	BRCS Strategy 2030 mentions that NS demands more diversity, equity and inclusion but does not make explicit commitments to PGI, PSEA and CEA.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: •	DM Manager is the focal point for BRCS risk monitoring system, and the team is sent to different areas according to NEMA standards to assess risk, vulnerability, and capacities. •	BRCS is represented on NEMA board when they establish their EOC.  •	BRCS obtains secondary data from government agencies and strategic partners; however, it does not always have staff capacity to collect primary data. VCAs have been completed for certain high-risk areas but not shared. Contribution of communities and local volunteers to regular update of mapping/VCAs is not done widely. •	Ability to analyse data depends on the seriousness of the situation. Information once received is disseminated to the DG or President, and action decisions are made. BRCS does not have updated national multi-hazard risk analysis and maps. •	BRCS does not have its own early warning system; it uses NEMA system.  •	Some BRCS volunteers were trained in epidemic control following Hurricane Dorian and as part of COVID-19 response. EPC training was conducted for HQs staff as well as volunteer representatives from branches.  •	There is no mandatory requirement for staff to be vaccinated.  •	BRCS has a very limited capacity to derive data from epidemic risk assessments and does not have an updated capacity mapping (e.g., health facilities).

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_responses.notes: •	Scenarios for all key hazards are given in the National Response Plan & Strategy but only at high-level - only COVID-19 scenarios are well elaborated.  •	NS is in process of developing contingency plans for the national level and for each branch.  •	For hurricanes, scenarios have been developed with a response strategy/plan for all high-risk areas. For a potential response to hydrometeorological hazards, NS has a direct connection with NEMA and with Meteorology office (e.g., for hurricane alerts, tsunami warnings).  •	Coordination and preparedness happen within the region at President and DG level. There is a mechanism to share best practices.    •	Acceptance, security and access during humanitarian operations are considered during planning.

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_responses.notes: •	BRCS does not currently have a systematic plan and separate unit to manage critical incidents; plan is pending since the 2020 assessment.  •	Overall risk management (RM) responsibility including management of critical risks lies with DG. President, DG and Board members mitigate the risks through mechanisms like treasury board, management board, insurance of assets, access/ privacy (information, sensitive matters etc.) and building security procedures.  •	RM is done for particular areas to identify risks involved before projects are started. NS needs to finalize control and compliance procedures within BRCS in the form of policy and admin manual (currently in draft form). •	For reputational and integrity risks, Board determines the impact and mitigation measures, as needed.  •	Now with COVID-19, NS has a procedure for managing sick staff. For volunteers, there is insurance but no specific policy in case contracting a disease. There are HR considerations and workplace related protocols in place.

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_responses.notes: •	DM Manager is the nominated focal point for disaster preparedness however, relatively new to position.  •	Preparedness actions are updated after every major disaster to look at gaps and challenges (e.g., after hurricanes Matthew, Irma, Dorian).  •	NS participates in national reviews (by NEMA) following major disasters.  •	BRCS does not have budget specific to capacity strengthening in a systematic or strategic way. However, during last couple of years, Hurricane Dorian response and PER assessment and project has helped covering some of the gaps. •	Resource Mobilisation is being discussed since before Hurricane Dorian; Fund Raising Strategy is currently being developed.  •	In collaboration with IFRC, NS is conducting programming for vaccine awareness, PPE distribution, sanitation and other activities.  •	In general, all the staff are becoming more aware of their roles and responsibilities during the emergencies; there are few people with institutional knowledge who are available as focal points and take the lead.  •	SOPs and engagement of finance manager (e.g., clarity on authorization limits, funds available etc.) and logistics/ warehouse personnel in preparedness/ planning could be strengthened.

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: •	No significant progress on this component/ mechanism has been made since 2020 assessment – no up-to-date and approved business continuity plan factoring in major emergency situations and prevalent risks is in place.  •	Communication procedures depend on the donor and is not formalized in writing. In past, NS has been able to reprofile Zika funding to COVID-19.  •	NS does not operate any blood banks, hospitals etc. The services they do run (feeding program, welfare checks) are included in the business continuity plan (not systematic) and have IPC considerations.

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_responses.notes: •	SOPs for areas of intervention and support services to respond to disasters and crises are in draft form since 2020 assessment. •	Elements like SOPs covering all relevant levels/ tiers and DRM phases, PGI considerations etc. to be confirmed once these are final. •	List of responsibilities for key staff as per response organogram exits in the National Response Plan & Strategy (draft).  •	Roles and responsibilities for epidemic response consider collaboration with and support to MoH.  •	BRCS does not have specific SOPs for epidemics. Draft SOPs refers to health emergencies.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_responses.notes: •	National Response Plan & Strategy exists - a decent document but still a draft and yet need to be finalized and validated/ evaluated. NS is planning to finalize this document early 2022. •	Sectors of intervention with key interventions are listed down. Response organogram and key SOPs are included however, capacity sections are not elaborated.  •	In the document, there is a reference to Movement principles and rules and other key documents as well as focus on PGI considerations and CEA. Plan mentions that response will be undertaken as guided by best practices supported by RC’s minimum standards for commitment (MSC) to GESI. •	Plan considers how to support self-recovery of affected population particularly livelihood, reconstruction, CBIs and resilience building. •	In general, staff, volunteers and executive committee members have been engaged in the process however, there is a potential gap in awareness about this document.  •	There are guidelines regarding accepting donations but not specific to medical items; NS follows MoH guidance regarding use and distribution of PPE; distribution is combined with some form of training.

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: •	BRCS DM team conducts regular meetings (once per month) with NEMA. These meetings also include other relevant stakeholders/partners active in emergency management in The Bahamas. During hurricane season meetings happen more often. •	NS is on the NEMA EOC, so has line of sight on all of the operations. Focal points responsible for various areas are aware of their related pre-disaster agreements (mostly verbal) and how they are to be operationalized.  •	There are some agreements in writing, mostly formalized with international partners. •	BRCS does not currently have a clearly documented capacity mapping of Movement partners.  •	Disaster Law clearly identifies the role of NS within NEMA (Social Services is part of the Act). NS has informal arrangements with Ministries which are relevant to disaster preparedness/response. •	Agreements with key suppliers are most likely based on the long-term relationships.  •	NS acts as an auxiliary to the government, and has an outlined role for collaboration with the MoH.

•	Evacuation is part of NS response. During Hurricane Dorian, NS worked with the MoH to help evacuate residents from Abaco and Grand Bahama. •	BRCS branches (e.g., Abaco and Grand Bahama) engage in this service as part of NEMA response plan e.g., by organizing buses and providing shelter support.  •	Door to door assessments have been done to identify vulnerable individuals during Hurricane Dorian response.  •	NS evacuation plan is not final and/or disseminated, and evacuation is not reflected in the recently done branch-level response plans (as per branches; no document shared to verify).

•	First Aid is part of the NS response strategy.  •	There is an ongoing training program for NS staff and volunteers. Recertification of training is regularly provided, and some branches have been trying to implement training of trainer initiatives. •	NS has a roster of people who are trained in First Aid and available for quick responses. •	During the pandemic, consultants were engaged to train staff on how to use PPE, and staff were briefed on IPC protocols.  •	Infectious disease outbreaks are not part of regular First Aid programming, but the NS has a good relationship with the MoH and would engage them for additional support, if required (e.g. during COVID-19 MoH has been using BRCS ambulance services).

•	NS can provide some WASH support as indicated in the National Response Plan & Strategy, but it is limited to the provision of certain items.  •	Although there are some procedures in place should WASH services be required, the branches do not have the appropriate training and equipment (it is stored at HQ). If branches require any of the supplies, they can request them from the national warehouse via email. •	BRCS does not have a dedicated WASH focal point, but there is a possibility to request surge support from IFRC, if needed.  •	NS coordinates with MoH and NEMA, should additional support beyond the provision of some items be required.  •	During epidemic response, the government provides WASH support. BRCS supports the government where needed.

•	Some communities have undertaken preparedness/contingency plans for specific projects (Zika). •	First Aid volunteers did health contingency planning in New Providence and the Family Islands, but the comprehensiveness and consistency of the training remains unclear.  •	CBHFA training does not include proper reporting of suspected health events and they are not actively engaged in simulation training and referral linkages with health facilities.  •	There is no regular training on communicable disease and epidemic control measures, there are no CBHFA simulations specific to epidemic. •	In one training some participants were made aware of the ECV toolkit, but it is unclear whether it has been utilized. •	CBS does not appear to be part of the services offered by the BRCS.

•	BRCS is represented on National Disaster Committee which is responsible for food security monitoring along with the Ministry of Health and Agriculture; information from this Ministry is shared with BRCS. NS does not have its own mechanism to monitor, analyse and document the relevant information. •	NS assesses individuals and provides food (parcels/vouchers) for the vulnerable (elderly, disabled) and economically poor population, mainly in Nassau and Abaco.  •	Considerable investments have been made in providing nutritious food and BRCS has generally increased the knowledge of Social Services and its own staff.  •	BRCS is partner with the Ministry of Social Services and other NGOs in Bahamas on relief supplies including food e.g., Hands for Hunger which transfers leftovers from hotels to the poor.  •	BRCS response strategies (including relevant SOPs) are in draft form, but safety standards are met by ensuring staff have food handling certificates.  •	BRCS does not have SOPs for food distribution in quarantine; this is the first time that NS has been involved in such a situation.

•	Search and Rescue is not reflected in the BRCS National Response Plan & Strategy as one of the response options however, branches have some engagement in this sector.  •	Search and Rescue is shared responsibility between NS and other partners (e.g. fire department, defence force, police force). BRCS is on NEMA consultative committee for disasters.  •	US Embassy provided a training and equipment (e.g., 2 boats and other equipment) to local authorities. Exuma branch team leader attended search and rescue training (provided by US embassy) from RC side.

•	NS ensures active participation of local populations in the assessment, design, planning of community-based preparedness activities via conclaves, town hall discussions, community feedback sessions, etc.  •	Public awareness raising and education sessions on disaster risks are done via different channels (radio, public service announcement, social media, etc.).  •	BRCS has partnered with community focal points to facilitate early action and to raise awareness on community-specific hazards. •	Community Early Warning Systems (CEWS) is not structured; mass email, SMS and social media are used. •	Branches have a varying system of CDRTs, some are under NEMA’s lead while others are under the branches. There are no contingency plans at community level to respond to relevant hazards.  •	During COVID-19 response, BRCS focused on working on vaccine hesitancy and misinformation. Depending on the type of activity, BRCS has the potential capacity to scale-up or down responses during outbreaks.

component_details.title: Mapping of NS capacities
component_details.description: A list of the NS capacities including HR (staff, response teams and volunteers) and equipment that are available for disaster/crisis response. Teams could include branch and national response teams. This should be defined by technical speciality where relevant.

component_responses.notes: •	BRCS maps its capacities for disaster response (human resources and equipment) in conjunction with NEMA.  •	Volunteers are specialized in specific areas of intervention (e.g., PSS, WASH, Logistics, etc.).  •	While resources are shared between HQ in New Providence and the Family Islands, the NS needs to improve coordination mechanisms to share resources across branches as well as the identification of gaps.  •	Branch Administrators do not have direct access to the databases for equipment and volunteers; they will have to go through higher management to obtain information.  •	Mapping of NS capacities needs to be done in line of the finalised National Response Plan & Strategy.

•	BRCS has some feedback mechanisms (e.g., hotline) but they are not consistently implemented across interventions.  •	NS helped combat rumours related to COVID-19 and does have a procedure in place for providing this support.  •	NS safety protocols are not specific to epidemics, and it is not involved in the management of dead bodies and infectious disease outbreaks.  •	Staff do have PPE and there is a warehouse with additional PPE should it be required and are regularly trained on how to use it.  •	There were a few trainings on IPC processes specific to COVID-19 but did not cover other epidemics. There was one training on ECV with some key participants. •	BRCS does not have a clearly identified role specific to epidemics and isolation and quarantine but will act as an auxiliary to the government if required as it does have resources that could be useful in an epidemic (roster of volunteers, vehicles, etc.).

component_details.title: Early Action Mechanisms
component_details.description: Designed to translate warnings into anticipatory actions to help reduce the impact of specific disaster or crisis events. They focus on consolidating available forecasting information and putting procedures in place to ensure that a NS can act ahead of any disaster/crisis. Forecast-based financing is included within the scope of this area.

component_responses.notes: •	In The Bahamas, NEMA is the main actor responsible for early warning system and keeps BRCS appraised with the most updated information.  •	BRCS branches closely coordinate with NEMA local offices and has a clear role within the national system. •	NS has a network of representatives located throughout the country with networks to inform local populations about alerts and early actions, while always following NEMA’s lead. •	NS has satellite phones for branches, uses zoom meetings, WhatsApp and email communications as well as the social media to communicate early actions. •	However, certain communication gaps during COVID-19 response were flagged. Some branches consider WhatsApp as the main/effective source for communication, whereas some important information was shared via email and missed.  •	NS does not have formalized early action mechanism with MoH for the epidemics.

component_details.title: Cash Based Intervention (CBI)
component_details.description: An effective and flexible way, including all forms of cash and voucher-based assistance, to support people affected by emergencies, maintaining their dignity and choice, while fostering local economies. Cash should also be mainstreamed into other sectors (including Relief, shelter, livelihoods) and services (Logistics, Finance, etc.)

component_responses.notes: •	While the BRCS has implemented 2 Cash Based Interventions as part of the Hurricane Dorian operation (in Abaco and Grand Bahamas, benefitting 600 individuals), there is not yet a formal CBI preparedness plan or budget.  •	Digital cash was most successful (using an intermediary company similar to Western Union). The beneficiaries' profiling was done in a structured way. Beneficiary had option of using the card on the site of company or they could withdraw the funds. It was very efficient to reach people in various areas.  •	Daily reports and tracking of disbursement were simplified. Now NS has some experience as well as learnings.  •	NS still needs to work to develop its CBI SOPs as well as its CBI toolkit, and it also needs to formalize its relationships with local money transfer providers and CBI partners. •	Appears that HR capacity built during Hurricane Dorian Response is gone now. •	BRCS does not have a cash transfer program tailored to face the challenges of infectious disease outbreaks.

component_details.title: Emergency Needs Assessment
component_details.description: Assess the extent and impact of the damage caused by the disaster/crisis and the degree of vulnerability of the affected population. The first step in any emergency response, such an assessment will identify the needs that require external intervention and the gaps to be filled. It is a vital component of the programme-planning process.

component_responses.notes: •	BRCS DM department has standard forms for secondary data collection and reporting but whether they are effectively utilized need to be verified.  •	Per the 2020 PER Assessment BRCS has trained personnel but whether these personnel are still with NS or their replacements has been made remains unclear.   •	NS bases its emergency plans of action on emergency needs assessments as well as the availability of funding. •	NS collects household level info which includes age, sex and disability.  •	There are no standardized templates for epidemic need assessments and NS does not conduct data collection specifically for epidemics.

component_details.title: Affected population selection
component_details.description: Identification and selection of target Affected population for interventions, using a pre-defined set of criteria based on need and vulnerability. This includes consideration of specific vulnerabilities such as disability, age and gender.

component_responses.notes: •	BRCS communicates selection criteria to affected population through collaborations with local partners (e.g., local community leaders) and works with these partners to identify vulnerability factors within the affected population.  •	NS cross-checks affected population lists with other agencies to verify inclusion and exclusion issues.  •	BRCS is working on improving sex, age, and disability disaggregation of data (SADDD) related to population selection and is considering the use of digital tools for future assessments of affected populations. •	Hard copy assessment information is kept in secure storage with restricted access. •	BRCS has been doing door to door assessments during Hurricane Dorian Response. Its volunteers have been engaged in beneficiaries’ registration during COVID-19 response (e.g., vaccination sites).

component_details.title: Emergency Operations Centre (EOC)
component_details.description: A central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions at a strategic level in an emergency situation. The common functions are to collect and analyze data; facilitate decision making that protects life and livelihoods; and disseminate those decisions to all concerned agencies and individuals. Generally located at the headquarter level of an organization.

component_responses.notes: •	BRCS has an appointed EOC focal point and a recently equipped physical space from which to operate its EOC. There is no designated phone line for EOC; HQ is in process of rerouting one of the current lines for EOC. •	NS relevant staff and volunteers received EOC training in August 2021. EOC SOPs are being developed and EOC would be activated according to defined national response levels. All decisions are based on a situational analysis.  •	EOC staff manage incoming information and regularly update all parties.  •	There is an intended space and a potential alternative option for the EOC that can be operational 24/7 with necessary equipment (telecommunication, satellite phones, laptops, etc.).  •	NS EOC is not linked to MoH EOC.

component_details.title: Information Management (IM)
component_details.description: Ability to manage information including requesting, receiving, analyzing and disseminating as per its procedures and partner requirements (IFRC and public authorities in particular). There should be a clear digital/paper trail that documents what, when and how the NS has acted and provides key information for the development of Emergency Plan of Actions. Includes IM between levels, between departments and Situational Reports, mapping, visualisation of data, GO platform (IFRC).

component_responses.notes: •	All approved policies and other documents are filed by PMER on SharePoint. However, it is a not a widespread practice for all departments and areas of emergency response.  •	NS IM system requires more work; there is a need for a dedicated IM focal point and defining filing method across departments.  •	BRCS has access to equipment for IM at HQ in Nassau, however further equipment needs to be deployed to the Family Islands. •	Family Islands have a template for sharing information, but not all of them use it. There is a Branch handbook with standard reporting forms. Branches have to submit monthly report but not consistent.  •	BRCS needs to further disseminate information on standard forms as well as a process of documenting and filing decisions. •	Specific SOPs for data sharing in epidemics are not available.

component_details.title: Testing and Learning
component_details.description: Drills and Simulations allow the organization to test, identify and learn from the results of these type of exercises and incorporate learning into future preparedness and response planning.

component_responses.notes: •	BRCS does test the response system through hurricane simulations but has not done in a while because of COVID-19. •	Community disaster management simulation (hurricane drill) used to happen every year for communities before COVID-19 (was done for volunteers, but open to public). •	BRCS participated in exercises organised by NEMA, MOH and Social Services along with other local organisations. It was noted that before COVID-19, this National simulation exercise was conduced every two years with different agencies to determine how overall response was to a mass casualty incident. •	NS has also participated in tabletop simulations with NEMA. •	BRCS did not participate in any epidemic specific simulations, but epidemic considerations were incorporate to some trainings (e.g., Shelter training). •	NS adapts its early actions based on the drills and simulations that are undertaken in the trainings but how lessons learnt are incorporated and to what extent remain unclear.

component_details.title: Activation of regional and international support
component_details.description: Procedures for requesting and accepting regional and international support in operations, including triggering coordination mechanisms for funding, materials and human resources deployments.

component_responses.notes: •	2020 PER Assessment findings for this component still remain relevant. •	Although key BRCS staff are familiar with available Movement support mechanisms and have experience with DREF and EA, the NS does not have written SOPs to request international support and facilitate coordination with IFRC.  •	Appears that SOPs will be in place for the upcoming hurricane season beginning June 1st.  •	DMM, DG and the President are the leads for preparedness and response including acting as counterpart to regional/international responders and leadership. •	In addition, SOPs for medical personnel and emergencies are not in place. NEMA has protocols in terms of who can support in ca

component_details.title: CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL, RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR (CBRN) EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS

component_responses.notes: •	Livelihood component is incorporated into the BRCS National Response Plan & Strategy. Livelihoods is a new area of intervention for BRCS as it has been introduced since Hurricane Dorian.  •	Some BRCS personnel have been trained on livelihood and food security but only from some areas of the country.  •	There appears to be no systematic capacity built on livelihoods and no focal point who could take the work forward for future responses.  •	BRCS has established relationships with Bahamas Social Services, Ministry of Agriculture, Bahamas Chamber of Commerce, Mercy Corps and World Central Kitchen – the agencies which are active in this sector.  •	BRCS has started Backyard Farming project with support of Ministry of Agriculture (will provide seeds and fertilizer). The plan is to expand the project to the communities.  •	Epidemic and IPC aspects related to this sub-component are absent.

•	BRCS ensures appropriate shelter response solutions in collaboration with NEMA and Bahamas Social Services; BRCS is a member of the shelter inspection team, and it follows government building codes.  •	During and after hurricanes BRCS provides Shelter Managers to the community shelters organized by Bahamas Social Services. •	BRCS has pre-positioned supplies in Family Islands; additional material is provided based on needs.  •	Few branches try to generate funds for cleaning items; also provide items like blankets to illegal immigrants. BRCS does not have a documented/agreed standard for NFI kit for pre-positioning.  •	BRCS has established relationships with vendors. Replacement of destroyed or contaminated NFI is considered in planning and inventory management.  •	NS has a plan for providing NFIs and shelter kits as an immediate response to hurricanes but not specific to epidemics and does not include replacing contaminated or destroyed supplies as NEMA would take the lead at that point.  •	Some adjustments were made in shelter management after COVID-19 e.g., measuring temperature, distancing of cots (6 ft apart), obligatory masks for visitors etc.

component_details.title: MANAGEMENT OF DEAD BODIES TO FACILITATE THEIR IDENTIFICATION

component_responses.notes: •	RFL services were conducted by the ICRC in coordination with NS during the relief phase of the Hurricane Dorian Operation. With the departure of and handover by the ICRC team, BRCS has continued follow-up on family tracing cases on different islands through its contacts. •	No procedures or agreements have been formalised with ICRC on RFL. •	NS currently does not have plans and procedures to carry out RFL in epidemics.

•	Key NS staff/volunteers are familiar with key recovery principles (DANA and Search and Rescue component of CDRT, at some branches). •	There is no CEA focal point. While PGI SOPs for case management, including safe protection referrals, were developed with a PGI delegate's support, continuous monitoring of referral pathways has been a challenge with no NS FP during the recovery phase. •	BRCS mandate for recovery is part of Bahamas National Disaster Plan and BRCS mandate is specific in food provision and WASH; this is formal and in writing as part of the Act.  •	Heavy support from IFRC for Dorian early recovery planning has been provided. •	NS made effort to decrease stigma during COVID-19 response through communication, resource mobilization and cooperation with department of social services.

component_details.title: NS-specific areas of intervention
component_details.description: Sector-specific or services provided by the NS in case of emergencies, it is in line with the NS mandate and legislation in country. It includes Community Based DP/DRR, Evacuation, Health in Emergencies, Epidemic and Pandemic, First aid, WASH, Food security and Livelihoods, Search and rRescue, Shelter, Management of dead bodies, RFL, Transition to recovery, and CBRN preparedness.

component_details.title: Coordination with External Agencies and NGOs
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and collaboration with Non-Governmental Organization (NGO), both local and international NGOs, civil society organizations (CSOs) and United Nations agencies in country.

component_responses.notes: •	BRCS has a collaboration with WHO/PAHO (Pan American Health Organization), UNICEF and UNHCR.  •	NS and IFRC coordinated closely with the DRA (Disaster Reconstruction Authority), especially in shelter programming in Abaco and Grand Bahama as part of Hurricane Dorian response. There were weekly meetings with DRA in 2020 and monthly meetings in 2021 and included BRCS, IFRC, UN agencies, and NGOs. •	BRCS has formal partnership agreements with certain NGOs and institutional donors (for example, USAID).   •	Although NS has a strong relationship with a lot of local NGOs, (especially for information exchange and affected population referrals), most of them are not formalised and don't have partnership agreements.  •	NS has strong relationship with NEMA and follows their and Ministry of Health lead during epidemic response.

component_details.title: Civil Military Relations
component_details.description: Dialogue and interaction with military actors, essential to protect and promote humanitarian principles, avoid competition, minimize inconsistency and, when appropriate, pursue common goals.

component_responses.notes: •	BRCS does not have direct communication with military (Defence Force); the collaboration can happen through NEMA and response mechanism. •	NS had some engagement with military during drill exercises organised by NEMA. •	NS has relationship and has access to defence force, police force, search and rescue services and could collaborate with them when needed.

component_details.title: Coordination with Movement
component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_responses.notes: •	BRCS adheres to coordination and cooperation principles and coordination mechanisms are established with IFRC and PNS in-country. •	SMCC structure is not in place in terms of a formal mechanism of coordination. Meetings with IFRC, ICRC and PNS are primarily bilateral. •	NS is active in Movement governance through CORI (every 2 years) and the Inter Americas Regional Meeting at the Senior leadership level of engagement with IFRC, ICRC and NSs (every 3 years).. Operational level exchange in the Caribbean Region is mainly through the IFRC with pre-Hurricane meetings and response planning. •	IFRC provided support to BRCS and lead on overall coordination with the Hurricane Dorian EPoA, published data analytics and documentation on the IFRC Go Platform, including comprehensive programming dashboards.  •	There is no framework for coordination with neighbouring NSs in response activities, but coordination happens for larger operations such as Dorian with IFRC support.

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_responses.notes: •	BRCS is formally part of the national humanitarian coordination system. NS maintains close coordination with government authorities to support response efforts as a part of its auxiliary role.  •	BRCS is a formal partner of NEMA as the main coordination body for emergency response at a national level with GoB and key agencies (sits in the national EOC).  •	At local level, BRCS branches are in direct coordination with local government offices, share resources, participate in joint assessments, and implement activities as per the National Response Plan & Strategy.  •	Key assets at the HQ level are managed and controlled directly by BRCS (staff, volunteers, equipment, fleet etc.) based on internal capacity (infrastructure, systems and operations).  •	Local level BRCS capacity in terms of operations varies and lack of branch infrastructure and support requires more reliance on GoB infrastructure (warehouse, vehicles, communications etc.) for operations.

component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_responses.notes: •	BRCS supports community level response systems in coordination with NEMA. •	There are no formal procedures for information sharing from HQ to branches. There are informal methods via group leaders and members of the Family islands, but it needs to be documented and formalized.  •	NS has recently created volunteer management committee to connect communities, branches, and volunteer manager at HQ. •	Information from communities is taken into consideration and this information is primarily shared via coordination meetings where local leaders are included and can discuss matters with members of NEMA and the NS.  •	Branches have a system to communicate with CDRTs, some are under NEMA’s lead while others are under the branches.  •	If needed, NS can support community level response (i.e., transportation via ambulance, food distribution, shelter management, etc.)

component_details.title: Cooperation with private sector
component_details.description: Mechanism that allows cooperation with private sector that often plays a strong role in response, particularly if there is impact on their staff and businesses. There is often a willingness to donate goods and services. Advance agreements help to expedite response actions.

component_responses.notes: •	NS Resource Mobilisation and Communications Manager   staff (no longer works at BRCS) has been using software for relationship management with donors and working closely with DG and the President on cooperation with private sector.  •	BRCS knows which agencies can be trusted and which ones have funding available, however, there are no written guidelines/procedures in place. A number of initiatives are done ad hoc as opposed to having a mechanism.  •	NS has a mapping of potential companies for financial donations (asks) available mainly with the President.  •	There is often willingness from private organisations to offer assistance (banks, hotels, schools etc.). •	NS receives grants and direct donations for welfare program (NFIs including sanitizers and PPEs).

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_responses.notes: •	Overall functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers. •	Initial volunteer orientation includes CoC, PSEA with subsequent additional training identified by each manager. Regular First Aid and recertification trainings are available as well.  •	BRCS responders/volunteers do not have official IDs, RC vests and T-shirts are used for visibility. •	BRCS is actively working on renewing the existing volunteer database (Excel) with IFRC to have all volunteers’ profiles, certificates, trainings etc. in one place •	BRCS Volunteers are insured through IFRC (covers up to 500 volunteers) but does not include COVID-19 coverage.  •	BRCS maintains diverse background/skills of responders and Volunteer Recruitment and Retention Strategy (approved February 2022) reinforces it. Plan for appreciation of volunteers is included in Volunteer Recruitment and Retention Strategy. •	NS does not have formal expedited procedures to incorporate spontaneous volunteers during emergencies however, there is a plan to reflect that in SOPs (currently under development).  •	There appears to be a challenge with the HR scale down after Hurricane Dorian response. Number of staff is reducing with the loss of IFRC and ARC support. Pandemic has also impacted resource mobilization to retain staff into 2022. •	EPC training has been conducted but not systematically.  •	NS takes measures for protecting its staff and volunteers during epidemics by following government mandates and protocols, and provision of PPEs. Vaccination is not mandatory but is encouraged.  •	CoC for Volunteers needs to be reviewed to include Zero Tolerance for Violence, PSEA, feedback mechanisms and whistle-blower policies. •	Systematic training and signing of HR Policy/Employee Handbook, CoC/PSEA and confidential reporting mechanisms need strengthening.

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_responses.notes: •	BRCS has some measures in place to protect staff and volunteers. •	The Safety and Security Policy is not developed as a stand-alone document, rather it is integrated into the Employee Handbook. •	Safety and Security risks and incidents are reported directly to managers however, BRCS does not have procedures where documentation is systematically collected, and strategies are developed to address them. •	Context and risk analysis information is provided to responders in closed Facebook groups, as well as WhatsApp chats. •	Some BRCS staff and volunteers have been trained on the Stay Safe. •	Safety and security management will be strengthened if a policy, a compliance system, and regular training are developed. The systematic analysis will improve safety and security of staff and volunteers.  •	Specific to epidemics, BRCS must consider PGI analysis and PGI specific requirements to ensure staff and volunteer safety during an epidemic response.

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_responses.notes: •	BRCS has a communication focal point at the HQ level. There are also trained communication volunteers.  •	President and DG are the designated spokespersons of BRCS.  •	Media platforms such as Twitter, WhatsApp, YouTube, Radio, etc. are used to disseminate preparedness and response information but there is no detailed social media plan specific to emergencies.  •	Some of the material produced included information on PGIE, CEA, COVID-19, public service announcements and information from the Ministry of Health.  •	There is a hotline that community members can utilize and call regarding any questions or feedback however, if this is functional needs to be verified.

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.
