component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_responses.notes: Se requierde definir mecanismos o procedimientos de para generar la informacion con la comunidad

component_details.title: Cooperation with private sector
component_details.description: Mechanism that allows cooperation with private sector that often plays a strong role in response, particularly if there is impact on their staff and businesses. There is often a willingness to donate goods and services. Advance agreements help to expedite response actions.

component_details.title: Coordination with External Agencies and NGOs
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and collaboration with Non-Governmental Organization (NGO), both local and international NGOs, civil society organizations (CSOs) and United Nations agencies in country.

component_responses.notes: La Sociedad Nacional, coordina de muy buena manera con las organizaciones no gubernamentales y de naciones unidas, ademas se tiene un reconomiento de la Sociedad Nacional como un lider humanitario, esto se muestra a traves de la confiabilidad de la informacion emitida y el liderazgo en la mesa humanitaria de pais

component_details.title: Civil Military Relations
component_details.description: Dialogue and interaction with military actors, essential to protect and promote humanitarian principles, avoid competition, minimize inconsistency and, when appropriate, pursue common goals.

component_responses.notes: Se mantiene buenas coordinaciones cívico militares, en los espacios oficiales, sin embargo se recomienda una mayor difusión de manera interna del DIH y directrices existentes a todo los niveles a sociedad nacional. Así como la protección del emblema con el cumplimiento de la ley 418.

component_details.title: Coordination with Movement
component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_responses.notes: Los mecanismos de coordinacion del movimiento es el resultados de las vivencias y expereincias que la SN ha tenido en crisis y desastres, lo que ha permitido su consolidacion.

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_responses.notes: Se mantiene excelente relacion con las autoridades publicas, sin embargo se recomienda establecer mecanismos de seguimiento a normativas ya establecidas como el manual de imagen para su cumplimiento ademas de realizar incidencia para la reactivacion de convenios.

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_responses.notes: Se debe de promover la actualizacion de las bases de datos SISVOL

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_responses.notes: Se requiere en algun momento vincular los Seguimientos y Monitoreos a Proyectos de Desarrollo, con las diferentes operaciones que se realizan en el país. Se necesita contar con información precisa de las operaciones.

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_details.title: DRM Strategy
component_details.description: An outline of the overall goal that the NS seeks to achieve in its disaster and crisis response operations. The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_details.title: Mapping of NS capacities
component_details.description: A list of the NS capacities including HR (staff, response teams and volunteers) and equipment that are available for disaster/crisis response. Teams could include branch and national response teams. This should be defined by technical speciality where relevant.

component_details.title: Early Action Mechanisms
component_details.description: Designed to translate warnings into anticipatory actions to help reduce the impact of specific disaster or crisis events. They focus on consolidating available forecasting information and putting procedures in place to ensure that a NS can act ahead of any disaster/crisis. Forecast-based financing is included within the scope of this area.

component_details.title: Cash Based Intervention (CBI)
component_details.description: An effective and flexible way, including all forms of cash and voucher-based assistance, to support people affected by emergencies, maintaining their dignity and choice, while fostering local economies. Cash should also be mainstreamed into other sectors (including Relief, shelter, livelihoods) and services (Logistics, Finance, etc.)

component_details.title: Emergency Needs Assessment
component_details.description: Assess the extent and impact of the damage caused by the disaster/crisis and the degree of vulnerability of the affected population. The first step in any emergency response, such an assessment will identify the needs that require external intervention and the gaps to be filled. It is a vital component of the programme-planning process.

component_details.title: Affected population selection
component_details.description: Identification and selection of target Affected population for interventions, using a pre-defined set of criteria based on need and vulnerability. This includes consideration of specific vulnerabilities such as disability, age and gender.

component_details.title: Emergency Operations Centre (EOC)
component_details.description: A central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions at a strategic level in an emergency situation. The common functions are to collect and analyze data; facilitate decision making that protects life and livelihoods; and disseminate those decisions to all concerned agencies and individuals. Generally located at the headquarter level of an organization.

component_details.title: Information Management (IM)
component_details.description: Ability to manage information including requesting, receiving, analyzing and disseminating as per its procedures and partner requirements (IFRC and public authorities in particular). There should be a clear digital/paper trail that documents what, when and how the NS has acted and provides key information for the development of Emergency Plan of Actions. Includes IM between levels, between departments and Situational Reports, mapping, visualisation of data, GO platform (IFRC).

component_details.title: Testing and Learning
component_details.description: Drills and Simulations allow the organization to test, identify and learn from the results of these type of exercises and incorporate learning into future preparedness and response planning.

component_details.title: Activation of regional and international support
component_details.description: Procedures for requesting and accepting regional and international support in operations, including triggering coordination mechanisms for funding, materials and human resources deployments.

component_details.description: An outline of the overall goal that the NS seeks to achieve in its disaster and crisis response operations. The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

component_responses.notes: The NS does not currently have a comprehensive DRM Strategy however, the DRM Strategy component is partially covered through the SRCS Resilience Strategy (valid for five years until 2024). A DRM framework was developed in 2017/ 2018 but it was not well understood or implemented by the NS. Even though there is no DRM Strategy in place yet a clear engagement with technical sectors and support services to deliver a meaningful response happens when there is a disaster or crisis.

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_responses.notes: The NS does not have its own DRM Policy nor has it adopted the recent IFRC policy. However, some relevant elements (in bit and pieces) are in place that have been guiding the NS’s DRM work so far. It was noticed that the NS involves various relevant sectors and services during response planning (mostly after a disaster or emergency) and actual response. It was also observed that there is a general lack of operationalization of policies and strategies that have been put in place; this may be related to lack of human/financial resources or lack of prioritization because of parallel engagements and the overall context.

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: It was noted that the NS benefited from special entitlements and exemptions during the 2017 Acute Watery Diarrhoea and other responses. SRCS does not pay import tax; the government (Ministry of Finance) provides a tax exemption to the NS’s imported items. No evidence was found if the NS has an IDRL humanitarian diplomacy action plan in place or is doing any implementation including relevant advocacy or testing/ tracking IDRL lessons for its future work. It was observed that the NS contributes to national adherence to International Health Regulations through its health programming.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_responses.notes: "The NS appreciates the importance of engaging communities and getting their feedback. It is working on a CEA system and plans to present the proposed system to senior management before the end of 2020. Community engagement and accountability was prioritized during drought and complex emergency responses via post-distribution monitoring, workshops with community leaders, community involvement in defining beneficiary criteria etc. however, this is not fully institutionalized. During the COVID-19 response, the PMERL Director gave trainings on CEA to active volunteers for collecting community feedback. Respondents expressed that this is difficult to measure concretely whether NS is following various standards; they suggested to develop easy/quick checklists (for instance on SPHERE standards for hygiene kits) for this. The NS references meeting Sphere standards related to safe water in their EPoA report.  CRC has recently provided technical support to SRCS for a new Child Protection Code of Conduct; it is under review and validation at the Hargeisa Coordination Office level. The next step will be sending it to the SRCS President for top level review and validation which is expected to happen before the end of 2020. A practice of PGI analysis is not in place at NS; this area still needs strengthening and guidance. SRCS completed PGI training for key staff recently."

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_responses.notes: The NS auxiliary role and mandate is well understood and appreciated by public authorities for a wide range of hazards including epidemics; this is also formalized through various agreements with Ministry of Planning and Development. For both the COVID-19 and desert locust response operations (referred to during the assessment), the NS has worked closely with authorities at the national as well as regional/ branch level. SRCS is also a key partner of the Ministry of Health Development for community-based health, CBS and epidemic response interventions. The NS mandate is aligned with RCRC Fundamental Principles and is reflected in available policies, strategies and guidelines, and is understood by staff and key volunteers. The assessment team could not find enough evidence if the NS is currently engaged in promotion of IHL and humanitarian diplomacy.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: The NS has developed a risk monitoring system through community volunteers, branch actions and response teams, and through coordination with government departments and external agencies. However, this system is not linked to preparedness and early actions at large except for integrated health services/health emergencies. In addition to primary data from the aforementioned information sources, the information about high risk communities also comes from other resources i.e. government agencies and UN system. The current/likely gaps and challenges to NS acceptance, security and access are not managed in a structured way; there has been no significant work on SAF since 2017. The NS does not coordinate risk monitoring for cross-border high risk areas and is not familiar with the capacities and procedures of neighbouring NSs. There is no mechanism in place to share information. SRCS community volunteers are well trained on epidemic preparedness and response. They use the CBS platform to report any type of disease to MoHD for immediate action. The CBS system currently operates in Togdheer and Awdal regions. SRCS and MoHD would like to expand the CBS system to all six regions, subject to funding.

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_responses.notes: The NS does not develop multi-sectoral scenarios for high-risk areas in the country, leading to the development of contingency plans thus, no contingency plans nor associated SOPs exist. For scenarios related to some sectors, the NS relies on the analysis of the respective clusters e.g. Food Security and Livelihood Nutrition. There has been a reactive approach for both the COVID-19 and desert locust responses – action plans for responses were developed only once emergencies had hit. However, the NS has clear guidance for some health emergencies/epidemics (e.g. CBS in case of cholera/AWD and COVID-19). Action plans to respond to epidemics consider the essential practices e.g. hygiene promotion and essential supplies, access to clean water.

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_responses.notes: The NS does not do risk management holistically across technical sectors, with mitigation measures identified and operationalized, and covering a wide range of risks including reputational ones. However, systematic finance procedures and internal control mechanism are in place for financial risks. Risk management responsibility has not been assigned to a trained and dedicated staff member. The NS has identified a wide range of stakeholders including military and nonstate actors, but they are using an informal mechanism for engagement. The NS does not have a crisis management unit/function to manage critical incidents in a systematic way. The NS ensures the protection of first responders; they are only deployed after necessary training and provision of essential PPE. No formal PS support is available for them. It was also noted that the NS has identified trusted sources of communication to ensure community engagement and public health messaging. In the case of COVID-19, the NS is disseminating government approved RCCE material and messages through loudspeakers and other means.

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_responses.notes: This component partially exists but the ongoing PER assessment process validates the commitment of SRCS towards this element. With the initiation of the PER process, the DRM Director is now a formal focal point for the NS’s preparedness work to respond to various disasters and crisis effectively. So far, the NS has been identifying preparedness gaps (including epidemics) on an ad hoc basis; overall, there is a lack of investment in preparedness. Preparedness gaps are not filled in a comprehensive way except for few specific sectors like CBS. It has been noted that necessary coordination exists among health and DRM/resilience teams for epidemic preparedness.

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: The NS has developed a business continuity plan for COVID-19. This is the first time SRCS has developed such a plan – such plans do not exit for other emergencies or situations. However, it was found that the business continuity plan for COVID-19 had not been disseminated or made known at the branch level. Health care facilities can adapt a quick plan (supported by SOPs) to ensure business continuity as happened during the COVID-19 response (masks, hand sanitizers, gloves, buckets, cleaning materials etc.) however, no formal plans exist. The NS has a communication mechanism to contact partners and donors for changes/repurposing of fund e.g. this happened during the COVID-19 response.

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_responses.notes: The NS does not have up-to-date and approved SOPs for most specific areas of intervention, operational capacity functions (e.g. EOC, IM) and support services to respond to disasters and crises. An absence of emergency response plans, contingency plans and most SOPs was highlighted as a major weakness of the NS. However, SOPs for some integrated health services are available e.g. CBS, ECV and CBHFA. It was also recommended that the NS will benefit from a user-friendly (one-page checklist) SOPs. SRCS has organogram and decision-making flowchart but that is genetic and not specific to a response.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_responses.notes: SRCS normally develops a response plan when a disaster or emergency has happened. It does not have up-to-date and approved multi-sectoral response plans for rapid deployment and efficient use of human and material resources. The NS has a practice to develop/adapt and approve donation protocols that communicate priority needs to the public in times of disaster and crisis. The NS follows WHO/MoH guidance regarding use and distribution of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE). Training is mandatory before any deployment and distribution/use of PPE. Community response plans for epidemics are available but only for a few communities which are supported by projects.

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: "Pre-disaster meetings (annual, periodic) with key stakeholders/partners do not take place in most cases. The NS typically takes a reactive approach and meetings take place when a disaster or emergency has hit. No formal mapping of capacity of Movement partners exists; only an overview is available. However, SRCS has a good idea of the in-country capacity of partners. Additional/potential capacity is explored after a disaster/emergency. A clear and strong working relationship exist with various levels of MoH.   Modalities and practices exist for coordination with relevant local and national key actors; MOUs exists with some line ministries and UNICEF (not necessarily focusing on disaster response). Agreements exist with public authorities to facilitate expedited import of humanitarian aid and visas for incoming personnel e.g. COVID-19 related supplies, delegates for various responses in the past, HR and material during the 2017 response to AWD. SRCS still needs to initiate agreements with key suppliers of goods and services with an agreed mechanism for activation in case of a disaster. SRCS has a 3-year framework agreement with Telesom for the period 2020-2022 to provide services for money transfer."

SRCS’s Health in Emergencies capacity is very strong as evidenced by their COVID-19 response. The NS has a good relationship with the Ministry of Health and is typically the first organisation contacted during an epidemic or pandemic. CEA systems exist at the branch level to collect relevant data and engage communities. Rumour managements was addressed via household visits and staff were equipped with PPE and training prior to deployment, The NS, however, could strengthen its capacity via epidemic scenario planning, structured safety protocols for staff and volunteers and further engagement in dead body management. Training, supplies and a formal agreement with the government are also needed to further engage in dead body management. Formal/approved SOPs for IPC are also missing.

component_details.title: Early Action Mechanisms
component_details.description: Designed to translate warnings into anticipatory actions to help reduce the impact of specific disaster or crisis events. They focus on consolidating available forecasting information and putting procedures in place to ensure that a NS can act ahead of any disaster/crisis. Forecast-based financing is included within the scope of this area.

component_responses.notes: EWEA is working well in cases of health emergencies/ epidemics through CBS; this allows the NS to support communities through community-based interventions. There is room for improvement when it comes to multi-hazards though. The NS has procedures to communicate alerts at all levels, though these are not yet formalized. In the case of Desert Locust, for example, community members would report to the branch, the branch to HCO and HCO to the Ministry of Agriculture. Similarly, branches inform communities of alerts via established local organisations, meetings, and community volunteers. SRCS uses more traditional early warning systems and could benefit from adopting newer technologies, like mobile phone alerts.

component_details.title: Cash Based Intervention (CBI)
component_details.description: An effective and flexible way, including all forms of cash and voucher-based assistance, to support people affected by emergencies, maintaining their dignity and choice, while fostering local economies. Cash should also be mainstreamed into other sectors (including Relief, shelter, livelihoods) and services (Logistics, Finance, etc.)

component_responses.notes: SRCS is very experienced and knowledgeable in CBI, having implemented many CASH projects in the past. The SRCS structure includes a CASH delegate, 6 field officers in the 6 branches in Somaliland, Volunteers who are trained on Cash (registration, verification, baseline, post-distribution monitoring (PDM)), as well as some branch secretaries who are also trained on CASH. While the NS does not have a CBI preparedness plan not a fully institutionalized approach, the NS has significant capacity to scale up CBI programming given the geographic reach and volunteer strength of the NS, as well as experience in CBI. SOPs have been developed for CBI with the support of the German Red Cross. While the NS has not completed a pre-disaster feasibility cash analysis, feasibility studies are always conducted before the beginning of a CASH project. Additionally, SRCS used a toolkit based off of the IFRC/ICRC Cash in Emergencies toolkit during its 2020 Drought, COVID19, and Desert Locust operations. SRCS also has a 3-year framework agreement with TELESOM from 2020-2022 to provide services for money transfers.

component_details.title: Emergency Needs Assessment
component_details.description: Assess the extent and impact of the damage caused by the disaster/crisis and the degree of vulnerability of the affected population. The first step in any emergency response, such an assessment will identify the needs that require external intervention and the gaps to be filled. It is a vital component of the programme-planning process.

component_responses.notes: SRCS has strong capacity and staff/volunteer resources to conduct robust Emergency Needs Assessments. The NS collects information from the affected population by age, gender, disability etc.  The branch does the assessment using KOBO collected at household level and through focus group discussions. SRCS is able to put together a multi-sectoral team depending on the need, and then cre4ates response plans based on the ENA results. SRCS could strengthen its ENA capacity by developing clear SOPs and guidelines for assessments.

component_details.title: Affected population selection
component_details.description: Identification and selection of target Affected population for interventions, using a pre-defined set of criteria based on need and vulnerability. This includes consideration of specific vulnerabilities such as disability, age and gender.

component_responses.notes: SRCS ensures that communities are informed of beneficiary selection criteria, often working with community leaders to make the selections. Criteria are based on vulnerability and take gender, diversity and needs of the affected population into account. Population data is protected by limiting access only to the NS individuals who need it, and staff/volunteers are trained in data collection beforehand. Triangulation and verification of population lists typically includes community leaders. The NS could strengthen its capacity in this area by standardizing and formalizing its processes and developing clear SOPs for affected population selection.

component_details.title: Emergency Operations Centre (EOC)
component_details.description: A central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions at a strategic level in an emergency situation. The common functions are to collect and analyze data; facilitate decision making that protects life and livelihoods; and disseminate those decisions to all concerned agencies and individuals. Generally located at the headquarter level of an organization.

component_responses.notes: SRCS has not established an EOC in its emergency response.

component_details.title: Information Management (IM)
component_details.description: Ability to manage information including requesting, receiving, analyzing and disseminating as per its procedures and partner requirements (IFRC and public authorities in particular). There should be a clear digital/paper trail that documents what, when and how the NS has acted and provides key information for the development of Emergency Plan of Actions. Includes IM between levels, between departments and Situational Reports, mapping, visualisation of data, GO platform (IFRC).

component_responses.notes: During the COVID-19 response SRCS has rolled-out trainings for staff and volunteers on collection of community feedback using Kobo and pre-developed templates, though these processes were somewhat ad hoc. Information was well-shared during this response, via a bi-weekly update letter distributed to the regions and daily email sitreps sent to SRCS partners. Weekly updates on CEA results were also shared with IFRC and ICRC. These information sharing activities, were primarily coordinated by the PMERL Director.

component_details.title: Testing and Learning
component_details.description: Drills and Simulations allow the organization to test, identify and learn from the results of these type of exercises and incorporate learning into future preparedness and response planning.

component_responses.notes: While SRCS undertakes a limited amount of testing, these are only occurring on a project-by-project basis. For examples the NS does some branch-level exercises supported by German RC. Volunteer trainings sometimes include distribution simulation when there is DRR programming. By and large, though, formal testing and simulation mechanisms do not exist. This is linked to the lack of contingency plans and response plans.

component_details.title: Activation of regional and international support
component_details.description: Procedures for requesting and accepting regional and international support in operations, including triggering coordination mechanisms for funding, materials and human resources deployments.

component_responses.notes: SRCS has a good procedure and significant experience in activating regional and international support for emergencies. Key staff are aware of the Emergency appeal and DREF application processes, and MoUs are in place with IFRC and ICRC. The NS informs IFRC within 24 hours when assistance is needed. There are no formal SOPs for this, and a Movement coordination agreement between IFRC, ICRC and SRCS (Global Agreement/ SMCC) is still to be finalised. The EPoA and DREF documents reviewed in this report are good examples of the NSs experience.

component_details.title: CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL, RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR (CBRN) EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS

component_responses.notes: Any Livelihoods activities implemented by the NS are tied to projects, and therefore not a part of any NS DRM strategy or approach. The Livelihoods Manager and Director PMER are both focal points for Livelihoods. They work closely with the Cash department where SOPs have been developed for cash transfers. While SRCS has not conducted a livelihoods mapping, they do coordinate with the Ministry of Agriculture, Ministry of Environment and NADFOR, and rely on the mapping of other actors. VCA processes and needs assessments are used to identify livelihood risk to the community. During the Desert Locust and COVID-19 responses, SRCS implemented a cash for work and cash for food program, respectively. NS distributed nutritional seeds/seedlings to the desert locust affected farmers, trained farmers on desert locust prevention and control, and distributed farming tools for digging trenches (mechanical control of desert locust). Despite these various project-based interventions, no pre-disaster tools or criteria have been developed. Criteria is developed (post emergency) for each project beneficiaries e.g. during COVID-19, cash for food was given specifically to those people impacted by the COVID-19 such as schoolteachers, women in teashops, substitute farmers etc.

component_details.title: MANAGEMENT OF DEAD BODIES TO FACILITATE THEIR IDENTIFICATION

component_responses.notes: The NS is interested in expanding its ability to offer this service but is limited by the need for government authorization (from the National Security and Criminal Investigation Departments). In the meantime, the NS has received some preliminary training, conducted by ICRC, and possesses some equipment (bags).

Even under challenging circumstances like the COVID-19 pandemic, SRCS continues to provide RFL services. ICRC is supporting SRCS’s RFL activities via funding, training and capacity building, and even conducted an assessment of the program in 2017/2018 aimed at filling gaps and improving the quality of the services. The constant movement of people, increasing number of IDP camps, high costs and limits to transportation and limited NS funding make this activity challenging to implement.

component_details.title: NS-specific areas of intervention
component_details.description: Sector-specific or services provided by the NS in case of emergencies, it is in line with the NS mandate and legislation in country. It includes Community Based DP/DRR, Evacuation, Health in Emergencies, Epidemic and Pandemic, First aid, WASH, Food security and Livelihoods, Search and rRescue, Shelter, Management of dead bodies, RFL, Transition to recovery, and CBRN preparedness.

component_responses.notes: NS is not engaged in this service because of low or no capacity.

Staff and volunteers are provided with First Aid training and First Aid is featured in the Community Resilience Strategy, among other key documents. FA is a priority for the NS and operations include details on IPC and PPE usage.

SRCS has significant WASH experience and includes WASH considerations in all of its response plans Branch teams and volunteers are trained in WASH and both CERT and BERT teams have access to necessary equipment, as stored in relevant regions of Somaliland (ceramic water filters, water purification equipment, solar panels, water pumps. The NS has developed WASH SOPs and the Community Resilience Strategy provides guidance on WASH interventions. SRCS participates in WASH cluster meetings organised by the Ministry of Water and is one of the most experienced members of the cluster. During the COVID-19 response, for example, SRCS has distributed hand-washing stations, soap, Jerry cans and dustbins to key locations like Ministry offices, Primary health care centres, Hospitals and SRCS branch locations.

SRCS is actively engaged in CBHFA. Volunteers are trained in Health in Emergencies, Communicable Disease Prevention, and Behaviour Change. For SRCS, First Aid is treated as a separate sector to CBHFA, which focuses more on health programming. The NS should work to clarify roles, responsibilities, services, capacities, and coordination between different teams. At the community level, assessments are conducted, and plans are created, but not in a systematic manner. Formal testing and simulations only happen at the project level, but all volunteers receive basic first aid training.

While food distribution is not a part of the SRCS mandate, the NS still engages in this service on a project-by-project basis. This file is currently overseen by the SRCS Livelihoods Manager, and information and analysis is obtained from the Food Security cluster. During the Desert Locust and COVID-19 responses SRCS implemented a cash for work and cash for food program, respectively. Food security interventions are always linked to projects, and thus not a systematic or institutional approach.

Community-based DP and DRR is a strength of the NS and is guided by a Community Resilience Strategy. Planning processes with communities are highly participatory and focus on the most vulnerable. Awareness raising is conducted via community and stakeholder meetings and VCA processes, though these activities are usually linked to projects. CBS is currently in place in two regions, with plans to expand to a third, while CDRTs are trained and active in all 6 regions of Somaliland. While the NS is strong on this component there is room for expansion including the development of contingency plans, resiliency plans for longer term risks, and expanded training and planning for community level response teams.

component_details.title: Mapping of NS capacities
component_details.description: A list of the NS capacities including HR (staff, response teams and volunteers) and equipment that are available for disaster/crisis response. Teams could include branch and national response teams. This should be defined by technical speciality where relevant.

component_responses.notes: SRCS has strong technical knowledge and expertise in all of its service areas. There are focal points for most areas of intervention, though these are often tied to specific projects. The NS has sufficient human resources including more than 180 staff members and some 8,000 volunteers, though the HR department is relatively new, and systems need to be developed for emergency responses. At this point SRCS does not conduct a systematic mapping of its capacities, nor does it engage with related scenario planning. SRCS does have capacity for sharing of staff between teams within Somaliland depending on competencies and personal preferences.

component_details.title: Coordination with External Agencies and NGOs
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and collaboration with Non-Governmental Organization (NGO), both local and international NGOs, civil society organizations (CSOs) and United Nations agencies in country.

component_responses.notes: SRCS is part of various inter-agency coordination clusters and sub-groups and attends joint meetings. For example, during the COVID-19 response, the PMERL Director has been part of inter-agency coordination meetings with the Ministry of Health, and WHO which was supporting government in developing a response plan.  SRCS also has an agreement with UNICEF, to outsource certain activities given their technical capacity and available human resources. During past emergencies, it was noted that SRCS regularly attended monthly coordination/cluster meetings at the HCO level. Here they would share progress updates with partners in the cluster. They would also discuss how each cluster member organisation were coordinating to better avoid duplication and optimise the limited resources available. A pre-developed mapping of capacities of partners could be conducted to ensure efficient response delivery.

component_details.title: Civil Military Relations
component_details.description: Dialogue and interaction with military actors, essential to protect and promote humanitarian principles, avoid competition, minimize inconsistency and, when appropriate, pursue common goals.

component_responses.notes: SRCS promotes the Fundamental Principles to state and non-state actors whenever there is any opportunity however, this needs to be further strengthened. The NS tries to avoid coordination with the military and use of their assets because of contextual complexity i.e. state and non-state actors in the country.

component_details.title: Coordination with Movement
component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_responses.notes: Although challenging given the context, coordination between coordination offices and among Movement partners occurs, but could be further strengthened. In addition to IFRC and ICRC, there are five PNSs supporting regular programs in the country. There is a strong need for all Movement partners to prioritize SMCC, to provide effective and coherent support to the National Society, such as ensuring a concerted approach to organizational development and capacity building. There is a positive attitude towards coordination and reports are shared from time to time. For example, for COVID-19, the PMERL Director provided updates to partners. Coordination meetings with Movement partners (also encouraged by partners) used to be held every month (before COVID-19) but there has not been a coordination meeting recently. SRCS is working on harmonising the process for building the capacity of the NS. There is coordination at a technical level (ex. health working group which includes SRCS, IFRC, ICRC and all PNSs supporting health. There is also a resilience working group engaging all the partners. These platforms offer a unique channel to speak and harmonize activities across the board.

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_responses.notes: In general, SRCS has a strong mandate as auxiliary to government. Despite this, it was noted that SRCS are independent and the public authorities do not dictate their actions, though SRCS always aligns with the government rather than working in isolation. SRCS are guided by the priorities of the ministries if in alignment with their priorities. SRCS collaborates with relevant actors within various government ministries (e.g. health) as well as various government task forces. They are seen as a principle partner of the government as it relates to disaster management and health. In general, SRCS is one of the first partners called upon by the government. It was noted that one way of improving coordination is through formalizing relationships with authorities (e.g. MoUs), strengthening pre-disaster agreements, developing joint contingency planning, and conducting joint simulation exercises.

component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_responses.notes: SRCS works very closely with community members by establishing local networks. In the beginning of working with a community, SRCS hosts a community meeting, familiarizes themselves with the community and asks them to establish local units to work with SRCS. Following this, SRCS provides training and conducts stakeholder meetings every three months to discuss challenges and gaps. SRCS community volunteers are trained in all parts of Somaliland. When SRCS starts a project, they always assign a community mobiliser. SRCS engages the community and uses information/feedback to prepare community action plans. In the case of a disaster, communities report to the branch which then reports to the HCO, and then to the relevant Ministry. There are approximately (12 types of) Actions Teams, each led by a team leader, in all six branches. Youth Clubs provide an opportunity for team members to get together. Unfortunately, the Hargeisa Branch does not have the space to host a Youth Club. During a response, teams are in touch with branches through cell phones and SRCS is able to send messages (e.g. alert) to a large number of volunteers at the same time. There are 48 community level Action Teams. Note: Volunteers are enrolled in the Action Teams based on their educational background, availability and interest, though not all volunteers are part of Action Teams. Not all Action Team are response teams. Community action plans are prepared with the support of a Community mobiliser.  Every year SRCS tries to add 2-4 new communities. Currently around 5% of Somaliland communities are supported by SRCS.

component_details.title: Cooperation with private sector
component_details.description: Mechanism that allows cooperation with private sector that often plays a strong role in response, particularly if there is impact on their staff and businesses. There is often a willingness to donate goods and services. Advance agreements help to expedite response actions.

component_responses.notes: Currently SRCS has no partnership with the private sector. No specific guidance exists on relationships with private sector or public donations. In general, SRCS’s use of the emblem is appropriate even though there has been limited opportunity to use it through private sector partnerships.

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_responses.notes: "In general, nearly all SRCS funding is from Movement partners. There is a need to enhance internal systems and capacities to attract more diverse funding and develop a fund for emergency response. There is no RM department. The Executive Director HCO and Coordinator for SRCS Nairobi CO lead this file. SRCS does not have any policy, strategy or guidelines for resource mobilization. SRCS Nairobi Coordination Office, together with ICRC, is working on developing a RM strategy. SRCS has done a market survey related to fundraising, but there has been no sensitisation of key staff on raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public or other in-country actors to support various responses. In general, few resources are allocated to preparedness work, but partners are usually eager to support response.  Sometimes SRCS gets support from mosques during emergencies. There are three rehabilitation centres (Hargeisa, Mogadishu and Galkayo) and some branches have business centres where income is generated. Some branches also rent their facilities to cover core costs."

LOGISTICS MANAGEMENT: SRCS’s logistics function is divided between (1) the Logistics Manager who covers warehouse management, fleet, dispatch of items, and (2) the DRM Director who covers procurement. It was noted that in general, there is no proper logistic system in SRCS, no emergency operating center to support prepositioning of stocks/relief items, not enough logistic staff, warehouse space, training (last in 2017) and in general, logistics roles, responsibilities and procures are not clearly defined. As a result, no analysis has been done as it relates to strategically or systematically pre-positioning stock (although some cases of this did occur during the COVID-19 response). Lack of funding has also been a challenge.  For internally procured goods, key SRCS staff are familiar with IFRC logistics procedures and liaise with IFRC logistics in Nairobi. Once the procurement process is done internationally, the SRCS Logistics Manager has a role to support customs clearance and tax exemptions from the government line ministries. SRCS does not have a cold chain system for medicine; the SRCS warehouse is only intended for non-medical items.//SUPPLY CHAIN MANAGEMENT: SRCS does not pay import tax, the government provides tax exemptions to SRCS imported items through the Ministry of Finance. One key role of the SRCS logistics function is to identify and apply for tax exemptions in the country. Once the shipment details are received from IFRC, ICRC or any other PNS, the logistics manager starts immediate action to prepare all the required logistics processes in the country including tax exemption paperwork, transporting and dispatching of items to the designed locations. Currently SRCS does not map out stocks and equipment available across the country or nor does it have an up-to-date list of all its resources. Further, SRCS does not have mapping of resources available by other stakeholders in-country. When branches require resources, they make a request by submitting list of items to the coordination office, then if the items are available at HCO in the warehouse, they are dispatched. Standard peacetime procedures are used but noted this was meeting the needs of branches.//PROCUREMENT: SRCS does not have a dedicated procurement person, but rather the Disaster Risk Management Director manages SRCS procurement and takes on that role as a Procurement focal point in addition to his other work. A draft procurement policy is under review, but this is not exclusively meant for emergencies (primarily for normal times). Although this draft policy is a good foundation document, it was noted in recent response reports that the tendering process took a long time and is an area where support is needed. Some adaptions can make the procurement process during emergencies more robust. In addition, some procurement documents and templates have been developed, but many needs revision/updating. With the exception of the pre-agreement with Telesom for cash distribution, SRCS does not have agreements with suppliers, or a pre-identified list of suppliers available for various goods or services in-country. In the recent COVID-19 response, various material including PPEs, facemask, hand sanitizer, thermometers, jerrycans, and soap were procured and distributed.//FLEET AND TRANSPORTATION MANAGEMENT: SRCS does not have a fleet manual containing road safety and security guidance, maintenance, etc. There is no insurance for vehicles (with the exception of IFRC operation vehicles) and there appears to be little adherence to the use of logbooks. It was noted that the existing fleet is not sufficient to meet response needs. Currently the NS has 4x4 vehicles and trucks available (but not owned). For the most part, vehicles are fitted with seatbelts, and weapon restriction stickers and contain fire extinguishers and first aid kits. Drivers have valid licenses, though no defensive driving training is provided.//WAREHOUSE AND STOCK MANAGEMENT: SRCS has a small warehouse in Hargeisa Coordination office and a large warehouse in Burao branch supported by IFRC. The warehouse in Burao was built during the ERU operation for the Cholera outbreak (AWD) in Burao Togdheer region in 2017. This warehouse is used for storing and dispatching all NFIs in the three eastern SRCS regions/branches. For the other three SRCS western regions like Saahi, Awdal and Maroodijeex, SRCS uses the warehouse in Hargeisa which does not have enough space. Ultimately, SRCS does not have enough warehouse space. No proper or recent training on warehouse management has occurred since the last training conducted by IFRC during the 2017 Burao cholera outbreak.18 participants attended from across six branches and the Coordination office.

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_responses.notes: HR policies and procedures are currently not adjusted to emergencies. In general, deployment of volunteers/responders is managed by branches. Branches provide briefings on safety and security risks before deployment however, no documented deployment procedures exist. An SMS system is used to activate responders. Staff engaged in response have do not have a written job description (i.e. response team TORs). A training needs assessment was completed for staff earlier this year, but a capacity assessment of the volunteers has also been recommended. Training on CEA has been provided by the PMERL Director during the COVID-19 response at branch-level. Trainings by the Gender and Diversity Manager and Primary Health Care Manager for PSEA and SGBV have been provided at the HCO and at branches for staff and volunteers. The following trainings are obligatory from HCO: (1) Overview of HR policy, (2) Employee Code of Conduct/Ethics, (3) Performance management training. First responders are only deployed after necessary training, including key staff trained in epidemic prevention and control. All staff sign the Code of Conduct/Ethics after their training/ induction in normal times. In emergencies, signing the Code of Conduct/Ethics is not possible, so after a quick orientation, paperwork is taken care of later. A responder online database, called Doktoz, has been developed. In general, staff and volunteers are appropriately insured. First responders are only deployed after necessary training and provision of essential PPE. There is no formal mechanism on analysis of the risks and its mitigation. All HCO staff and branch coordinators have IDs, but some field staff do not. Retention of volunteers is a big challenge, despite having appreciation as part of the Volunteer Management Guidelines. There are some plans to retain volunteers through Youth Clubs, by giving access to computers/internet, and offering courses on computer skills, team work etc.

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_responses.notes: There are currently no safety and security guidelines within SRCS. There is no formally appointed function of Safety and Security at the NS, however it was noted that this role is taken on by the FA Director and Branch Coordinators in a more informal manner. For instance, SRCS checks from community leaders for access and acceptance before a response. Branch Coordinators generally conduct analysis and provide briefings to responders, on topics such as the nature of response or services to be provided, before deployment, however it was noted that there is no formal mechanism for reporting security incidents and security monitoring during real time operations does not exist. In general, it appears that staff and volunteers (particularly the Action Teams) are familiar with Stay Safe, but no significant work has been done related to Safer Access since 2017. The Volunteer Management Guidelines document mentions methods for sending complaints but there is no formal mechanism specific to security.

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_responses.notes: SRCS has a Communications Director leading the communications office at the Hargeisa Coordination Office working primarily in two branches (i.e. Lasanod and Erigavo). Guidelines for communications in emergencies do not exist, though communication to the public is typically provided with 2-3 days. There are no standard templates (e.g. press release template) or tools for communications in emergencies. In emergencies, a spokesperson is assigned by the Executive Director depending on the event. If the Executive Director is not the focal point it may be the Head of Program, Health Director, Comms Director, but it is not always the same person or pre-determined. Messages to the public are created on a more ad hoc basis during emergencies using traditional communication channels (e.g. microphones/megaphones, internal dissemination). During COVID-19, IFRC has worked closely with SRCS to develop messages. IFRC and CRC have helped SRCS with press releases during the COVID-19/Desert Locust crises. During COVID-19 the primary messages have been for hand washing, social distancing, and mask usage following the IFRC universal messages. Messages are developed on an ad hoc basis for epidemics. Although SRCS publishes annual reports for public authorities, ministers, and partners this material does not advocate on behalf of communities, but rather describes SRCS activities. Although social media usage is new for SRCS with limited presence online, SRCS has developed social media guidelines for Staff and Volunteers including ways to avoid damage to SRCS’s reputation. For the COVID-19 response, SRCS HCO and branches have used a local management system, to respond to rumours by disseminating clear information about the pandemic and exact steps to be taken.

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_responses.notes: The PMERL function within SRCS was newly established in 2020, made up of one core staff: the PMERL Director. Since the role was established, there have been some immediate positive contributions during the recent COVID-19 and Desert Locust responses. The PMERL function is largely under-resourced, however there is hope/intention to expand the unit and decentralise some of its functions to branches. Before the function was established there were no standardised reporting templates, however since, there has been reporting from field-level, to branch-level, to coordination office-level (first reporting from field using new reporting templates October 2020). Data is consolidated to produce monthly/quarterly monitoring reports which are shared with partners. During 2019 Drought Operation, Post-Distribution Monitoring (PDM) assessments were done in all targeted locations under Sahil and Awdal Regions. The purpose of the PDMs were to ensure Quality and Accountability to beneficiaries and track any changes in terms of the logframe indicators. It was noted that there are some operational documents and guidelines which need to be developed, such as having a standard template for EPoAs, as well as formulating high-level outcome statements, generic response actions/activities, indicators and targets to guide operational planning. Opportunities exist with the MCO PMERL function to ensure consistency and standardisation. During the COVID-19 response, there have been daily email updates provided to partners. With the establishment of the PMERL function, the NS is taking a lead role in coordinating and cooperating with partners on planning, monitoring and reporting. It was noted that overall project management capacities of technical staff could be improved to ensure that PMERL across the organisation is enhanced.

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_responses.notes: SRCS uses SAGE financial software for its accounting system. The NS uses the same financial procedures for normal times as it does for emergencies – there are no dedicated or specific emergency financial procedures or authorisation levels. There are some procedures in the existing finance manual to facilitate transparency.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_responses.notes: In general, SRCS does not provide equipment to key staff and volunteers. Hardware, such as laptops, is typically supplied by projects. Most staff and volunteers utilise their own personal phones for their work. Vehicles do not have radios or any other communication equipment. There is no radio room function within SRCS. The NS does not have a dedicated frequency for emergency radio communication. Additionally, the NS does not have any portable generators to maintain operational continuity in the event there is no electricity. The NS does have internet functionality available for Hargeisa Coordination office and 6 branches.

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.notes:
La CRCI n'a pas encore activement engagé de travail dans ce domaine. Quelques initiatives ont eu lieu mais sans suite. 
Une étude IDRL commanditée par la CRCI en 2015, auprès d’un cabinet en Côte d’Ivoire, avait révélé qu’il n’existait pas de lois en matière de gestion des catastrophes. Un plaidoyer ponctuel avait été mené par la CRCI suite à cette étude mais le travail s’en est arrêté là. 
Un pool de points focaux (nombre exact méconnu) a été formé sur les questions IDRL et DIH en 2016 mais ces personnes ne sont pas clairement identifiée et a priori pas apte à intervenir en cas d’urgence.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_responses.notes:
L’application systématique de l’approche CEA et PEAS est observée dans toutes les opérations, interventions, projets de la CRCI. 
Les projets d’urgence sont présentés aux communautés pour mettre en place les activités ensemble, établit des moyens de communications, et de collecte de feedback des communautés ou des plaintes en liens avec PSEA, corruption chantage et autre. Cependant, les sensibilisations et formations des comités locaux et volontaires ne sont pas fréquentes, car la capacité financière de la CRCI est très réduite.
Il existe seulement un draft incomplet de politique CEA. Son élaboration et plan d’action et sa mise en place est prévu à travers des financements de la CRNL pour 2023. 
Des systèmes de retour communautaires existent mais ils sont différents selon les zones géographiques et souvent pas entièrement opérationnel.

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_responses.notes: Le mandat de la CRCI a été développé. Il est bien mentionné dans le PSD et connu des staff clés. Cependant il n’est pas assez connu du reste du staff et des volontaires ainsi que des autorités gouvernementales locales et nationales. Un travail de diffusion reste à faire en interne et en externe.

component_details.title: DRM Strategy
component_details.description: An outline of the overall goal that the NS seeks to achieve in its disaster and crisis response operations. The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

component_responses.notes:
La CRCI prend appui sur l’existant au niveau interne et national des documents suivants : 
1) Le Plan Stratégique de Développement (CRCI) 
2) Le Plan National des Risques et de Gestion des Catastrophes 
3) Le Plan National de Développement.
 Mais elle n’a pas encore de stratégie de GRC spécifique à la CRCI

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_responses.notes: La CRCI ne dispose pas de politique de GRC. Au cours de ses opérations les équipes utilisent des facto la politique de GRC de la Fédération.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_responses.notes:
Un système de surveillance des risques existe mais rien de précis et systématique. Il faut le rendre plus formel et le vulgariser. 
Pas de SAP a proprement dit. 
Existence d’un groupe WhatsApp avec les PF sureté et sécurité en charge de communiquer tout type d’information sur tout type de risques. Branches reçoivent les alertes localisées météo, relayées sur une plate-forme WhatsApp CRCI GRC. Cette plateforme couvre toutes les zones à risque. Pas de système de collète et d’analyse de données. La collecte de quelques données primaires est effectuée par les branches locales et l’analyse au niveau du siège mais le mécanisme reste quelque peu inopérant. Besoin d’un outil performant tel que QRISKA alerte. Besoin d’élargir le réseau des points focaux. 
Une coordination transfrontalière avec CR Guinéenne faite en 2021 concernant les risques liés à l’alerte Ebola.

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_responses.notes: Aucun scénario n’a été élaboré à ce jour. Les plans de contingence existant n’en possède pas. Une ébauche de scénario existe dans le plan elections (pas dans le plan inondations) mais l’identification des causes profondes/ facteurs de risques y est juste survolée.

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_responses.notes: Existence d’un DM et d’une unité de gestion générale des risques (DM et fonctions de soutien). La SN a réalisé une analyses de risques couvrant le pays mais ce travail n’est pas mis à jour régulièrement. Une analyse plus poussée est réalisée en temps d’élections avec le CICR et des mesures régulières liées au Safer Access sont mise en place au niveau du terrain. Certains comités locaux ont identifié des acteurs locaux qu’ils engagent régulièrement pour discuter de leurs activités mais ce travail reste ad hoc, ni systématique ni généralisé. Une politique de lutte contre la fraude mise en place au niveau national. Elle ne définit pas comment éviter la fraude et corruption mais définit les mesures à prendre en cas de fraude/ corruption. Un travail de révision de la politique et de sa mise en place est en cours.

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_responses.notes: La DM est la point focal préparation. Le travail d’analyse des gaps et d’approche pour renforcer la préparation est en cours au travers de la mise en place de ce premier cycle d’approche PIE

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: La CRCI ne dispose pas de plan de continuité des activités.

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_responses.notes: Aucun SOP n’a été développé à ce jour.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.
