component_responses.notes: In place of a DRM Strategy, SIRCS has a DRM Plan which includes the NS mandate, SI hazard contexts, operational objectives, activities, and success indicators. The DRM plan likewise includes specific roles of various programs and support units within the National Society. Developed in the early 2010s, the DRM plan was set to be reviewed in 2017 but was postponed. Since then, no other reviews were scheduled to revisit the DRM Plan. SIRCS is looking towards the PER process to inform the review and revision of the DRM plan. Lack of dissemination among the staff and volunteers especially at the Branch level was raised.

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_responses.notes: SIRCS does not currently have a DRM Policy but uses the IFRC DRM policy as a reference.

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: Although there are ongoing discussions between SIRCS, NDMO, and CCD-Pacific on the International Disaster Response Law (IDRL), no concrete plan is in place to move the IDRL work forward. No training on disaster law or IDRL was conducted in SIRCS. However, the Communications Coordinator is the focal point for the International Humanitarian Law, supported by ICRC. SIRCS enjoys entitlements from the SI government in the form of tax-free privileges and Customs exemptions for imported goods and supplies, though on an ad-hoc basis. Since 2019, SIRCS consistently included lobbying with parliamentarians for the review and amendment of the Red Cross Act. This is intended to have the RC Act updated with the evolving role of SIRCS and the fast-changing humanitarian contexts.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_responses.notes: SIRCS adheres to international standards for disaster relief and strives to achieve SPHERE minimum standards in its disaster response operations. Program and service delivery are guided by National Society policies on Child Protection (CP), Protection Gender and Inclusion (PGI), and Prevention and Response to Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA). In response operations, SIRCS relies on its emergency assessment process in integrating concerns of the affected population into operations planning. Although a Community Engagement and Accountability (CEA) training was conducted in 2018, the trained staff and volunteers were not given specific roles in rolling out the CEA approach. However, several SIRCS program processes are already practicing CEA. This is evident in the community-based processes used in SIRCS resilience programming and most recently with the messaging activities in COVID 19.

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_responses.notes: SIRCS is mandated by law through the Red Cross Act passed by the parliament of the Solomon Islands (SI). However, the RC Act has no implementing rules and regulations that can provide the scope and limitations of SIRCS auxiliary role in responding to crisis and disasters. Collaboration with the SI government is usually on an ad hoc basis, there are no MoUs or MoAs that exist between the SIRCS and the SI government. The current Strategic Plan of SIRCS embodies its mandate and is widely disseminated to its partners in the RC/RC Movement, government, INGOs, UN, and donor agencies. The SIRCS mandate and policies form an integral part of the induction package for staff and volunteers. Strategic Goal 3 of the SIRCS Strategic Plan 2017 – 2020 highlights the need to maintain its relationship with relevant government ministries, strengthen its auxiliary role and advocate the 7 Fundamental Principles. The IHL Parliamentarian Handbook is the main advocacy toll for SIRCS towards the government. The IHL Handbook is due for review and updating since it was launched in 2014.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: Although there is no monitoring and early warning system in place, an ad hoc system is being used by SIRC by linking with NDMO, MET, and IFRC to access daily weather updates (MET), early warning messages (NDMO), and seasonal forecast (IFRC) of up to 3 months. Information received are the relayed to the Branches. The DRM Manager is the focal point in SIRCS for hazard monitoring and early warning. The current level of SIRCS hazard monitoring is focused on hydrometeorological hazards, specifically on tropical cyclones but there are no trigger mechanisms identified for slow-onset hazards such as dry spells and drought. SIRCS response to hazard events are guided by the DRM Plan which includes the mechanism for the response, along with various color-coded alert and response levels. Although these color codes are different from the NDMO color coding and are unique to SIRCS, the response actions are coordinated closely with the NDMO and the Country Sector Committees. At the community level, people depend mostly on traditional knowledge and indigenous practices in reading weather patterns. Although SIRCS is well placed to gather and analyze data on emerging human-induced hazards, the NS do not have any written obligation, policy or operational guidelines to pursue this. To address concerns on the safety and security of staff and volunteers, SIRCS main reference is the Safer Access Model. However, the last training on Safer Access was conducted back in 2014. SIRCS received no other safety and security training since then. The VCA process is central to disaster risk assessments at community level to promote community participation and ensuring an inclusive approach. VCAs are also used to gather sex and age disaggregated data (SADD) and PWD information in high-risk communities. Although the VCA process itself is only done

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_responses.notes: Although there is no standard written simulation exercise guide with structured scenarios and phased inputs for the exercise, SIRCS has experienced conducting simulation exercises at the community level based on ad hoc scenarios. These scenarios are all related to hydro-meteorological hazards only. However, in the advent of COVID-19, the first actual scenario planning was initiated by SIRCS on how the pandemic may evolve and its impact on NS operations. The scenario planning became the basis for SIRCS in developing the Business Continuity Plan (BCP). Although concentrated on the pandemic, this is the first BCP developed by the NS and will gradually be expanded into a multi-hazard continuity plan.

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_responses.notes: Responsibility for risk management in SIRCS rests with the Secretary General (SG), being accountable to address the operational, institutional, financial and reputational risks of the National Society. To manage these risks, the SG regularly meets with both the NS Senior Management Team and the National Governing Board. The experience of the National Society derived from the development of its first Business Continuity Plan (BCP) at the onset of the pandemic in the Pacific provided a template for a holistic approach on risk management. SIRCS have systems and procedures in place to prevent fraud and corruption which includes the NS Finance Manual and the Anti-Fraud and Corruption Policy. There are currently no specific unit in SIRCS assigned to handle critical incidents. Staff and volunteers are trained in Safer Access and First Aid in conflict.

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_responses.notes: The focal point for disaster preparedness is the Disaster Management Coordinator. The DMC is supported by the Resilience Coordinator at the national level and the Branch Officers at the provincial level. To address preparedness gaps, SIRCS conducts capacity analysis at the end of every calendar year which are used as basis for capacity building for staff and volunteers. The ongoing USAID resilience funding and the Australian Red Cross institutional response preparedness support addresses financial gaps in preparedness and early action. There is no resource mobilization strategy in place at the moment the IFRC CCD is supporting SIRCS in developing an overall resource mobilization strategy. The NS has an existing bank account specific for disaster relief operations but has no reserve funds.

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: SIRCS developed the first BCP during the impending pandemic lockdown in March 2020. The BCP was specific for COVID-19 only. There are no written guidelines for repurposing funds.

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_responses.notes: Existing SOP is an integral part of the SIRCS DM Plan whereby roles and responsibilities of key staff are outlined. The DM Plan includes procedures for response, alert and response levels and decision-making flowcharts. However, the DM plan is overdue for review and is not disseminated widely among the staff and volunteers, particularly at the Branch level.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_responses.notes: The SIRCS DM Plan is an all-in-one document that includes the NS’s response plan. The Response Plan was designed based on the technical areas of non-food items and emergency shelter and aligns with IFRC global standards and templates. The DM plan was developed by staff and volunteers at HQ and Branch level, there was no participation from the community and governance. The NS does not directly engage in recovery but support agency partners in joint recovery assessments. The DM plan, along with its recovery component not been reviewed for the last several years. The review will provide the opportunity to have the PGI components integrated into the response plan based on the PGI policy passed by the governing board in 2020.

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: SIRCS attends the annual pre-disaster meetings with other stakeholders organized by the NDMO. Key SIRCS staff have defined roles in pre-disaster agreements as indicated in the SIRCS DM Plan. Coordination and management arrangements with other stakeholders are reflected in the governments national DRM plan. To ensure preparedness at all levels, SIRCS conducts annual discussions with Movement Partners through partnership meetings and the Pacific SG Network. Although unaware of Movement Coordination agreements, SIRCS follows the lead of IFRC in Movement coordination. SIRCS is yet to ensure that all its contractors sign the Code of Conduct prior to engagement. This has never been practiced in the past. There are no existing official agreements, instead SIRCS uses the Red Cross Act as the reference point for collaboration and coordination with stakeholders. Part of the SI Red Cross Act is the exemption of SIRCS in customs duties in receiving imported relief supplies during times of emergencies. There are no framework agreements signed with any logistics and service providers, however SIRCS maintains a list of potential suppliers mapped out across the country. This list has not been updated. There are no existing social protection agreements with the government. However, SIRCS have access to pre-existing data bases of vulnerable population through the NDMO.

SIRCS has been conducting disaster preparedness activities in communities as part of their disaster risk reduction approach. This is further strengthened under the current community-based approach in enhancing community resilience which puts the community to lead the process. Although the current set-up of early warning systems in the community is on an ad-hoc basis, regular hazard awareness raising are being done by volunteers in their own communities. The current ERT system of SIRCS is general and have no distinction between community, Branch or national level as the same ERT training is rolled out at all levels. There are no community-level contingency plans.

component_details.title: Mapping of NS capacities
component_details.description: A list of the NS capacities including HR (staff, response teams and volunteers) and equipment that are available for disaster/crisis response. Teams could include branch and national response teams. This should be defined by technical speciality where relevant.

component_responses.notes: SIRCS periodically conducts inventory of materials and equipment and recommendations being submitted to the Senior Management Team for action. Available human resources comprised of volunteers inducted into the SIRCS Emergency Response Team (ERT). However, available response equipment is only suited for small-scale response to disasters. An annual mapping of response capacity is being conducted by SIRCS based on the indicators in the DM plan. Report is shared with IFRC. Mechanisms are in place for Branch-to-Branch peer to peer support. IFRC previously facilitated cross-NS peer support.

The SIRCS DRM plan has no component on multi-sectoral responses for any epidemic scenarios. However, the existing SOPs can be used for mobilization of volunteers and for coordination with government agencies

component_details.title: Early Action Mechanisms
component_details.description: Designed to translate warnings into anticipatory actions to help reduce the impact of specific disaster or crisis events. They focus on consolidating available forecasting information and putting procedures in place to ensure that a NS can act ahead of any disaster/crisis. Forecast-based financing is included within the scope of this area.

component_responses.notes: The early action methodology of SIRCS is included in the DM and contingency plans based on prevailing hazard and vulnerability conditions. The DM and contingency plan likewise provide the guidelines to anticipate and respond to hazard events alongside the NDMO. The SIRCS communication tree outlines the flow of information via text messages. The Disaster Management Coordinator is the focal point for the SIRCS alert system. Branches work collaborates with their government counterparts in the provinces for send alert messages to the communities, strictly following NDMO alert protocols.

component_details.title: Cash Based Intervention (CBI)
component_details.description: An effective and flexible way, including all forms of cash and voucher-based assistance, to support people affected by emergencies, maintaining their dignity and choice, while fostering local economies. Cash should also be mainstreamed into other sectors (including Relief, shelter, livelihoods) and services (Logistics, Finance, etc.)

component_responses.notes: SIRCS assessment templates are used in sequence to build up assessment information from incident report to more detailed assessments. The NS deploys its program units to conduct thematic multi-sectorial detailed assessments which are often deployed alongside the NDMO and other agencies. Assessment information are analyzed according to specific relief needs, existing community capacity, access and safety of volunteers and includes disaggregated data of affected populations which then are used in the formulation of emergency plan of action (EPoA). The SIRCS Assessment Form 1C in particular is used to assess secondary risks.

component_details.title: Emergency Needs Assessment
component_details.description: Assess the extent and impact of the damage caused by the disaster/crisis and the degree of vulnerability of the affected population. The first step in any emergency response, such an assessment will identify the needs that require external intervention and the gaps to be filled. It is a vital component of the programme-planning process.

component_responses.notes: SIRCS assessment templates are used in sequence to build up assessment information from incident report to more detailed assessments. The NS deploys its program units to conduct thematic multi-sectorial detailed assessments which are often deployed alongside the NDMO and other agencies. Assessment information are analyzed according to specific relief needs, existing community capacity, access and safety of volunteers and includes disaggregated data of affected populations which then are used in the formulation of emergency plan of action (EPoA). The SIRCS Assessment Form 1C in particular is used to assess secondary risks.

component_details.title: Affected population selection
component_details.description: Identification and selection of target Affected population for interventions, using a pre-defined set of criteria based on need and vulnerability. This includes consideration of specific vulnerabilities such as disability, age and gender.

component_details.title: Emergency Operations Centre (EOC)
component_details.description: A central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions at a strategic level in an emergency situation. The common functions are to collect and analyze data; facilitate decision making that protects life and livelihoods; and disseminate those decisions to all concerned agencies and individuals. Generally located at the headquarter level of an organization.

component_responses.notes: The DM Coordinator is the appointed focal point for the EOC at the headquarters level. The Branch Officers are designated focal points at provincial level. However, SIRCS has no SOP to run an EOC. The main reference document for the EOC is the SIRCS DM plan. Activation of EOC is done by the DM Coordinator, guided by the response level from the DM Plan. Included in the DM Plan are the roles and responsibilities of key SIRCS staff in the EOC. The defined space for the EOC is the multi-function hall in the headquarters building, recently upgraded with internet telecommunication equipment. Depending on the scale of emergency, the EOC can be operational 24/7. There is no electric power back-up since the generator has broken down. There is no identified alternative location for the EOC in case the headquarters building is damaged. The SIRCS communication tree is regularly updated. SIRCS is license to operate radio communication equipment and has designated frequency provided by the government. Strategic decisions on the emergency operation are based on assessments and secondary data sources and are reached by consensus among the members of the SIRCS senior management team which also functions as the emergency management team of the EOC. Official information coming out from the EOC goes through a validation and analysis to ensure factual information.

component_details.title: Information Management (IM)
component_details.description: Ability to manage information including requesting, receiving, analyzing and disseminating as per its procedures and partner requirements (IFRC and public authorities in particular). There should be a clear digital/paper trail that documents what, when and how the NS has acted and provides key information for the development of Emergency Plan of Actions. Includes IM between levels, between departments and Situational Reports, mapping, visualisation of data, GO platform (IFRC).

component_responses.notes: SIRCS has available equipment to process, visualize and share information. Although the NS has a centralized electronic filing system, this is currently non-functional while waiting for the complete installation of the IT-in-a-box. As such the bulk of the data are spread out among the various units in their laptops which are not backed up in the shared drive. SIRCS can access hazard and vulnerability data from the government through the National Statistics Office and the NDMO. The NS has a standard situation report format. Depending on the sensitivity of the data, information is commonly shared through the SIRCS social media page, the national press, emails and mobile communication.

component_details.title: Testing and Learning
component_details.description: Drills and Simulations allow the organization to test, identify and learn from the results of these type of exercises and incorporate learning into future preparedness and response planning.

component_responses.notes: SIRCS does not have a regular simulation exercise or drills to enhance its emergency procedures other than those small scenarios in the ERT training. However, SIRCS joins the annual tsunami drills organized by the government. In 2020, SIRCS took part in the COVID 19 simulation exercises organized by the MoH and NDMO.

component_details.title: Activation of regional and international support
component_details.description: Procedures for requesting and accepting regional and international support in operations, including triggering coordination mechanisms for funding, materials and human resources deployments.

component_responses.notes: The SIRCS senior management team are aware of the available support that can be extended by IFRC, ICRC and the other Movement Partners. Although there are no written guidelines, there is an adhoc system that enables SIRCS to rapidly contact and request support through IFRC. There is no SOP in the NS for requesting and incorporating global/regional teams into SIRCS emergency response operation. SIRCS follows and is familiar with the guidelines from IFRC on international support and is able to inform IFRC within 24 hours following the occurrence of an emergency. The DM Coordinator is the focal point for emergency response operations as indicated in the SIRCS DM Plan.

component_details.title: CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL, RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR (CBRN) EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS

component_responses.notes: SIRCS is co-chair of the national shelter cluster. Shelter tool kits, along with non-food relief items (NFI) and personal protective equipment (PPE) are prepositioned in all Branches. SIRCS coordinates with IFRC and Movement Partners on the replenishment of prepositioned stocks. Branch staff and volunteers are trained in Branch Level Emergency Shelter Training (BLEST). Included in the BLEST package are various emergency shelter designs using available materials from the shelter tool kit and other locally available materials. There are no framework agreements in place with local and national suppliers although SIRCS maintain a list of suppliers available in the capital city.

component_details.title: MANAGEMENT OF DEAD BODIES TO FACILITATE THEIR IDENTIFICATION

component_responses.notes: SIRCS is not involve in reintegrating survivors of epidemics into communities.

Previous responses of SIRCS to largescale disasters reflects continuity and transition from immediate relief phase to early recovery interventions. Although SIRCS did not include recovery in their DM Plan, transition to recovery is realized by support the government and partner agencies. In general, SIRCS involvement in recovery is on an ad hoc basis until such time this is properly defined in in strategy papers and enabling systems are established for transition from relief to longer-term recovery intervention, including human resources and support services as well as entering into partnership agreements.

component_details.title: NS-specific areas of intervention
component_details.description: Sector-specific or services provided by the NS in case of emergencies, it is in line with the NS mandate and legislation in country. It includes Community Based DP/DRR, Evacuation, Health in Emergencies, Epidemic and Pandemic, First aid, WASH, Food security and Livelihoods, Search and rRescue, Shelter, Management of dead bodies, RFL, Transition to recovery, and CBRN preparedness.

component_responses.notes: First Aid is a recognized component of the SIRCS DM Plan but focusing more towards ERT personal safety. SIRCS has no strategy on the deployment of volunteers to provide First Aid in emergency situations. In 2020, SIRCS has started to integrate First Aid along with PGI into their current ERT training program. Although volunteers are trained in First Aid, no kits and equipment are provided to them. The current resilience program will include community First Aid as a component of the community-based approach and will provide the necessary kits and equipment to enable functional community level first aid teams.

Although emergency WASH is considered as part of SIRCS response strategy, there is no specific WASH Officer or WASH Unit in the NS. There was previous emergency WASH training conducted to train HQ and Branch staff and volunteers in the use of water filtration equipment. A pair of NOMAD portable filtration machines are available at the headquarters but requires maintenance. However, the NS is more known for its rural WASH projects which were part of the USAID funded DRR projects in previous years. SIRCS has existing partnership with the MoH for rural WASH.

CBHFA was the flagship program of the SIRCS Health Unit but due to unavailability of funding, this was not continued. However, the current Resilience Program has integrated CBHFA and will be adapting approaches that has been effective in the past. These practices included inclusion of health risks in contingency planning and annual community health and safety assessments, community first aid training with periodic refresher courses.

component_details.title: Coordination with External Agencies and NGOs
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and collaboration with Non-Governmental Organization (NGO), both local and international NGOs, civil society organizations (CSOs) and United Nations agencies in country.

component_responses.notes: SIRCS is an active member of the humanitarian community for coordination and efficiency of response. Roles of the SIRCS technical leads is agreed and is reflected in the national DM arrangements with government. SIRCS is aware and supports the IFRC’s role in shelter cluster coordination. The NS is likewise aware of parallel appeals being launched by the UN system for disaster response but has not been involved in making or launching joint appeals. However, SIRCS work in partnership with INGOs operating in the Solomons in both preparedness and response which are supported by formal agreements.

component_details.title: Civil Military Relations
component_details.description: Dialogue and interaction with military actors, essential to protect and promote humanitarian principles, avoid competition, minimize inconsistency and, when appropriate, pursue common goals.

component_responses.notes: The government of Solomon Islands has no standing military force other than the police that are responsible for safety and security. The only instances that SIRCS used military transport as a last resort to transport NFIs to the provinces in 2014. The military transport was from the foreign military forces support the Solomons government for relief operations. SIRCS do not currently provide international humanitarian law orientation to police personnel.

component_details.title: Coordination with Movement
component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_responses.notes: SIRCS is not familiar with the Strengthening of Movement Coordination and Cooperation (SMCC) principle but has been enjoying an excellent relationship with Movement Partners. SIRCS organizes an annual Movement Partners meeting which is used as a venue to renew commitments and strengthen Movement cooperation. Through the SG, SIRCS regularly shares information to Movement Partners at before and during an ongoing emergency response operation. This information includes assessment data, progress reports and identified gaps in the operation. Information is likewise shared by the SIRCS DM Coordinator to IFRC which then disseminates information to NS in the Pacific region. Framework agreements for solicited international support is guided by IFRC. However, SIRCS has to develop guidelines for addressing unsolicited support coming in from various sectors, both at national and international levels.

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_responses.notes: SIRCS plays a key active role in the national humanitarian coordination system and is a member of the National Disaster Operating Committee which is the highest advisory level in the national DM system. SIRCS technical leads are part of the country cluster system. SIRCS is likewise fully aware of the government’s capacity in disaster management and complements this with their auxiliary role. During emergency response operations working alongside the government and other agencies, SIRCS maintains control over its assets, goods, and ensures the proper use of the Red Cross emblem. However, SIRCS sees the need to have more robust advocacy for the creation of a law specific on the Red Cross emblem to avoid misuse by the business sector.

component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_responses.notes: The SIRCS communication tree is the main dissemination tool for relaying information from headquarters to Branches to communities and vice versa. Information provided by the community is the foundation for informed decision making at Branch and Headquarters. SIRCS supports community level response through their Branches working with the village disaster response committees which are part of the government’s national DM structure.

component_details.title: Cooperation with private sector
component_details.description: Mechanism that allows cooperation with private sector that often plays a strong role in response, particularly if there is impact on their staff and businesses. There is often a willingness to donate goods and services. Advance agreements help to expedite response actions.

component_responses.notes: Thorough background check is done by SIRCS before entering into any partnerships with both the humanitarian and private sectors. SIRCS has declined receiving donations from tobacco, mining, and logging companies. The NS will formalize these guidelines through a policy paper. The Solomon Islands Government Red Cross Act passed in 1983 provides the safeguards against misuse of the Red Cross emblem. Although this provides safety nets on the Red Cross visual identity, there still needs to have a more robust campaign against misuse of the emblem by business establishments and companies. Ad hoc guidelines are in place in training and deploying volunteers from corporate partners. These guidelines will need to be formalized through an update on the SIRCS Volunteer Policy.

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_responses.notes: Key SIRCS staff at headquarters are aware of fund-raising options for emergency operations. Most preparedness activities are funded under the One Plan approach of the resilience program. There is an existing resource mobilization strategy within SIRCS which is currently applied in their fund generation activities. However, there are no specific fundraising mechanism with the private sector. Although the Branch has the autonomy to conduct fund generation activities, most of the funding for Branch operations are provided by the Headquarters from various funding source within and outside the Movement. Although there is a SIRCS bank account specific for receiving funding for emergency operations, there is no system for maintaining a specific amount for emergency funding and no replenishment mechanism.

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_responses.notes: Responders are equipped with the required PPEs when deployed under DREF operations. However, this may not be the case for localized emergencies when volunteers are deployed to address small-scale, community level emergencies. Volunteers are not fully equipped with vests and standard visibility items. There is no system in place for responders to have a learning program to gain other competencies. There is also no distinction between the community, Branch and national level responders. Not all responders are insured under the Movement insurance scheme. The current ERT program of SIRCS has yet to integrate accountability standards, SPHERE and PGI. There is no specific SOP for the management, maintenance and deployment of ERTs other than what is included in the general DM Plan. There are no historical and updated databases of the list of trained ERT members. There are no organized volunteers with sector-specific expertise, no database of professional volunteers. SIRCS is also yet to update its volunteer policy to include professional volunteers and volunteer recruitment done spontaneously during emergencies. There is also a need for volunteer recognition for services rendered in response operations. Although safer access guidelines are being used to update and analyze existing and emergent risks to responders, very few are aware of the Safer Access model. Only key staff and volunteers were oriented on self-care, violence and harassment and is not included in the ERT training. SIRCS Code of Conduct is explained to and signed by volunteers that are deployed to emergency response missions.

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_responses.notes: SIRCS adheres with the guidelines provided by the Safer Access model in safety and security of staff and volunteers. However, there are no trained staff appointed at headquarters and Branch levels that are responsible for the safety and security protocols. There are no safety and security policy in SIRCS. Context and risk analysis are part of the mission orientation of staff and volunteers before being deployed on emergency operations. These information and analysis are regularly updated from data coming from the field. There is a need to train volunteers on safer access as the last training was conducted several years ago and most of the trained volunteers are already inactive or have left. There are ad hoc procedures in place for safety and security but only a few staff at headquarters are aware of these. The SIRCS communication tree is being used as the incident reporting system.

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_responses.notes: The SIRCS Secretary General is designated as the official spokesperson in an emergency. Although communications focal points were already identified in the Branches, they are yet to be trained. SIRCS has a communication plan in place and maximizes the use of social media and the national press to raise awareness on preparedness and to launch an appeal to support emergency response operations. There is no social media policy, but the draft guidelines are used in the interim. Standard templates for communications are used. Key messages are likewise developed and shared with the staff and volunteers. SIRCS has communication focal points in the Branches that can track negative media and be able to address these. However, SIRCS will require support for a more thorough training of its communication focal points in the Branches.

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_responses.notes: SIRCS has a dedicated PMER function for regular programming. However, there is a need to clarify function during emergencies and to be included into the PMER Officer’s job description. Lessons learned from both response operations and regular programming are incorporated into the planning processes. The IFRC emergency plan of action (EPOA) template is the standardized framework for disaster response operational planning. Preparedness planning is integrated into resilience programming and uses the One Plan approach for planning processes. Plans are updated periodically to reflect the dynamics of the operations. Operational updates and reports use information gathered from the community and Branches which are compiled, analyzed and provided to IFRC and Movement Partners.

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_responses.notes: SIRCS uses an automated accounting and financial system which tracks, and reports funds received. The logistics unit is responsible for managing and reporting in-kind resources received. SIRCS has trained staff in finance and logistics to support emergency operations. There are no finance and administrative procedures in place. Instead, SIRCS follows the standard procedures outlined in their finance manual related to regular programming. The SIRCS Finance Management Manual includes guidelines for to facilitate transparency and fraud prevention.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_responses.notes: SIRCS provides mobile phones and phone credits to all staff at headquarters and branch levels. Program Coordinators are likewise provided with mobile data allowances to ensure 24/7 connectivity. Contact lists are stored in mobile phones and emails. The communication tree serves as the emergency notification protocol for the NS. SIRCS has a social media account which is regularly updated. Internet conferencing is done through MS Teams, Zoom and Skype. Although SIRCS has a dedicated radio frequency provided by the government, all base and handheld radios are not functioning. Satellite phone sim cards are all expired, last time this was used was in 2013. No SOPs relating to internet and telecommunications. Diesel generator at the headquarters has been out of order for several years and needed replacement. Internet access are through individual mobile phones or internet dongles as SIRCS cannot use a common server account due to its outstanding debt to the national internet provider. There are no trained staff that can address technical issues, repairs are outsourced to local computer technicians. SIRCS is still waiting for the completion of its IT-in-a-box installation from New Zealand Red Cross.

component_responses.notes:
La Société Nationale (SN) intègre pleinement les risques liés à la santé publique et les interventions connexes dans ses initiatives de Gestion des Risques de Catastrophes (GRC). Cependant, son action repose principalement sur des outils opérationnels spécifiques notamment le SOP dédiés à la préparation et à la réponse aux urgences. Ces outils incluent :
• Risques naturels : cyclones, crues soudaines, sécheresses.
• Mouvements de population : réfugiés, déplacés internes, migrants, troubles civils.
• Épidémies et pandémies : diarrhée, choléra.
• Risques environnementaux : accidents de la route, accidents industriels, incendies.
Parmi les documents opérationnels disponibles :
• Une SOP pour la distribution des kits (2017).
• Un plan de contingence pour les accidents de la route (2017).
• Un plan de contingence pour les inondations (2021), ciblant 2 500 personnes.
• Un plan de contingence pour les incendies (2017), visant 2 400 personnes.
• Un plan de contingence pour les mouvements de population (2017), prévoyant l’accueil de 300 personnes par jour sur six mois.
• Un Protocole d’Action Précoce (PAP) 2022-2024, couvrant 2 500 personnes.
Ces outils permettent à la Croissant-Rouge de Djibouti (CRD) de fournir une réponse rapide et coordonnée face aux crises, même en l’absence d’une stratégie unifiée.
Implications : 
L’absence d’une stratégie claire et nationale limite l’engagement coordonné des différents secteurs et services techniques, freinant l’élaboration de plans d’intervention cohérents et complets. Les branches locales planifient leurs actions en s’appuyer sur des objectifs opérationnels définis au niveau national, ce qui peut réduit l’efficacité des interventions. L’adoption d’un Protocole d’Action Précoce (PAP) marque une avancée majeure pour la SN. Toutefois, il serait crucial de développer davantage de PAP conformes aux SOP, renforçant ainsi la préparation et la capacité d’intervention rapide face aux urgences. Cette dynamique proactive constitue une opportunité pour la CRD de se doter d’une approche intégrée et d’améliorer sa résilience face aux crises futures.

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.notes:
Actuellement, aucun plan ou action précise n’est mis en œuvre concernant la diplomatie humanitaire fondée sur le Droit International Humanitaire, notamment en matière de réponse aux catastrophes. De plus, il n’existe pas de collaboration systématique avec le gouvernement pour :
• Aligner la législation nationale sur la Loi-type relative à la facilitation et réglementation des opérations internationales de secours et d’assistance au relèvement initial.
• Promouvoir l’adhésion au Règlement Sanitaire International (RSI) en cas de catastrophe.
Bien que la Société Nationale (SN) bénéficie d’exonérations douanières sur la base de documents officiels, elle demeure soumise au paiement de la TVA sur les achats locaux. Un plaidoyer est en cours pour obtenir une exonération totale, y compris pour la TVA, afin de réduire les coûts et d’optimiser les interventions humanitaires.
Par ailleurs, il n’existe actuellement ni points focaux en IDRL ni en DIH, au sein de la SN ou des structures étatiques. Bien qu’une commission des droits de l’homme soit en place, elle ne couvre pas spécifiquement le DIH. Le Comité International de la Croix-Rouge (CICR) a initié des efforts pour combler cette lacune, mais les résultats concrets se font encore attendre.
Implications :
• L’absence d’alignement des législations nationales freine la coordination entre les acteurs humanitaires et les autorités publiques, entraînant des délais dans les interventions.
• Le maintien de la TVA sur les achats locaux constitue une contrainte budgétaire qui pourrait être allégée grâce à une exonération totale.
• L’absence de points focaux en IDRL et DIH limite les capacités de la SN à plaider efficacement pour des réformes législatives et à répondre aux obligations internationales.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_responses.notes:
La Société Nationale (SN) s’appuie sur plusieurs outils pour répondre aux catastrophes, notamment :
• Une SOP pour la distribution des kits (2017).
• Un plan de contingence pour les accidents de la route (2017).
• Un plan de contingence pour les inondations (2021), ciblant 2 500 personnes.
• Un plan de contingence pour les incendies (2017), visant 2 400 personnes.
• Un plan de contingence pour les mouvements de population (2017), prévoyant l’accueil de 300 personnes par jour sur six mois.
• Un Protocole d’Action Précoce (PAP) 2022-2024, couvrant 2 500 personnes.
Ces outils soutiennent des interventions conformes aux normes Sphère dans certaines activités, avec des enquêtes PDM (Post-Distribution Monitoring) menées après les distributions. Toutefois, plusieurs lacunes importantes subsistent.
Bien que des approches CEA (Engagement Communautaire et Redevabilité) et PGI (Protection, Genre et Inclusion) soient intégrées, il n’existe pas de procédures claires ou de politiques formalisées pour garantir la participation active des communautés dans la planification, la mise en œuvre et le suivi des interventions.
Actuellement, les mécanismes pour recueillir et traiter les retours, y compris les feedbacks sensibles et les préoccupations des bénéficiaires, sont sous-développés.
Bien qu’une formation PSEA ait été réalisée dans le cadre de l’opération MDRDJ005, aucun mécanisme structuré et systématique n’est en place pour garantir une prévention et une réponse efficaces aux abus/exploitations sexuels.
Malgré la formation des volontaires, l’application des normes PGI n’est pas suffisamment documentée, ce qui rend difficile l’évaluation de l’impact des mesures de protection et d’inclusion.
Implications :
L’absence d’implication systématique des populations dans les processus de décision peut entraîner une inadéquation entre l’aide fournie et les besoins réels des bénéficiaires. Cela risque de réduire l’efficacité et l’impact positif des interventions. 
Les mécanismes actuels de gestion des retours ne permettent pas de recueillir efficacement les préoccupations des communautés, ce qui peut nuire à la confiance des bénéficiaires envers la SN.
Sans des procédures solides pour prévenir les abus/exploitations sexuels et inclure les groupes marginalisés, certaines interventions pourraient involontairement exposer les populations vulnérables à des risques supplémentaires.

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_responses.epi_considerations: Au cours des cinq prochaines années, notre objectif est de travailler avec les communautés pour renforcer leur capacité à gérer les problèmes de santé primaires et les épidémies.(Paln de contingence)
component_responses.notes:
La Société Nationale du Croissant-Rouge de Djibouti (CRD) est reconnue comme société de secours volontaire et auxiliaire des pouvoirs publics. Elle agit conformément à l'article 26 de la Première Convention de Genève et à l’Ordonnance n° 77-042/PR. 
Mission : Collaborer avec les communautés pour réduire leur vulnérabilité et répondre efficacement aux catastrophes. 
Vision 2022-2026 : Construire une société où chaque individu peut répondre à ses besoins fondamentaux et vivre avec dignité. 
En pratique, la SN complète les efforts du gouvernement en matière de santé, notamment pour la gestion des épidémies et des catastrophes. Activités guidées par les Principes Fondamentaux. 
Les branches définissent des rôles différents auprès des autorités locales en se basant sur les orientation su siège.  
Les politiques, plan stratégique… ne reflètent pas de manière claire le rôle de la SN en épidémies. 
Implications : L’absence d’un accord-cadre clair et d’une structure de tutelle pour le Croissant-Rouge de Djibouti (CRD) limite sa visibilité, sa reconnaissance, et la compréhension de sa mission. Cette situation complique l’accès à l’information, retarde les réponses d’urgence, et est aggravée par l’absence de procédures validées avec les autorités.

Pas d’orientations concernant la gestion des urgences de santé publique
component_responses.notes:
Actuellement, la Société Nationale ne dispose pas d’une stratégie intégrée ni d’orientations spécifiques pour la gestion des risques de catastrophes, y compris les risques liés à la santé publique et les interventions associées. Par ailleurs, aucun pourcentage précis de la population affectée à soutenir n’a été défini. Toutefois, le plan de contingence national prévoit un objectif d’assistance à 5 000 familles.
Implications :
L’absence d’une stratégie nationale structurée freine la collaboration entre les différents secteurs et services techniques, compromettant l’élaboration de plans de préparation et d’intervention intégrés et cohérents.
Les branches locales ne disposent pas de directives opérationnelles claires ni d’objectifs prédéfinis pour planifier leurs actions. Cela affecte la cohérence et l’efficacité des interventions sur le terrain, notamment en situation d’urgence.
En l’absence d’un consensus préalable sur les objectifs opérationnels et le nombre de bénéficiaires à couvrir, la mobilisation des fonds devient plus lente. Une fois la catastrophe survenue, le temps requis pour définir les interventions prioritaires et identifier la population cible retarde significativement la réponse humanitaire.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_responses.epi_considerations: Une collaboration existe entre la CRD et le ministere mais à travers l'UNICEF qui accompagne la SN dans les acatvites lies à la santé. Il sera necessaire de faire un plaidoyer pour renforcer le lien entre les deux structures
component_responses.notes:
La Société Nationale (SN) dispose des opportunités pour répondre à divers risques grâce à l’existence d’une certaine synergie d’action grâce à la collaboration entre les comités locaux et les autorités locales, ainsi qu’au travail conjoint de la coordination WASH avec le ministère de la Santé sur les épidémies. Cependant, des lacunes persistent, notamment l’absence de diagnostics clairs pour identifier les difficultés rencontrées par la SN, ainsi que le manque d’évaluations des risques au niveau communautaire et de cartes multi-aléas actualisées au niveau des comités locaux. La SN peut collecter des données via ses volontaires, mais elle nécessite un renforcement significatif de ses capacités d’analyse. Le processus d’Évaluation de la Vulnérabilité et des Capacités (EVC), actuellement en cours avec le soutien de la IFRC, constitue une étape importante, mais il n’existe pas encore de mécanismes pour ventiler et exploiter efficacement les données collectées. Par ailleurs, bien que la collaboration avec le ministère de la Santé soit facilitée par l’UNICEF pour des activités liées à la santé, il reste crucial de renforcer le lien direct entre la SN et les structures étatiques par le biais d’un plaidoyer soutenu.
Implications :
L’absence de diagnostics précis et d’outils analytiques freine une compréhension approfondie des défis rencontrés par la SN et entrave l’efficacité de ses interventions. L’absence de cartes multi-aléas et d’évaluations communautaires des risques limite la planification stratégique et la priorisation des actions. Par ailleurs, un manque de reconnaissance institutionnelle et de collaboration directe avec les autorités publiques réduit le soutien apporté à la SN, compromettant ainsi la durabilité de ses interventions.

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_responses.notes:
La Société Nationale (SN) dispose d’un plan de contingence global intégrant des scénarios sectoriels avec des indicateurs spécifiques pour les abris, la sécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle d’urgence (SAME), le WASH (eau, assainissement et hygiène) et la santé. Ce plan est aligné sur les stratégies des pouvoirs publics, facilitant une coordination générale des réponses aux crises. Toutefois, la SN n’a pas encore élaboré de scénarios humanitaires spécifiques pour chaque zone à risque élevé, ce qui limite l’adaptation des interventions aux particularités des contextes locaux. De plus, les scénarios actuels et les plans de contingence, bien que détaillés au niveau central, ne sont pas systématiquement déclinés au niveau des comités locaux. Cela réduit leur efficacité opérationnelle, particulièrement dans les zones éloignées ou présentant des besoins spécifiques. Par ailleurs, les scénarios ne prennent pas en compte les défis liés à l’acceptation, la sécurité et l’accès pendant les opérations humanitaires, éléments pourtant cruciaux pour garantir une réponse efficace en milieu complexe. Un Protocole d’Action Précoce (PAP) inondation est en place pour 2022-2024, avec un déclencheur permettant de répondre aux besoins de 2 500 personnes, mais son application reste limitée
Implications :
L’absence de scénarios spécifiques et de déclinaisons locales limite la capacité de la SN à répondre rapidement et efficacement aux crises dans des contextes variés. Cette lacune réduit l’adaptabilité des interventions et compromet leur pertinence au niveau communautaire. De plus, l’omission des problématiques d’acceptation, de sécurité et d’accès dans les scénarios peut entraîner des retards dans les opérations et exposer les équipes humanitaires à des risques accrus. Enfin, la coordination locale avec les comités reste insuffisante, ce qui nuit à l’efficacité de la réponse sur le terrain.

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_responses.epi_considerations: Les procédures sont définies, mais elles nécessitent des améliorations pour mieux tenir compte des réalités actuelles, afin d'assurer une mise en œuvre plus adaptée et efficace.
component_responses.notes:
La Société Nationale ne dispose actuellement ni d’un personnel dédié à la gestion des risques ni d’un point focal spécifiquement chargé des questions de sécurité. Bien que le code de conduite et le manuel du personnel soient disponibles, leur mise en œuvre n’est pas soutenue par une unité ou une fonction dédiée à la gestion des risques, tant au niveau national que local. Les procédures existantes, bien que définies, nécessitent des améliorations pour mieux refléter les réalités actuelles et garantir une mise en œuvre plus adaptée et efficace.
Implications :
L’absence d’une structure et de ressources dédiées à la gestion des risques et à la sécurité fragilise les capacités de la Société Nationale à anticiper et répondre aux menaces potentielles. Cela peut exposer le personnel, les volontaires et les bénéficiaires à des risques évitables, tout en affectant la continuité des opérations humanitaires en cas de crise. De plus, sans un point focal ou une unité responsable, les efforts pour harmoniser et améliorer les pratiques existantes restent limités, compromettant ainsi la sécurité globale de l’organisation.

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_responses.epi_considerations: la SN ne dispose pas d'un departement santé mais il existe une coordination des acation entre le WASH et la DM
component_responses.notes:
La Société Nationale (SN) dispose d’un responsable chargé de la gestion globale des catastrophes, bien qu’il n’y ait pas de spécification particulière sur la préparation aux catastrophes. Aucune documentation ne rapporte actuellement les lacunes en matière de préparation, ce qui complique l’identification des points faibles dans ce domaine. Cependant, la SN dispose d’une stratégie globale de mobilisation des ressources, ce qui lui permet d’avoir un cadre pour obtenir les fonds nécessaires à ses interventions. Un des outils clés de la SN est le protocole d’action précoce pour les inondations (2022-2024), visant à répondre aux besoins de 2 500 personnes, et facilitant ainsi le déclenchement rapide des réponses en cas de catastrophe. En ce qui concerne la santé, bien que la SN ne dispose pas d’un département santé spécifique, une coordination efficace existe entre les départements WASH (eau, hygiène et assainissement) et DM (disasters management), permettant une collaboration pour une réponse intégrée.
Implications :
L'absence de spécification sur la préparation aux catastrophes et l'absence de documentation sur les lacunes en matière de préparation rendent difficile l’évaluation et l’amélioration continue des capacités de la SN pour se préparer efficacement aux crises.
Bien que la mobilisation des ressources soit bien encadrée, le manque de détails sur la préparation pourrait retarder la réactivité de la SN lorsqu'une crise survient.
La coordination entre WASH et DM est un point positif, mais l'absence de département santé distinct pourrait limiter la capacité à répondre de manière cohérente aux besoins en santé publique dans les interventions.

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.epi_considerations: la SN disposent d'un centre de sante qui fonctionnet uniquement au heurs de service
component_responses.notes:
Actuellement, la Société Nationale (SN) ne dispose pas de plan de continuité du travail, ce qui limite sa capacité à assurer un fonctionnement ininterrompu en cas de crise. Bien que la SN dispose de plusieurs outils opérationnels, dont le Mécanisme de Réponse aux Urgences (DREF), d'autres instruments de gestion des catastrophes sont utilisés, mais leur coordination reste insuffisante.
Implications :
L’absence de plan de continuité du travail expose la SN à des interruptions de service pendant les crises, empêchant une réponse rapide et constante.
L'absence de coordination claire entre les différents outils opérationnels pourrait entraîner des chevauchements ou des lacunes dans les interventions, limitant l’efficacité globale des réponses.
Le fonctionnement du centre de santé uniquement pendant les heures de service empêche une prise en charge optimale des populations, notamment en cas d’urgence en dehors de ces horaires.

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_responses.epi_considerations: Le SOP ne tiens pas compte des roles et responsabilites de la SN
component_responses.notes:
La Société Nationale (SN) dispose d'un SOP (Procédure Opérationnelle Standard) datant de 2018, qui nécessite une révision complète afin de tenir compte des évolutions des pratiques et des défis actuels. Actuellement, ce SOP est uniquement diffusé au niveau du siège, ce qui limite son accessibilité et son application à l’échelle des branches et des communautés. Les Procédures Opérationnelles Standard (POS) en place décrivent les grands rôles et responsabilités des intervenants à différents niveaux (stratégique, opérationnel, management), mais elles restent trop générales et nécessitent des améliorations substantielles.
Les SOP, bien qu'elles définissent des procédures pour certaines phases d'intervention, ne couvrent pas toutes les étapes nécessaires à une réponse complète. De plus, elles ne prennent pas en compte un organigramme précis, ce qui rend difficile une coordination fluide et claire des rôles et responsabilités au sein de la SN. Le SOP ne tient pas compte non plus des rôles et responsabilités de la SN elle-même dans son ensemble, ce qui crée des zones d’ombre dans la gestion de la réponse.
Implications :
L'absence d’une SOP mise à jour et d’une version complète des POS limite la capacité de la SN à répondre de manière cohérente et efficace aux catastrophes. Les rôles mal définis et la dispersion des responsabilités nuisent à la coordination des interventions.
L'absence d'un organigramme et de procédures précises pour toutes les phases d’intervention peut entraîner des chevauchements de responsabilités et des retards dans la mise en œuvre des actions.
Le SOP obsolète ne reflète pas les évolutions récentes des risques, des défis logistiques et des besoins des populations, ce qui compromet l’adaptation des réponses humanitaires.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_responses.notes:
Actuellement, la Croissant-Rouge de Djibouti (CRD) ne dispose pas d’un plan d’intervention global, bien que plusieurs documents spécifiques soutiennent les interventions en cas de catastrophe. Parmi ces outils, on trouve une Procédure Opérationnelle Standard (SOP) pour la distribution des kits, datée de 2017, ainsi que des plans de contingence pour les accidents de la route (2017), les inondations (2021, visant à assister 2 500 personnes), les incendies (2017, ciblant 2 400 personnes), et les mouvements de population (2017, prévoyant l’accueil de 300 personnes par jour pendant six mois). En outre, un protocole d’action précoce couvrant la période 2022-2024 a été élaboré, visant à répondre aux besoins de 2 500 personnes.
Malgré ces documents, l'absence d’un plan d’intervention centralisé entraîne des lacunes en termes de cohérence et de coordination des actions. Cela limite la capacité de la CRD à répondre de manière rapide et efficace aux catastrophes, en particulier lorsque des événements multiples ou complexes surviennent simultanément. De plus, l'absence de stratégie unifiée complique l’harmonisation des interventions entre les différents secteurs, rendant difficile la gestion optimale des ressources et la priorisation des actions.
Implications :
L’absence de plan d’intervention global entraîne une coordination limitée entre les différentes interventions et un manque de synergie entre les acteurs de terrain. Cela compromet l’efficacité et la rapidité de la réponse face aux catastrophes.
L'absence de plan d’intervention centralisé pourrait engendrer une gestion inefficace des ressources, ce qui pourrait ralentir la prise en charge des besoins urgents des communautés affectées.
Sans un cadre unifié et flexible, la CRD pourrait rencontrer des difficultés pour ajuster ses interventions en fonction de l’évolution des besoins sur le terrain, limitant ainsi son efficacité opérationnelle

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes:
Les membres clés de la CRD ne sont pas familiers avec les accords pré-catastrophes, limitant leur réactivité. 
La CRD a un accord avec l’UNICEF pour la gestion des épidémies, notamment le choléra. 
Aucun accord formel n’existe avec les autorités étatiques, mais le statut d’organisation auxiliaire facilite l'importation de biens et l’assistance en cas de crise.
Des partenariats informels peuvent être activés en fonction des besoins.
Lors de l’opération MDRDJ005, un programme de CASH a été mis en œuvre, montrant la capacité de la CRD à déployer une réponse financière.
Implications: 
L'absence de familiarité du personnel avec les accords pré-crises limite la réactivité de la CRD. 
L'absence d'accords formels avec les autorités et fournisseurs crée des incertitudes logistiques et administratives. 
L'absence de partenariats formels avec les fournisseurs peut entraîner des retards d'approvisionnement, mais la mise en œuvre réussie du programme CASH montre la capacité d'adaptation de la CRD et la nécessité de structurer ces partenariats.

component_responses.epi_considerations: N'existe pas
component_responses.notes:
Une évaluation des besoins des communautés est effectuée avant les opérations, comme pour le MDRDJ005. 
Des sensibilisations ont lieu dans certaines préfectures, mais manquent de moyens.
Il n'y a pas de système d'alerte précoce clair ni de CDRT. 
Des améliorations sont nécessaires sur les thématiques abordées et la couverture des informations utilisées dans les opérations.
Implications:
L'absence de moyens suffisants pour la sensibilisation et des systèmes d'alerte précoce complique la réponse aux urgences. 
Les communautés risquent de ne pas être suffisamment préparées, entraînant une gestion des risques inefficace.
L'absence de CDRT limite la mobilisation locale et la prise de décision rapide. 
Il est essentiel d'améliorer la couverture des thématiques et renforcer les systèmes d'information pour une meilleure gestion des risques.

component_responses.epi_considerations: inexitance du departement santé et d'un Staff
component_responses.notes:
L'évaluation d'urgence se concentre principalement sur le WASH, sans inclure les besoins liés à la santé.
Le responsable communication est formé sur le CEA et utilise régulièrement les outils dans les opérations.
La CRD gère la désinfection des milieux contaminés, notamment en cas de choléra.
La SN dispose d'EPI, mais les formations de recyclage sont seulement effectuées pendant les opérations.
Il n'y a pas de rôle défini dans les cas d'isolement, ni de département santé ou de personnel dédié.
Implications: 
L'application sporadique des outils CEA limite l'intégration durable de l'engagement communautaire dans la stratégie de la SN.
L'absence de département santé et de personnel qualifié réduit la gestion efficace des crises sanitaires, notamment le choléra.
Le recyclage des EPI uniquement pendant les opérations peut entraîner des lacunes dans la préparation.
La santé manque de visibilité et de rôle clair au niveau régional, limitant l'impact local.
L'absence de protocoles pour l'isolement des cas nuit à la gestion des infections et à la prévention de leur propagation

component_responses.epi_considerations: la SN dispose pas de docuemnt à ce propos
component_responses.notes:
Les premiers secours sont intégrés au plan stratégique de la CRB, mais un manque criant de formateurs limite les capacités d’intervention. 
Une formation des formateurs est organisée pour renforcer les compétences internes en réponse d’urgence. 
La SN ne dispose pas de politiques ou de procédures pour la prévention et le contrôle des infections lors de flambées de maladies infectieuses.
Implications :
L'absence de formateurs suffisants limite la capacité de la SN à dispenser des formations de premiers secours à grande échelle, ce qui réduit le nombre de personnes formées et prêtes à intervenir lors de catastrophes.
L'absence de documents opérationnels sur la formation des formateurs empêche la mise en place d'un cadre clair et cohérent pour le développement et le suivi de ces formations, affectant ainsi la pérennité du programme.
Le manque de formateurs compétents entraîne des difficultés à déployer rapidement des équipes de secours formées, ralentissant ainsi la réponse en cas de catastrophe.

L'évaluation d'urgence se concentre principalement sur le WASH, sans inclure les besoins liés à la santé.
Le responsable communication est formé sur le CEA et utilise régulièrement les outils dans les opérations.
La CRD gère la désinfection des milieux contaminés, notamment en cas de choléra.
La SN dispose d'EPI, mais les formations de recyclage sont seulement effectuées pendant les opérations.
Il n'y a pas de rôle défini dans les cas d'isolement, ni de département santé ou de personnel dédié.
Implications: 
L'application sporadique des outils CEA limite l'intégration durable de l'engagement communautaire dans la stratégie de la SN.
L'absence de département santé et de personnel qualifié réduit la gestion efficace des crises sanitaires, notamment le choléra.
Le recyclage des EPI uniquement pendant les opérations peut entraîner des lacunes dans la préparation.
La santé manque de visibilité et de rôle clair au niveau régional, limitant l'impact local.
L'absence de protocoles pour l'isolement des cas nuit à la gestion des infections et à la prévention de leur propagation.

component_details.title: MANAGEMENT OF DEAD BODIES TO FACILITATE THEIR IDENTIFICATION

component_responses.notes:
Le personnel et les volontaires disposent des compétences nécessaires pour offrir des services de RLF de qualité. 
Des procédures et des accords relatifs aux activités de RLF sont établis en collaboration avec le CICR.
Implications:
Le personnel et les volontaires sont formés pour offrir des services RLF de qualité. 
Des procédures et accords avec le CICR encadrent les activités.  
L'implication des parties prenantes renforce la coordination et l'efficacité.

component_details.title: CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL, RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR (CBRN) EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS
Mapping of NS capacities
component_details.description: A list of the NS capacities including HR (staff, response teams and volunteers) and equipment that are available for disaster/crisis response. Teams could include branch and national response teams. This should be defined by technical speciality where relevant.

component_responses.notes:
De nombreux domaines au sein de la Société Nationale (SN) manquent de personnel dédié, soulignant l'urgence de recruter pour renforcer les capacités et répondre aux besoins opérationnels.
Des formations pour les volontaires sont organisées, mais leur renforcement reste nécessaire.
Une base de données existe pour le matériel et les équipements, tandis que celle des volontaires est encore gérée manuellement.
L'insuffisance de volontaires et de personnel limite la capacité de la SN à répondre efficacement aux besoins humanitaires et à mettre en œuvre ses activités. 
Implication: 
L’insuffisance de personnel et de volontaires compromet la capacité d’intervention rapide et efficace face aux crises, augmentant les risques pour les populations affectées.
L’absence de systèmes modernes pour gérer les données des volontaires ralentit leur mobilisation et empêche une planification stratégique adéquate.
Sans renforcement des ressources humaines, les efforts de formation et de coordination risquent de demeurer inefficaces, compromettant la crédibilité et la réactivité de la SN.

component_details.title: Early Action Mechanisms
component_details.description: Designed to translate warnings into anticipatory actions to help reduce the impact of specific disaster or crisis events. They focus on consolidating available forecasting information and putting procedures in place to ensure that a NS can act ahead of any disaster/crisis. Forecast-based financing is included within the scope of this area.

component_responses.notes:
L'utilisation de mégaphones est un moyen efficace pour diffuser des informations auprès des communautés. De plus, des connaissances internes existent au sein des branches régionales, bien qu'elles nécessitent un renforcement pour améliorer la communication et la coordination locales.  
La Société Nationale (SN) fait face à une insuffisance de volontaires et de personnel, ce qui limite sa capacité à répondre efficacement aux besoins humanitaires et à assurer la mise en œuvre de ses activités.  
Les branches disposent de réseaux qui nécessitent cependant une mobilisation accrue des volontaires.
Implications:
Le manque de personnel et de volontaires compromet la capacité à répondre rapidement aux crises, augmentant le nombre de victimes et les impacts négatifs sur les communautés affectées.
L'absence de systèmes adéquats de gestion des données des volontaires ralentit leur mobilisation et empêche une utilisation optimale des ressources humaines disponibles, réduisant l'efficacité des interventions.
Le manque de ressources humaines et de formation pourrait nuire à la réputation et à l'efficacité de la SN, compromettant ainsi sa capacité à répondre de manière crédible et rapide aux besoins urgents.

component_details.title: Cash Based Intervention (CBI)
component_details.description: An effective and flexible way, including all forms of cash and voucher-based assistance, to support people affected by emergencies, maintaining their dignity and choice, while fostering local economies.
