component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_details.title: Cooperation with private sector
component_details.description: Mechanism that allows cooperation with private sector that often plays a strong role in response, particularly if there is impact on their staff and businesses. There is often a willingness to donate goods and services. Advance agreements help to expedite response actions.

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_responses.notes: The organization ensures affected populations are involved in all stages of the response to meet their needs. It has trained CEA focal points, with 18 trained in August 2023. A comprehensive CEA plan is implemented, integrated into strategic plans, and includes standard procedures. Feedback and complaints mechanisms are in place but need strengthening. The organization has a Protection for Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) policy and adheres to various international standards for gender, disability, and violence prevention. Procedures and policies support protection services, and the "do no harm" principle is followed. Indicators for gender, disability, and diversity are used in all project stages.

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_responses.notes: The NS  is well established through an act of parliament (ZRCS Act). Its mandate is further clarified under the CPU Act.

component_details.title: DRM Strategy
component_details.description: An outline of the overall goal that the NS seeks to achieve in its disaster and crisis response operations. The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

component_responses.notes: NS does not have a standalone DRM strategy, but has a   strategic plan which addresses key benchmarks under the DM strategy

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_responses.notes: The organization has a Disaster Risk Management (DRM) policy adopted in 2022, though it requires revision. This policy incorporates guiding principles and values from the Red Cross and Red Crescent (RCRC) fundamental principles, particularly in sections 8 and 9, ensuring a principled approach to decision-making in responses. It also includes comprehensive technical and support services, covering sectors such as water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH). Moreover, the DRM policy is effectively integrated into response plans and procedures, and is adhered to by both staff and volunteers.

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: The organization has an IDRL humanitarian diplomacy plan based on the IFRC's IDRL Checklist, although relevant legal facilities in national legislation are not fully identified. Management understands public health laws, including data sharing and quarantine. While staff are trained in IDRL and IHL, additional training is necessary. The organization has the capacity to advocate for disaster relief legislation but has not prioritized this effort. IDRL lessons from response operations are tracked to improve future humanitarian diplomacy.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: The National Society is urged to bolster its Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) to improve its ability to monitor environmental conditions and forecast independently, lessening dependence on the meteorological department. It is recommended that the EOC implement a toll-free hotline to streamline volunteer reporting of emergencies and foster better community engagement. Furthermore, there is a notable absence of a Disaster Management library or a comprehensive repository for crucial Red Cross assessments, disaster response data, and insights gained from previous incidents. To address these gaps, it is essential to strengthen the EOC's capabilities and establish a functional repository to enhance disaster risk management efforts comprehensively.

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_responses.notes: The National Society's scenario planning assessment reveals a robust multi-sectoral approach, with well-developed humanitarian scenarios and closely aligned contingency plans with public authorities. Response strategies involve local branches, addressing challenges in acceptance, security, and access during operations. Clear triggers for activation are integrated, especially for prolonged crises, alongside regional coordination for epidemics and pandemics. Annual reviews ensure readiness, highlighting a need for enhanced coordination with government and other sectors to strengthen overall disaster management efforts. Areas for improvement include bolstering coordination mechanisms and ensuring continuous engagement to optimize disaster response effectiveness.

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_responses.notes: All provinces and units maintain current risk mapping profiles. The National Society prioritizes high-threat risks where communities lack sufficient capacity to respond independently, necessitating external support.

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_responses.notes: The National Society primarily relies on DREF funds for disaster response, lacking additional funding to initiate disaster preparedness activities and consistently train DCPU and PCPU members in readiness for effective responses.

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: The National Society possesses an up-to-date and approved business continuity plan developed during the Covid-19 era in 2021. However, there is a significant need to disseminate this plan effectively among staff and volunteers. Additionally, the organization has an approved procedure to communicate with donors for reallocating funds to address unexpected or emerging needs, supported by crisis modifier funds available for disaster response.

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_responses.notes:
The NS has Emergency Response SOPs, but they need to be updated. 
SOPs needs to be disseminated.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_responses.notes: The National Society maintains an up-to-date and approved multi-sectoral response plan that integrates gender, age, disability, and diversity considerations, alongside community capacities. The plan involves inputs from community members, staff, volunteers, governance, and technical experts from IFRC where applicable. It adheres to Principles and Rules, DRM policies, and the Red Cross's fundamental principles. The plan also aligns with IFRC global standards and addresses secondary disasters while acknowledging actions of other responders. It is regularly updated with lessons learned from exercises and real-time events, with processes in place for adaptation to evolving contexts and needs.

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: Overall, the National Society (NS) effectively conducts pre-disaster meetings with key stakeholders at least once a year and has formalized coordination and management arrangements with relevant local and national actors. However, there is a need to disseminate information on pre-disaster agreements among key staff and operationalize crisis agreements more effectively. Capacity mapping of Movement partners is currently not up to date, and agreements with contractors, suppliers, and money transfer providers still need to be formalized. Additionally, NS lacks agreements with social protection systems to facilitate access to databases of vulnerable populations. Development of codes of conduct and formal agreements with suppliers are also outstanding tasks to strengthen disaster preparedness efforts.

The national society is performing well in community-based disaster preparedness and risk reduction, with active community involvement and established early warning systems. However, there are inconsistencies in public education implementation, limited reach of early warning systems, and inadequate training and sustainability of Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs). To enhance effectiveness, it is recommended to standardize and expand awareness programs, extend early warning systems to all areas, and develop comprehensive training and resource mobilization strategies for CDRTs. Strengthening the integration of Protection, Gender, and Inclusion (PGI) principles across all activities is also essential.

The national society effectively integrates evacuation into its response strategy, playing a crucial role in moving people to safety in various scenarios and high-risk areas. However, there is a need for enhanced coordination, dissemination of evacuation plans, and the development of clear evacuation notes. Recommendations include establishing robust coordination mechanisms, conducting regular evacuation drills, creating comprehensive evacuation guides, and engaging communities in high-risk areas. Strengthening partnerships with emergency services and ensuring adequate resource allocation are also critical for improving evacuation efficiency.

The national society has made significant progress in health emergency preparedness, with established multi-sectoral response plans, community engagement mechanisms, and procedures for managing rumours. However, there are critical gaps in infection prevention and control protocols, personal protection equipment management, and roles during isolation and quarantine scenarios. To enhance overall effectiveness, it is recommended to develop systematic procedures for community engagement, strengthen IPC protocols, ensure adequate PPE and training, and clearly define roles during isolation and quarantine periods. Collaboration with public authorities and regular training will also be crucial for improving response capabilities.

The national society effectively integrates First Aid into its response strategy and includes First Aid training as part of its broader disaster management efforts. However, the absence of a comprehensive First Aid strategy and a Community-Based Disaster Risk Reduction (CBDRR) strategy with Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) needs to be addressed. Additionally, although volunteers are well-trained, they lack the necessary First Aid kits for effective response. To improve, it is recommended to develop and integrate a detailed First Aid strategy, establish a CBDRR strategy with clear SOPs, ensure all volunteers are equipped with First Aid kits, and conduct regular practical simulations to enhance preparedness.

The national society demonstrates a strong commitment to addressing water and sanitation humanitarian consequences, with appropriate training, skills, and equipment for its response teams. The organization has effective partnerships and coordination mechanisms with WASH authorities and networks. However, there is a need for systematic development of SOPs for equipment procurement and continued prepositioning of WASH materials. To improve further, it is recommended to enhance training programs, develop comprehensive SOPs, and maintain robust coordination with WASH partners and networks.

The overall assessment indicates substantial gaps in the NS's food security capabilities, particularly in monitoring food security levels, training technical staff, and developing comprehensive action plans for food aid distribution. While there are strengths in coordination with other organizations and integrating food distribution in response strategies, significant improvements are needed in training for epidemics, urban food security programming, and climate & environmental considerations.

While some benchmarks, such as having an agreed standard NFI kit with clear SOPs and standard emergency shelter designs, are met, others, including mechanisms for consultation with the target population and pre-positioning of shelter supplies in high-risk areas, require attention.

component_details.title: MANAGEMENT OF DEAD BODIES TO FACILITATE THEIR IDENTIFICATION

component_responses.notes: NS does not do management of dead bodies

The Restoring Family Links (RFL) sub-component has achieved the benchmarks related to staff and volunteers providing quality RFL services, as well as having procedures and agreements with ICRC in place. However, there are notable gaps in addressing epidemics and urban contexts. While there were SOPs for COVID-19 during the outbreak, further development of plans and procedures for RFL in epidemics is necessary. Additionally, limited financial resources hinder the NS's ability to rapidly scale up services, including tracing and communications, in urban contexts. Integration of climate and environmental considerations also requires improvement to ensure comprehensive and effective RFL services.
The focus of the NS is on relief. There is less focus on long term support to recovery. The response materials for the NS focus on relief materials in the warehouse.

component_details.title: CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL, RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR (CBRN) EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS

component_responses.notes: This does not exist in the NS

Overall, there are areas where the Community Based Health & First Aid (CBHFA) sub-component is performing adequately, but there are also notable areas for improvement, particularly in standardizing training and engagement activities across all projects and ensuring that all benchmarks are consistently met.

component_details.title: Mapping of NS capacities
component_details.description: A list of the NS capacities including HR (staff, response teams and volunteers) and equipment that are available for disaster/crisis response. Teams could include branch and national response teams. This should be defined by technical speciality where relevant.

component_details.title: Early Action Mechanisms
component_details.description: Designed to translate warnings into anticipatory actions to help reduce the impact of specific disaster or crisis events. They focus on consolidating available forecasting information and putting procedures in place to ensure that a NS can act ahead of any disaster/crisis. Forecast-based financing is included within the scope of this area.

component_responses.notes: There are notable areas for improvement, particularly in utilizing new technologies for alerts, enhancing personnel availability for communication and early action, and strengthening local networks for community engagement.

component_details.title: Cash Based Intervention (CBI)
component_details.description: An effective and flexible way, including all forms of cash and voucher-based assistance, to support people affected by emergencies, maintaining their dignity and choice, while fostering local economies. Cash should also be mainstreamed into other sectors (including Relief, shelter, livelihoods) and services (Logistics, Finance, etc.)

component_responses.notes: The NS possesses relevant documents such as SOPs, preparedness plans, and HR resources (though limited), and actively engages in relevant activities. Additionally, the NS has successfully implemented CVA programs over the past three years. However, the NS lacks an up-to-date, approved CBI toolkit tailored to its specific contexts, including adaptation of CiE tools, establishment of a database, among other necessary components.

component_details.title: Emergency Needs Assessment
component_details.description: Assess the extent and impact of the damage caused by the disaster/crisis and the degree of vulnerability of the affected population. The first step in any emergency response, such an assessment will identify the needs that require external intervention and the gaps to be filled. It is a vital component of the programme-planning process.

component_responses.notes: While assessment templates are available within the NS, they are not consistently utilized across all branches, indicating a need for revision and validation. Furthermore, the multi-sector emergency team, referred to as the NDRT by the NS, requires training and additional members, as a significant portion of the team has departed from the NS.

component_details.title: Affected population selection
component_details.description: Identification and selection of target Affected population for interventions, using a pre-defined set of criteria based on need and vulnerability. This includes consideration of specific vulnerabilities such as disability, age and gender.

component_responses.notes: The NS effectively employs vulnerability indicators to clearly target beneficiaries. However, there is a pressing need to enhance the capacity of the response team, including a substantial requirement for training.

component_details.title: Emergency Operations Centre (EOC)
component_details.description: A central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions at a strategic level in an emergency situation. The common functions are to collect and analyze data; facilitate decision making that protects life and livelihoods; and disseminate those decisions to all concerned agencies and individuals. Generally located at the headquarter level of an organization.

component_responses.notes: The National Society (NS) has made significant progress in establishing a functional Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) with a formally appointed focal point, up-to-date SOPs, and defined strategic decision-making processes. However, there are critical areas needing improvement, particularly in training staff on SOPs, integrating sector procedures, clarifying roles, enhancing telecommunications infrastructure, equipping the EOC, and maintaining functional equipment. Addressing these gaps through targeted training, infrastructure development, procedural integration, and equipment procurement will strengthen the EOC's operational capacity and ensure efficient emergency response.

component_details.title: Information Management (IM)
component_details.description: Ability to manage information including requesting, receiving, analyzing and disseminating as per its procedures and partner requirements (IFRC and public authorities in particular). There should be a clear digital/paper trail that documents what, when and how the NS has acted and provides key information for the development of Emergency Plan of Actions. Includes IM between levels, between departments and Situational Reports, mapping, visualisation of data, GO platform (IFRC).

component_responses.notes: NS is performing highly on this component although it requires some improvement on independent data collection.

component_details.title: Testing and Learning
component_details.description: Drills and Simulations allow the organization to test, identify and learn from the results of these type of exercises and incorporate learning into future preparedness and response planning.

component_responses.notes: NS is performing well in this component, and needs to improve in cross-border collaboration.

component_details.title: Activation of regional and international support
component_details.description: Procedures for requesting and accepting regional and international support in operations, including triggering coordination mechanisms for funding, materials and human resources deployments.

component_responses.notes: NS should focus on developing SOPs procedures to request and incorporate regional and global support/teams (RDRTs, FACT, ERUs, HEOps) into their response system, including prior to imminent crisis/disaster.

component_details.title: Coordination with Movement
component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_details.title: Coordination with External Agencies and NGOs
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and collaboration with Non-Governmental Organization (NGO), both local and international NGOs, civil society organizations (CSOs) and United Nations agencies in country.

component_details.title: Civil Military Relations
component_details.description: Dialogue and interaction with military actors, essential to protect and promote humanitarian principles, avoid competition, minimize inconsistency and, when appropriate, pursue common goals.

component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_responses.notes: The NS has a good communications structure but need to enhance Communications in Emergencies (CiE) and recognize the importance and potential risks if CiE protocols are not standardized. This includes identifying and training key spokespersons for the NS as well as ensuring staff and volunteers take care in communicating, even as individuals, in social media.

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_details.title: DRM Strategy
component_details.description: An outline of the overall goal that the NS seeks to achieve in its disaster and crisis response operations. The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

component_responses.notes:
• DRM Strategy & Alignment: IRCS does not yet have a dedicated Disaster Risk Management (DRM) strategy, though the 2024 NS strategy establishes emergency response as a key pillar. While the government maintains a national risk registry, IRCS has not reviewed it for relevance. There is clear recognition that a written framework is needed, as response and preparedness cannot depend on individuals.
• Review & Dissemination: Without a stand-alone DRM strategy, there is no structured process for review, integration into response planning, or systematic dissemination to staff and volunteers. The new strategy offers momentum to address this gap and strengthen organizational preparedness.
• Comprehensiveness & Technical Engagement: Engagement with technical sectors and support services remains ad hoc and personality driven. Consolidating knowledge and good practices into institutional systems is now seen as a priority to ensure more consistent and comprehensive responses.

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_responses.notes:
• DRM Policy & Principles: IRCS does not have its own Disaster Risk Management (DRM) policy and has not formally adopted the IFRC policy. As a result, there are no agreed guiding principles or values to frame decision-making on response approaches and actions.
• Inclusiveness & Sector Engagement: In the absence of a policy, inclusiveness and engagement with relevant sectors and services are not formally articulated, limiting opportunities for a coordinated and comprehensive response.
• Integration & Adherence: The lack of a DRM policy also means there is no integration into response plans or procedures, and no common framework for staff and volunteers to follow. Establishing such a policy will be critical for coherence, accountability, and alignment with strategic objectives.

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.notes:
• IDRL Planning & Legal Facilities: IRCS does not have an IDRL humanitarian diplomacy plan, with efforts instead focused on IHL. While the IFRC IDRL policy is informally followed, there is no formal adoption or systematic approach. Ireland currently has no legislation on IDRL, and the NS has not identified relevant legal facilities or exemptions. The 2012 amendment of the RC Act has not been fully reviewed for entitlements, though advocacy attempts have opened some dialogue.
• Capacity & Training: IDRL knowledge is limited to the technical focal point and has not been disseminated across the organization. There is no designated IDRL focal point for emergencies, and capacity remains basic. In contrast, IHL has a clear focal point, with structured trainings, including specialized modules (e.g., CBRN) planned from 2025. Expertise on IDRL is accessed mainly through academic partners.
• Advocacy & Learning: IDRL has not been prioritized. The NS is not advocating for adoption of the Model Act or testing lessons, though future plans are under consideration.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_responses.notes:
• Community Engagement & Accountability: IRCS has some mechanisms to engage affected populations, particularly through migration programs, but approaches remain inconsistent. Feedback processes exist, though not systematically applied—for example, the closure of the Ukraine HUB was not preceded by consultation with the community. Safeguarding is in place, but there is no streamlined CEA framework or trained focal points at HQ or branches. A CEA plan, templates, and SOPs are not yet developed. A new role under recruitment will have CEA as one of its responsibilities, which may strengthen future practice.
• Feedback & Complaints: Mechanisms exist, including a complaint module on the website, a safeguarding helpline, and an external appeal board. However, local-level processes are complex, not widely promoted, and cannot be considered accessible.
• Protection, Standards & Do No Harm: A PSEA policy is drafted and pending approval, while safeguarding training is mandatory every three years. Sphere standards, do-no-harm, and PGI minimum standards are not systematically applied, though policies for children and elderly are strong.

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_responses.notes:
• Auxiliary Role & Mandate: IRCS’s mandate is firmly established through two acts, including the 1939 law, and reinforced in the national emergency framework. Its auxiliary role is clear, with activation by national stakeholders in major emergencies and capacity for independent local response. The main challenge remains translating this legal clarity into consistent operational practice.
• Alignment with Principles & Dissemination: The mandate aligns with the Fundamental Principles, especially independence, though public perception risks remain, as seen during the Ukraine crisis. Policies and strategies reflect the mandate, but dissemination is uneven. Staff training is structured, yet local branches and volunteers require stronger tools to ensure consistent understanding at all levels.
• IHL & Humanitarian Diplomacy: Promotion of IHL has expanded with a comprehensive strategy, dedicated personnel, and strong youth engagement. While government recognition is still limited, visibility and humanitarian diplomacy capacity are steadily increasing.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_responses.notes:
• Risk Monitoring & Early Warning: IRCS does not have a formal risk monitoring system or designated focal point. Monitoring occurs informally, with some units maintaining links to local authorities that track hazards. There is no structured early warning system, no thresholds established, and no mechanisms to communicate or activate early action.
• Data Collection & Risk Analysis: The NS does not currently have capacity to systematically collect or analyse primary and secondary data on political, social, or economic trends. Multi-hazard risk analysis and maps are not updated or shared with branches, and community-level contributions to mapping or VCAs are absent. Risk assessments also do not incorporate analysis of community connectors, dividers, or diversity-related vulnerabilities.
• Cross-Border Coordination: Gaps, barriers, and risks to NS acceptance, security, and access have not been identified. Cross-border risk monitoring and coordination remain informal, with some ad hoc collaboration seen in 2020 but no formal mechanisms in place.

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_responses.notes:
• Scenario Analysis & Contingency Planning: IRCS does not have a systematic process for scenario analysis across sectors such as health, livelihoods, and protection. Limited work has been done in migration, but broader multi-sectoral approaches are absent. Humanitarian scenarios for high-risk areas have not been developed, and contingency plans are not aligned with public authorities.
• Response Strategies & Operational Challenges: There are no response strategies linked to scenarios, and branches are not engaged in shaping strategies that would affect their areas. Scenarios also do not identify challenges related to NS acceptance, security, or access during operations, leaving critical gaps in preparedness.
• Triggers, Regional Coordination & Review: Contingency plans do not include triggers for activation, nor do they address slow-onset or protracted crises. Regional coordination mechanisms with neighbouring countries are not in place, despite a strong appetite for such arrangements. Contingency plans for high-risk scenarios are neither developed nor reviewed annually.

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_responses.notes:
• Risk Management Systems & Processes: Responsibility for risk management sits with a dedicated department, with overall accountability clearly defined. Risks are identified and addressed, but the process is not yet systematic risks are often managed as they arise, rather than through active monitoring. Sector-wide engagement is stronger, with workshops conducted across technical teams and risk registers maintained at departmental level. However, branch-level capacity remains weak and requires support.
• Fraud, Integrity & Stakeholder Engagement: While there is no stand-alone fraud policy, automated financial systems and internal practices help mitigate risks. Access risks have not been systematically analysed but may become more visible through high-level risk registers. Stakeholder engagement takes place, but not in a structured way. Reputational and integrity risks are regularly discussed at Governing Board meetings, with risk management a standing item every two months.
• Crisis Management: A crisis management unit is not formally established. Insurance systems and communication procedures are in place, and an international security manual is planned, but domestic procedures for managing critical incidents and crisis management training remain gaps.

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_responses.notes:
• Preparedness Focal Point & Gap Identification: IRCS is in process of recruiting a qualified focal point for disaster preparedness. However, preparedness gaps are not systematically identified. Current practice is reactive, with program managers engaging the grant manager and finance team when funding shortfalls arise. This approach does not replace structured preparedness planning.
• Remedial Actions & Resource Mobilisation: Preparedness gaps are not yet addressed through consistent remedial actions. While the fundraising team is active and supportive, efforts remain focused on applications for specific opportunities rather than a broader preparedness agenda. Financial gaps for preparedness and early actions are not identified, and a resource mobilisation strategy is not in place. Following the PER, the priority action will be to request the Board to establish unrestricted funding for preparedness and response, supported by emergency financial procedures.
• Budgeting & Updates: Preparedness actions are not updated on a regular cycle. There is currently no flexible budget “pot” that allows funds to shift between actions. Policies to allocate budgets are limited, with no dedicated funding at branch level. A national emergency fund, similar to DREF, is under consideration but not yet operational.

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes:
• Business Continuity Planning: IRCS has some elements of business continuity planning in place, but an up-to-date, approved plan does not currently exist. While a plan was developed in the past, it is unclear if it has been updated, leaving a gap in preparedness for major crises that could affect the NS’s ability to operate.
• Donor Communication Procedures: There are semi formal procedures for communicating with donors to repurpose funds during unexpected or emerging needs. Engagement occurs on an ad hoc basis, when necessary, but a standardized approach has not been developed.

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_responses.notes:
• SOP Development & Coverage: IRCS has some SOPs regulating “peacetime” activities and ad hoc procedures created in response to requests, but there is no up-to-date, comprehensive set of SOPs for disaster and crisis response. Existing documents were developed under a previous structure and do not reflect current operations. While SOPs exist for specific Units (e.g., Ambulances), branch-level SOPs for crisis response are absent. There is a general appetite to update and expand SOPs to align with the new structure and emerging operational needs.
• Dissemination & Awareness: Some SOPs are available online and accessible to volunteers, but they function more as guidelines than binding procedures. Dissemination is inconsistent; branches apply them differently, and they are not systematically integrated into staff or volunteer induction. Auditing and structured implementation are lacking.
• Roles, Processes & Structures: HQ has some procedures to form a crisis unit, but formal roles and responsibilities are not clearly outlined. SOPs do not yet include procedures for all response phases, scaling alert levels, decision-making flowcharts (beyond Units), or organograms with accessible contact details.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_responses.notes:
• Multi-Sectoral Response Planning: IRCS does not yet have an up to date, approved multi-sectoral response plan for rapid deployment and efficient use of resources. Mobilization has been positive in past responses but not guided by formal procedures. Current efforts are focused on collecting experiences to inform a plan and standardize good practices.
• Inclusiveness, Alignment & Standards: The plan has not been developed with input from communities, staff, volunteers, or governance, and does not yet incorporate gender, age, disability, or diversity considerations. Alignment with the Principles and Rules, DM policy, Fundamental Principles, and IFRC standards such as EPOA is absent. While secondary risks and recovery planning are not formalized, IRCS’s recovery mandate is clear and recognized within the Major Emergency Framework, which defines activities beyond the seventh day as “Recovery.” Many IRCS activities fall into this category.
• Adaptation, Learning & Transition: There are no established processes to adapt plans to changing contexts or capture lessons from simulations, though First Aid exercises provide useful reflections. IRCS has experience transitioning from relief to recovery, particularly through UKR-related funds, though volunteer availability in recovery phases is a challenge. Familiarity with DREF/EA exists, but no formal procedures are in place. Donation protocols are under development.

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes:
• Pre-Disaster Engagement & Agreements: IRCS maintains some regular meetings with local authorities and stakeholders, though these are patchy, often limited to ambulances or specific services, and not consistently shared across the organization. Broader pre-disaster agreements remain absent, with Civil Defence and others more systematically engaged. While the Major Emergency Framework (MEF) offers a reference point, it is not fully disseminated. Government response practices rely heavily on informal engagement (“picking up the phone”), and there is growing momentum to establish a more professional framework. Meetings with HSE emergency leads are planned, reflecting strong efforts to strengthen infrastructure quickly.
• Familiarity, Coordination & Movement: The mandate and role of IRCS are being clarified, with some agreement already in place with the authorities, though further alignment is still needed. Key staff are partly familiar with the organization’s role, but volunteers and branch members have limited awareness. Coordination with NGOs, INGOs, UN, and public authorities exists but is project-based and reactive. Movement capacity mapping is up to date, and thematic agreements (e.g., RFL, Prison Program) are in place and shared with IFRC.
• Suppliers, Contractors & External Agreements: Contractors have not systematically signed the Code of Conduct. Agreements with public authorities, suppliers, money transfer providers, and social protection systems are not yet formalized, though informal relationships and interest in developing them are present.

• Search & Rescue Capacity: IRCS is affiliated with two search and rescue (SAR) teams – one specialized in mountain operations and one in water. These teams are technically strong and well connected within the SAR community, maintaining their own networks and coordination with external stakeholders. However, they function largely as standalone units, without structured collaboration between them or integration into the broader IRCS disaster response system.
• Integration & Strategy: There is no formal SAR strategy, and SAR is not explicitly embedded in the NS’s response planning or scenarios. The teams are highly specialized and respond only within their specific operational domains. Coordination with state authorities is limited, as SAR is not typically an area where the state formally calls upon IRCS.

component_details.title: MANAGEMENT OF DEAD BODIES TO FACILITATE THEIR IDENTIFICATION

component_responses.notes:
• Restoring Family Links (RFL) Capacity: RFL services are delivered primarily by staff within the International and Migration Department, with one person dedicated to RFL and another to tracing. Volunteers are not trained for RFL, though they occasionally assist with transport or similar support. This reliance on staff ensures service quality but poses challenges for scale-up in emergencies, such as large boat arrivals, when surge capacity would be required.
• Services & Beneficiaries: RFL activities include tracing, Red Cross messaging, and travel assistance, operated in collaboration with IOM Ireland for people with refugee and subsidiary protection. Unaccompanied minors frequently approach IRCS for tracing and family reunification, though housing remains a barrier for reunification cases. These services demonstrate the essential humanitarian value of RFL, even as resourcing remains tight.
• Procedures & Collaboration with ICRC: Formal agreements with ICRC are in place, including access to the ICRC database. IRCS also collaborates closely with the ICRC delegation in London and contributes to the development of the RFL strategy, ensuring alignment with Movement standards.

• Recovery Principles & Practice: IRCS staff have some practical experience in applying recovery principles, such as trauma management and community participation, but there is no documentation or standardized approach. One example of good practice exists, yet it remains isolated and not institutionalized, highlighting a gap between practice and systematization.
• Mandate & Systems: The mandate for recovery has not been formally agreed with public authorities, though discussions are ongoing. While the Major Emergency Framework identifies “Recovery” as activities beyond the seventh day, IRCS has not embedded this into its role. Enabling systems to support transition from relief to recovery are absent, with no dedicated HR, planning, or support services in place to manage early recovery interventions.
• Coordination & Partnerships: IRCS does not coordinate recovery efforts with public authorities or other humanitarian actors through joint assessments or national recovery planning. Sectoral integration has not been considered, and external partnerships to cover non-strategic recovery needs have not been explored, leaving recovery a significant institutional gap.

component_details.title: CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL, RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR (CBRN) EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS

component_responses.notes:
• Mandate & Planning: IRCS does not have a defined role or responsibilities in national, regional, or local emergency plans related to technological or biological hazards. Consequently, no action plan exists to guide response to such incidents, and no SOPs or safety protocols are in place.
• Focal Points & Expertise: There is no designated focal point for technological or biological hazards. Staff and volunteers have not received specific training to prepare for or respond to incidents of this type.
• Systems & Preparedness: Without a clear mandate or formalized role, IRCS lacks the enabling systems, procedures, and specialized resources required to contribute meaningfully in this area. This creates a significant preparedness gap, as technological and biological hazards are not integrated into IRCS’s current strategy, planning, or operational structures.

component_details.title: Mapping of NS capacities
component_details.description: A list of the NS capacities including HR (staff, response teams and volunteers) and equipment that are available for disaster/crisis response. Teams could include branch and national response teams. This should be defined by technical speciality where relevant.

component_responses.notes:
• Focal Points & Training: IRCS has focal points across areas of expertise who provide technical guidance. Training systems are strong, supported by a live database tracking courses for staff and volunteers. Staff benefit from a wide range of updated training opportunities, ensuring good technical capacity.
• Materials, Equipment & Human Resources: Branches maintain annual inventories accessible to HQ, with gaps noted. Human resources are generally sufficient for initial response, but equipment availability is uneven. HQ holds no equipment and cannot directly support branches, though during COVID-19 it supplied essential items. Sharing between branches is ad hoc, with some reluctance to release assets.
• Response Levels & Resource Sharing: There is no formal classification of emergencies (Green – Yellow – Red), limiting structured resource planning. Volunteer sharing across branches is possible but not always straightforward. Equipment-sharing mechanisms remain weak, while ad hoc collaboration with sister NSs (e.g., British Red Cross) has occurred but is not systematic.

component_details.title: Early Action Mechanisms
component_details.description: Designed to translate warnings into anticipatory actions to help reduce the impact of specific disaster or crisis events. They focus on consolidating available forecasting information and putting procedures in place to ensure that a NS can act ahead of any disaster/crisis. Forecast-based financing is included within the scope of this area.

component_responses.notes:
• Early Warning & Methodology: IRCS does not have an early warning/early action (EWEA) system integrated into national preparedness mechanisms. There is no established methodology to determine when and where to act based on vulnerability, exposure, or triggers. Forecast-based financing and disease surveillance are not part of current approaches.
• Mechanisms & Technology: While some elements of proactive coordination exist with national authorities, there are no formalized mechanisms for anticipating or responding to hazards. New technologies such as SMS, email, or social media alerts are not systematically tested or used to trigger early action.
• Communication & Branch Networks: There are no permanent procedures or staff dedicated to issuing alerts or initiating early action within the NS structure. At branch level, local networks with authorities and communities are active, but communication remains reactive rather than anticipatory. There is no formal system defining what information should be shared, when, or how it should be escalated across levels of the NS.

component_details.title: Cash Based Intervention (CBI)
component_details.description: An effective and flexible way, including all forms of cash and voucher-based assistance, to support people affected by emergencies, maintaining their dignity and choice, while fostering local economies. Cash should also be mainstreamed into other sectors (including Relief, shelter, livelihoods) and services (Logistics, Finance, etc.)

component_responses.notes:
• Preparedness Plans & Capacity: IRCS has no dedicated CBI preparedness plan, budget, or resourcing or personnel. Vouchers were distributed during the Ukraine response through supermarket chains, with protocols and acceptance forms in place, but no tools or processes were developed further afterwards. The only structured cash scheme currently in place is the national flood scheme, which targets businesses rather than households. There is no database of CBI-trained staff or volunteers, and no broader preparedness planning for scalable emergency CBI.
• Analysis, SOPs & Tools: There are no pre-disaster market analyses, baselines, or frameworks in place. Coordination with other actors is minimal, limited to one charity store. SOPs are absent, with no clear roles or responsibilities defined for CBI responses. Apart from the flood scheme, there are no NS-specific CBI tools or toolkits, and no processes for systematically updating them based on lessons learned. 
• Delivery Mechanisms & Coordination: Flood scheme reimbursements operate through the IRCS bank account but are not linked to external financial service providers. No mapping of service providers exists, though it is being considered. There are no agreements with money transfer providers, nor an internal or external CBI coordination mechanism.

component_details.title: Emergency Needs Assessment
component_details.description: Assess the extent and impact of the damage caused by the disaster/crisis and the degree of vulnerability of the affected population. The first step in any emergency response, such an assessment will identify the needs that require external intervention and the gaps to be filled. It is a vital component of the programme-planning process.

component_responses.notes:
• Templates & Teams: IRCS does not have standardized templates for primary or secondary data collection specific to emergency needs assessments (ENA). Elements of secondary data review exist—mainly through monitoring news and media—but these are not formalized. A trained, multi-sectoral ENA team does not exist; instead, occasional briefings are provided to volunteers and staff involved in ad hoc data collection.
• Use of ENA for Planning: Emergency plans of action are not systematically based on ENA results. Assessments, when conducted, are used to flag acute needs that require immediate action rather than to inform structured operational strategies. Some results have been applied to trigger interventions in specific cases, but this remains reactive rather than strategic. 
• Disaggregation & Analysis: When ENA has been conducted, data was disaggregated by gender and age, but other elements of analysis are not systematically applied. Accessibility, availability, quality, use, and awareness of goods and services are not assessed. Nor are secondary risks, coping mechanisms, or self-recovery capacities. Likewise, existing national and international response capacities and gaps are not systematically considered.

component_details.title: Affected population selection
component_details.description: Identification and selection of target Affected population for interventions, using a pre-defined set of criteria based on need and vulnerability. This includes consideration of specific vulnerabilities such as disability, age and gender.

component_responses.notes:
• Selection Criteria & Communication: IRCS does not systematically communicate or apply selection criteria across operations. The Migration team has developed effective practices, such as using case workers and Telegram channels to share eligibility information, and communication for the Flood Scheme has been clear and effective. However, these practices are not formalized across the NS. 
• Criteria Development & Data Protection: Selection criteria are not consistently based on vulnerability considerations such as gender, age, disability, or diversity. Data protection is a stronger area: IRCS complies with GDPR and other national legislation, ensuring appropriate handling of sensitive information.
• Training & Data Collection: Responders have not received systematic training in data collection, and standardized templates are not in use. GDPR training is being developed for all members, and efforts are made to minimize the amount of data collected by branches, but these are still in progress.
• Verification & Inclusion: Cross-checking beneficiary lists with community leaders, authorities, or other agencies happens occasionally but is not systematic. Agreements to share predefined data exist but are not consistently applied across responses.

component_details.title: Emergency Operations Centre (EOC)
component_details.description: A central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions at a strategic level in an emergency situation. The common functions are to collect and analyze data; facilitate decision making that protects life and livelihoods; and disseminate those decisions to all concerned agencies and individuals. Generally located at the headquarter level of an organization.

component_responses.notes:
• Structure & Focal Points: IRCS does not have an Emergency Operations Centre (EOC), and therefore no formally appointed focal point, SOPs, or defined activation procedures. Staff and volunteers are not trained on roles, responsibilities, or SOPs, and technical sectors and support services do not have integrated procedures.
• Facilities & Equipment: There are premises that could be repurposed into an EOC if needed, but no dedicated, equipped, or self-sufficient facilities exist. There is no backup for power, water, or telecommunications, and no alternative location is identified should the main site be inaccessible.
• Coordination & Processes: Contact lists for relevant personnel are in place, and IRCS holds certified licenses for emergency frequencies. However, systematic information management (maps, operational details, situation reports) is not yet operationalized. Strategic decision-making processes, levels of authority, and 24/7 functionality are not defined. While some initiatives to track updates during responses exist, they remain ad hoc and not institutionalized.

component_details.title: Information Management (IM)
component_details.description: Ability to manage information including requesting, receiving, analyzing and disseminating as per its procedures and partner requirements (IFRC and public authorities in particular). There should be a clear digital/paper trail that documents what, when and how the NS has acted and provides key information for the development of Emergency Plan of Actions. Includes IM between levels, between departments and Situational Reports, mapping, visualisation of data, GO platform (IFRC).

component_responses.notes:
• Templates & Equipment: Information management (IM) is uneven across the NS. Branches are not familiar with IM templates or methodologies, though HQ has signalled appetite to prioritize this area. Equipment gaps remain significant, as many branches lack premises or basic tools such as printers or projectors, limiting their ability to compile and visualize data.
• Systems & Data: Despite these challenges, systems that work are in place. File storage and sharing is partially functional, and official government data provides updated demographic and socio-economic information, disaggregated by gender, age, and disability. These sources are used in operations, though not systematically across the NS.
• Documentation & Reporting: Decisions are documented and filed, albeit without a standardized approach. Situation reports are produced and have directly informed response planning in recent emergencies, though formats vary.
• Information Sharing: Regular coordination mechanisms—including calls, email groups, and SMT meetings—ensure information flows across levels, sectors, and services. While not standardized, these practices demonstrate that working systems exist, even if improvements are needed for consistency.

component_details.title: Testing and Learning
component_details.description: Drills and Simulations allow the organization to test, identify and learn from the results of these type of exercises and incorporate learning into future preparedness and response planning.

component_responses.notes:
• Simulations & Drills: IRCS does not have a structured system of simulations or drills for early action and response. No formal training or procedures are in place, and emergency procedures themselves are lacking. While drills were previously conducted and included aspects such as Fundamental Principles, these practices have not been sustained.
• Branch-Level & Thematic Testing: Some branch-level testing takes place in areas prone to natural hazards, though this is usually linked to SAR training organized by external actors. These activities provide some indirect preparedness, but they are not part of a formalized IRCS system.
•  Safe Access & Security: Personal protective equipment (PPE) use is consistently tested during drills, but broader safe access—including perception, acceptance, and security for vulnerable groups—is not systematically addressed or trained.
• Coordination & Cross-Border Work: Cross-border simulations have not been conducted in over two decades, reflecting a significant gap. However, IRCS does participate in simulations and training exercises led by national authorities or other organizations, showing willingness to coordinate even in the absence of its own structured program.

component_details.title: Activation of regional and international support
component_details.description: Procedures for requesting and accepting regional and international support in operations, including triggering coordination mechanisms for funding, materials and human resources deployments.

component_responses.notes:
• Familiarity with Support & Contacts: IRCS’s key staff are well informed about the technical, financial, material, and HR support available from IFRC/ICRC. Contacts with IFRC are known, and staff understand how to activate support. However, formal mapping of technical focal points still needs to be developed. SOPs to guide this process are not consistently in place, though knowledge exists informally.
• Procedures & Integration: There are no established IRCS SOPs outlining procedures to request and integrate regional or global support teams, either in preparedness or in imminent crises. Requests for bilateral assistance and assigned focal points for international responders are not relevant in the Irish context.
• Emergency Funding & Communication: IRCS staff are familiar with IFRC emergency funding mechanisms such as DREF and Emergency Appeals and know the associated requirements (EPoA). Forecast-based Financing remains an area where capacity is limited. To date, IRCS has never requested IFRC support for a response, reflecting both national context and limited relevance of some benchmarks.

• Community Participation & Preparedness: IRCS does not have structured mechanisms to ensure community participation in preparedness activities. One project proposal on community-based preparedness was developed but not approved, and no dedicated initiatives currently exist. Community assessments, planning, and response are not systematically inclusive of gender, diversity, or conflict sensitivity.
• Awareness & Early Warning: The NS does not conduct regular public education or awareness-raising on disasters or crises. Community-based early warning and early action systems are not in place, though IRCS has identified this as a future priority.
• Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs): There are no trained or equipped CDRTs within IRCS structures. Contingency or response plans aligned with local authorities and resources are absent, and no systematic engagement with local actors is currently in place.

• Epidemic Scenarios & Community Engagement: IRCS has not identified multi-sectoral response needs for epidemics or cross-border outbreaks, and no hazard mapping exists. Community engagement in prevention and response is limited. Two funded projects (EU for Health and AMIF) provide MHPSS and trauma therapy for displaced people, migrants, and applicants for international protection, with services now expanding. A core team delivers PFA online and face-to-face, supported by Ukrainian, Russian, and Arabic-speaking therapists. These initiatives show strong practice but are not yet integrated into epidemic preparedness or response planning.
• Rumour Management & Communication: There are no formal rumour management procedures, but Telegram and other channels provide strong infrastructure to counter misinformation.
• Safety Protocols & PPE: Infection prevention protocols follow HSE guidelines, applied mainly to volunteers. PPE is accessed through partners rather than stockpiled, with disposal practices in place.
• Roles & Preparedness: IRCS has not clearly defined roles in pandemics, isolation, or quarantine. COVID-19 lessons remain undocumented, though volunteers provided PFA in vaccination centres. Migrants face particular gaps in healthcare access, highlighting IRCS’s potential role in preparedness and coordination with state stakeholders.

• First Aid as a Core Service: First Aid (FA) is central to IRCS’s mandate and one of its strongest capacities. It consistently features in response, supported by decades of FA competitions and a large network of trained volunteers. Even without formal approval in strategic documents, FA is de facto a guaranteed element of IRCS’s emergency response.
• Training & Community Outreach: Volunteers routinely receive FA training, though it is not mandatory. Community-level dissemination is weaker: while positive initiatives exist, such as awareness sessions in schools and one branch with strong outreach, there is no systematic approach to training communities in basic life-saving skills. Clinical FA training and community-focused awareness remain separate. Expanding this outreach would greatly enhance resilience, particularly in previously affected areas.
• Volunteer Teams: IRCS has trained and equipped FA teams potentially capable of rapid deployment. Their effectiveness is proven, but linking FA more closely with community resilience efforts would maximize its impact.

component_details.title: Coordination with Movement
component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_responses.notes:
• SMCC Principles & Coordination Mechanisms: Coordination and cooperation within the Movement follow SMCC principles, though the benchmark is less relevant in the Irish context, as ICRC is the only Movement partner present in-country. When coordination is required, it adheres to the established rules. 
• Information Sharing & National Coordination: In-country coordination mechanisms with Movement partners are established to share information on assessments, plans of action, and emerging gaps, though application remains limited to specific cases, such as joint grant proposals. Overall, the benchmark is less applicable to the context.
• Cross-Border & International Collaboration: IRCS maintains a strong historical relationship with the British Red Cross, particularly around youth activities, and has recently shared lessons learned in technical areas. Collaboration with other National Societies is gradually developing. The benchmark on frameworks for managing international assistance is not currently relevant, as such mechanisms have not been required.

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_responses.notes:
• National Coordination & Auxiliary Role: IRCS is formally part of the national humanitarian coordination system and participates regularly in coordination mechanisms. While the benchmark on informing partners of Movement capacities in case of international support is less relevant, the NS is actively engaged at the national level.
• Authorities’ Capacities & Service Identification: IRCS is aware of the roles and capacities of national authorities and is in the process of identifying which services it can reliably provide during a response. Once these services are clearly defined, the NS intends to proactively communicate its auxiliary role to government stakeholders.
• Independence & Control: IRCS maintains full control over its assets, resources, and use of the emblem when cooperating with public authorities, ensuring operational independence.
• Local Coordination: Coordination mechanisms with local and national authorities are established across most areas of intervention, though there are seven counties without IRCS presence.

component_details.title: Coordination with External Agencies and NGOs
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and collaboration with Non-Governmental Organization (NGO), both local and international NGOs, civil society organizations (CSOs) and United Nations agencies in country.

component_responses.notes:
• Humanitarian Community Engagement: IRCS is an active member of the humanitarian community, engaging with UN and NGO partners to support coordination and strengthen response efficiency. Much of this engagement, however, is through informal mechanisms, which now need to be formalized to ensure consistency and sustainability.
• Cluster Roles & Strategic Awareness: Some benchmarks are less relevant in the Irish context, such as cluster membership and participation in UN-led appeal processes. Nonetheless, IRCS is aware of IFRC’s role in shelter cluster coordination, ensuring alignment with Movement responsibilities if required.
• Partnership Agreements: Partnerships with UN and NGO actors exist, though primarily linked to migration. Two formal agreements are in place covering migrant-specific emergency response, with information shared between headquarters and branches. These partnerships provide an important platform for operational coordination and could serve as a foundation for broader, more formalized engagement across other sectors in future responses.

component_details.title: Civil Military Relations
component_details.description: Dialogue and interaction with military actors, essential to protect and promote humanitarian principles, avoid competition, minimize inconsistency and, when appropriate, pursue common goals.

component_responses.notes:
• Military Coordination & Principles: IRCS has no operational procedures governing relations with the military beyond its auxiliary role, which exists on paper. Engagement is largely formal, with two examples during floods and the Ukraine crisis. An army officer also sits on the IRCS board. However, in Ireland the military is not considered a first responder, and arrangements do not fully exist as described in the benchmarks, which are not fully applicable to the context.
• Movement Guidance & Use of Assets: IRCS does not directly approach the military and therefore does not systematically apply the Movement’s 2005 guidance. Military assets are not used in operations, making benchmarks on last resort use, armed transport, or armed protection not relevant in practice.
• Promotion of Principles & Engagement: IRCS promotes awareness of the Fundamental Principles and appropriate use of the Movement emblems in interactions with authorities, including the military. As part of engagement, IRCS provides free first aid training for soldiers, reinforcing its humanitarian role and independence.

component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_responses.notes:
• Information Flow & Decision-Making: IRCS has procedures to manage information between communities, branches, and headquarters, though these could be strengthened to ensure more consistent upward and downward flow. At times, branch–community engagement occurs without HQ being fully informed. Community input is systematically considered during BOCA sessions, and while this process exists, it can be better integrated into decision-making. Overall, approaches remain somewhat reactive, though grounded in collaboration with communities.
• Branch Coordination & Local Structures: Branches maintain systems to communicate and coordinate with community volunteer groups, which function similarly to CDRTs in Ireland. Local branches are often recognized by others as coordinators due to their experience and standing within the community
• Support to Community Response & Preparedness Context: IRCS supports community-level response systems either directly or in partnership with local authorities, with SAR teams considered part of this capacity. A preparedness plan existed in the past, but today planning often reflects the broader national context. Given Ireland’s strong national preparedness and relative safety, IRCS sees space for more targeted plans, though this remains difficult to prioritize.

component_details.title: Cooperation with private sector
component_details.description: Mechanism that allows cooperation with private sector that often plays a strong role in response, particularly if there is impact on their staff and businesses. There is often a willingness to donate goods and services. Advance agreements help to expedite response actions.

component_responses.notes:
• Due Diligence & Donations: IRCS has a policy in place to ensure due diligence when selecting partners and accepting donations, with screening applied to large donations and corporate partners. However, enforcement is weak due to a reactive approach and limited time for systematic checks. As a result, while there is cautious awareness, the policy is not consistently operationalized.
• Emblem Protection & Visual Identity: The appropriate use of the emblem and protection of IRCS’s visual identity are prioritized, supported by branding guidelines.
