component_responses.notes: DM is reflected in the MRCS’s Strategy 2020 but it does not include analysis of country context, trends, operational objectives or success indicators. Engagement with technical sectors and support services is informal and not documented.

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_responses.notes: MRCS references IFRC policy as they have no DRM policy.  Some departments have guiding principles and SOPs that are used as a reference in times of disaster response but there is no cross-departmental, organisation-wide policy.

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: Due to a lack of resources the MRCS does not have a specific IDRL humanitarian diplomacy plan. However when the opportunity arises the NS advocates with the government for IDRL guidelines to be implemented. The NS is reviewing its constitution to identity possible changes to strengthen the act of parliament and articulate the role of the NS to support the government specifically in areas of disaster. The NS has a legal officer who is the focal point for IHL and IDRL. As noted in Component 1, although IHL is an area of focus for the NS, it does not actively promote IHL but rather coordinates with ICRC when they are engaged in IHL promotion. IDRL has less priority currently. When the situation arises the NS advocates the government to enact legislation in line with the Model Act for the facilitation and regulation of International Disaster Relief and Initial Recovery Assistance but this is not always in a strategic way (more ad hoc).

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_responses.notes: Some MRCS DM staff are trained and aware of the Sphere standards. These standards are generally followed during response. MRCS has an approved Child Protection and Gender Diversity Policies that have not been fully disseminated and understood at all levels of the NS. For RFL and unaccompanied minors the NS follows IFRC and government guidelines. The NS has no formal mechanism to ensure affected populations are involved in all stages of response or a communication system to allow for feedback from beneficiaries. The NS has a close informal working relationship with the Government’s Welfare Department who are involved at the community level. The NS believes they follow PGI standards but dissemination and understanding in limited.

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_responses.notes: MRCS is recognised under the 1965 “Malaysian Red Crescent Society Act”. Here their role is articulated as an organisation that “shall be open, without any discrimination on the grounds of religion, race or politics, to all persons in Malaysia to...(a) in time of peace or war, to carry on and assist in work for the improvement of health, the prevention of disease and the mitigation of suffering...(b) in time of war, to furnish voluntary aid to the sick and wounded both of armies and non-belligerents, to prisoners of war and to civilian sufferers...in accordance with the spirit and covenants of the Geneva Conventions...(c) to perform all the duties devolved upon a national society by each nation which has acceded to the said Conventions”.  Their role is further articulated through National Security Council Directives (NSC) 18, 20, and 21. Their specific responsibilities include, in coordination with various government bodies (e.g. Ministry of Health, Ministry of Women, Family and Social Development, Rescue Agencies), assisting emergency medical services, preparing and providing food, providing first aid, manning relief centres, maintaining evacuation centres, evacuating individuals, distributing relief items, doing registration and rehabilitation, assisting agencies with rescuing and evacuating victims.  Although the mandate is clear, it was noted that the broader role of the NS as it relates to DM can  be further articulated and defined (e.g. preparedness, response and recovery). The NS mandate is reflected in some organisational documents. The NS mandate has not been fully disseminated to all the branches and this has lead to a lack of  awareness and understanding. Their mandate is aligned with the Fundamental Principles, referencing volunteerism, impartiality and neutrality in the Act.  It is noted that in  practice the MRCS auxiliary role is not clearly understood by public authorities or the general public, often considering them as an NGO. This may even extend to members of the NS living in rural areas. The government is in the process of reviewing/updatings Directives 18, 20 and 21. The NS does not actively promote IHL but coordinates with ICRC when they are engaged in IHL promotion.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: The MRCS has no risk monitoring systems in place. They receive all their data from the government (NADMA) and also participate in coordination meetings organised by NADMA. The NS does no data collection, analysis or identifying of risks. There is also no procedure in place for early warning and actions. 2 VCA’s have been done in Cameron Highlands and Alor Setar and a plan to do a VCA in Jahor is in place. Cross-border risk monitoring is done by the government.

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_responses.notes: Currently the NS does not have any up-to-date scenario plans based on hazard-risk analysis. It is noted that the NS had developed a multi-hazard contingency plan in 2010, but no specific hazard scenario plans.

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_responses.notes: Although the NS does not have a formally designated person responsible for risk management, different areas of risk (e.g. financial risk) are managed by different departments. There is no centralised and holistic risk register, and the NS does not systematically evaluate and mitigate potential risk. It is noted that NS has procedures to minimise fraud and corruption in their financial policy and handbook #2.

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_responses.notes: MRCS has a DM Officer, responsible for preparedness, who reports to the SG. Overall the SG overseas all preparedness work. It was noted that MRCS has not identified all of the preparedness gaps, including its corresponding financial gaps/requirements. Different projects address NS preparedness actions (e.g. Red Ready), but there is no overall/comprehensive preparedness plan that are based on identified gaps. It was noted however that through the PER process, preparedness gaps will be identified, which can be used to secure funding with donors through work-plans.

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: Currently the NS does not have any business continuity plans.

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_responses.notes: MRCS has DM Standard Operating Procedures, but it is noted this is out-of-date (2014). Different departments have their own emergency procedures, however it was noted these have been developed independently and remain siloed and not aligned. The DM SOPs have been disseminated, but generally not understood by all. SOPs focus on response but not on early warning, early action or recovery. Existing DM SOPs do not contain up-to-date response structure or decision-making flowchart.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_responses.notes: The MRCS does not have templates for standardised response plans. These are done on an ad hoc basis and is not included in SOPs. In times of disaster response the DM committee advises the NEB to create a Task Force. This Task Force will draft a response plan to be approved by the NEB. The response plan incorporates input from staff, management and technical areas but currently this does not include community input. 7 Fundamental Principles are considered when drafting the response plans but this process in not systematic due to lack of  DM policies and SOPs. The NS data collection focuses on number of families and their needs and does not include detailed information like age, gender, disability, diversity complexities or community capacities. This being said the NS is in the process of mainstreaming the concept of Gender and Diversity within all its activities including data collection. With changes in context and/or emerging needs,  the Task Force will alter the response plans accordingly, but these are more tactical. The NS’s DREF plans aim to align with IFRC global standards, but as these plans are drawn up on an ad hoc basis the NS is unaware if the plans actually meet global standards. The NS response plans do not consider how to reduce and address secondary risks or acknowledge response or recovery actions of other actors. Depending on financial resources the NS can develop recovery activities on a needs basis. Lessons learnt from real time or simulated exercises are not fed back into plans.

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: Twice a year MRCS has pre-disaster meetings with NADMA and additional meetings can also be requested if a disaster is approaching. The NS also has pre-disaster meetings with local authorities but not with other movement actors. The NS is in the process of reviewing its legal base and this will include having contractors sign a Code of conduct. At the moment the NS has no pre-disaster agreements with any other actors (e.g. Movement partners, vendors). Although they are looking at developing agreements with money transfer providers as part of their CTP plan.

MRCS supports the government in providing mass cooking services in shelters during disaster responses. The NS has trained staff and members in mass cooking but does not do food security as this function is performed by the government. The NS participates in the food aid coordination mechanism established by the government. It is noted that this is a new NADMA initiative still in development. MRCS has food distribution (mainly mass cooking in relief centres and some food deliveries to communities) integrated in response actions as per Directive 20 and follows exact safety standards.  The NS follows the “food and beverage menu” guidelines as specified in the DM SOP. These guidelines are aligned with government guidelines and the Ministry of Health does random checks to confirm the safety of the food.

Search and rescue is part of MRCS’s mandate and is included in Directive 20, clause no.2. “Roles and responsibilities of MRCS. It does not define specific areas of rescue as it can be applied to different search and rescue scenarios.

MRCS has 2 programs focused on DRR being implemented in some areas of Malaysia. These programs include one referred to as “Adopt a Village” (a package that covers services for the community, including preparedness) and another for targeted communities (focused on disaster preparedness). These programs include participation from the community and also includes coordination with the local authorities. The NS conducts awareness activities but these are more on an ad hoc basis. It is noted that awareness is part of the NS’s  Adopt a Village program and includes early warning, evacuation and preparedness. In the districts of Kelantan and  Terengganu the NS has developed the Adopt a Village program with activities in  early warning and early action. The NS trained Community Based Action Teams’s (CBAT) in 2015 and their effectiveness was seen during the 2017 Kelantan and Terengganu responses. The CBAT responses are coordinated and aligned with local authorities.

component_details.title: Mapping of NS capacities
component_details.description: A list of the NS capacities including HR (staff, response teams and volunteers) and equipment that are available for disaster/crisis response. Teams could include branch and national response teams. This should be defined by technical speciality where relevant.

component_responses.notes: At national level the MRCS has an identified focal point for each area of intervention to provide technical guidance and support. Depending on their resources the NS aims to have area specific training for staff and volunteers at least once a year. All trainings are centralised, and both the courses and records are held at HQ. These records would include specific type of training and also who attended it. The NS has no updated or centralised database of response material or equipment. It is noted that the warehouse uses a paper-based sign-in/out tracking system. It is also noted that at district level some branches have a database of resources owned by members and used in response actions. At district level it is noted that MRCS branches do not have enough volunteers to cover the initial response needs. For responses in KL, HQ would cover the initial response till branches can take over if the need is there to do so.
This component was not assessed as in disasters this role is performed by the Malaysian Ministry of Health.

component_details.title: Early Action Mechanisms
component_details.description: Designed to translate warnings into anticipatory actions to help reduce the impact of specific disaster or crisis events. They focus on consolidating available forecasting information and putting procedures in place to ensure that a NS can act ahead of any disaster/crisis. Forecast-based financing is included within the scope of this area.

component_responses.notes: The MRCS does not have early warning early action systems in place as it follows the NSC directive 20 and uses this to coordinate with the government during responses. The NS has not yet developed forecast based financing. The NS’s DM SOPs do not cover early action triggers. The NS receives messages on potential hazards from the Met office at both HQ and branch level and uses this information to define actions. Information sharing between HQ and branches to communicate warning messages are done via WhatsApp. The community leaders receive warning messages from the local government district officer via the branch leaders. The process of how the branches communicate messages to the district officer is not formalised. The MRCS use email and fax to communicate alert messages but this process is not formalised.

component_details.title: Cash Based Intervention (CBI)
component_details.description: An effective and flexible way, including all forms of cash and voucher-based assistance, to support people affected by emergencies, maintaining their dignity and choice, while fostering local economies. Cash should also be mainstreamed into other sectors (including Relief, shelter, livelihoods) and services (Logistics, Finance, etc.)

component_responses.notes: Cash Based Interventions has not been implemented in the MRCS. The NS has 3 staff and 17 volunteers trained in CBI. The NS has not done pre-disaster cash analysis and baseline about market systems, prices and seasonality, mapping of other actors and coordination structures yet. This is planned under the Red Ready project but is yet to be approved.

component_details.title: Emergency Needs Assessment
component_details.description: Assess the extent and impact of the damage caused by the disaster/crisis and the degree of vulnerability of the affected population. The first step in any emergency response, such an assessment will identify the needs that require external intervention and the gaps to be filled. It is a vital component of the programme-planning process.

component_responses.notes: The MRCS has standardised templates for primary and secondary data collection and reporting. The template for disaster needs assessment is included in the DM SOPs but this yet to be updated. The NS has no specific team for assessments but the staff and volunteers in different sectors fulfill this role. NS emergency plans of actions incorporate some information captured in the assessments (e.g number of people/families and specific needs) but does not contain information regarding gender and diversity. More detailed information is collected by the government welfare department. The NS’s ENA form in the DM SOP analyses accessibility, availability, quality and use of goods and services. However, not all sections of the form are completed including section E “local financial material and human resources” as this information is sometimes difficult to obtain. The NS’s ENA form does not include a section for national or international capacities although some branches do collect information on other actors responding in the community. It is noted that the NS does acknowledge the need to have information of other actors doing response as this would prevent duplication of actions and wasted resources. The NS does not have the capacity (manpower or technical) to analyse data collected during the needs assessments.

component_details.title: Affected population selection
component_details.description: Identification and selection of target Affected population for interventions, using a pre-defined set of criteria based on need and vulnerability. This includes consideration of specific vulnerabilities such as disability, age and gender.

component_responses.notes: Communication with beneficiaries are mainly done by the government and community leaders and this makes it difficult for the NS to communicate selection criteria to the affected population. The NS does not have its own selection criteria and relies on the government and local authorities’ criteria when providing services during emergencies. The government criteria does consider gender, diversity, age and disabilities. The NS does not have a data protection policy and some branches keep the information collected from beneficiaries for 2 years, thereafter it is destroyed. The NS Acknowledges the importance of data protection and plans to develop a workshop in October to align with government data protection regulations. The NS cross-checks all its collected data with the Social services department.

component_details.title: Emergency Operations Centre (EOC)
component_details.description: A central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions at a strategic level in an emergency situation. The common functions are to collect and analyze data; facilitate decision making that protects life and livelihoods; and disseminate those decisions to all concerned agencies and individuals. Generally located at the headquarter level of an organization.

component_responses.notes: The MRCS has no formally appointed focal point for EOC and currently, in an emergency the DM officer is in charge of the EOC, although this is not formally included in the JD.  The NS has no specific EOC SOPs. The DM SOP includes a list of tasks for the Operation Room and this is used as guidelines in time of disaster and activation of EOC.  The DM SOP does not include a documented activation of EOC based on the response level.  It is noted that the activation of the EOC is the responsibility of the Director of Operations as stated in the DM SOP. Staff and volunteers in the EOC know their roles although they have received no formal training. The NS has an updated contact list of all relevant personnel and a hardcopy is available at HQ. The designated EOC has sufficient space and equipment and has a sufficient supply of electricity, a water tank and radio communications. The NS does not have an identified alternative EOC location. The NS has legal access and designated use of emergency radio frequencies. It is noted that the licence for radio frequencies has just been renewed. NS EOC information is updated regularly and printed and displayed on walls in the EOC. This information includes standardised sitreps, maps, equipment and human resources. The DM unit is responsible for collecting information from the field and relaying it to the Task Force in the EOC. Recommendations are made by the SG, Vice Chairman and DM Chairman. On these recommendations the Task Force reaches a decision and reports to the NEB. The information received is enough to make immediate tactical decisions but is not necessarily reflected in response plans. The last operation MRCS responded to occurred in 2017, so the process may need to be clarified and simplified in order to avoid delayed and/or inappropriate response actions. The NS EOC is operational 24/7 and the volunteers operational shift is less than 24hrs. However, if there are not enough volunteers available to fill specific roles staff may exceed the 12 hr/shift.

component_details.title: Information Management (IM)
component_details.description: Ability to manage information including requesting, receiving, analyzing and disseminating as per its procedures and partner requirements (IFRC and public authorities in particular). There should be a clear digital/paper trail that documents what, when and how the NS has acted and provides key information for the development of Emergency Plan of Actions. Includes IM between levels, between departments and Situational Reports, mapping, visualisation of data, GO platform (IFRC).

component_responses.notes: Information Management is acknowledged by the NS as an area which requires significant improvement, especially given its cross-cutting nature. Currently MRCS does not have an overarching information management framework for all aspects of their work. There is no focal point for IM at NHQ or Branch levels who would provide the overall support, and establish information standards, templates, procedures and filing structures. NS does have hardware but does not have the software and capacity to utilise it to collect, manage and analyse data. It is noted that during a response, the NS follows a standard situation report (SitRep) template to summarise response actions and to share information. MRCS does review the SitReps to help inform immediate response actions, although not through a structured response plan. The SitReps do also inform recovery plans (if funding is available). MRCS does have informal structures to share information at different levels (e.g. HQ to Branch), but it was noted that as a result of these informal structures, information often is not fully made aware at all levels.

component_details.title: Testing and Learning
component_details.description: Drills and Simulations allow the organization to test, identify and learn from the results of these type of exercises and incorporate learning into future preparedness and response planning.

component_responses.notes: The MRCS participates in annual simulations and drills organised by the government for both country and cross-border scenarios. The NS also organises internal simulations as part of their NDRM program. These simulations are done country-wide in cooperation with the Fire Department, Ministry of Health and Civil Defence with NADMA in an observing role. Some branches within the NS would organise annual simulation exercises at state level. Simulation exercises are primary to expose participants to the DM SOP and capturing lessons learned is not the objective. In some cases, lessons learned are captured and passed on to HQ but this is not systematic. Evidence of this is the DM SOP not being updated. The NS tests their response systems at branch level and in particular those in high risk areas. The NS has developed scenarios to test the NS’s access and security but acknowledges that this is an area that needs further development.

component_details.title: Activation of regional and international support
component_details.description: Procedures for requesting and accepting regional and international support in operations, including triggering coordination mechanisms for funding, materials and human resources deployments.

component_responses.notes: Key staff of MRCS (e.g. DM and Finance) are familiar with the IFRC supports available. The NS does not have SOPs that describe when or how to accept regional and/or global support within the Movement. Sometimes, the wrong people are completing the forms. In part, it is acknowledged that the NS is bound by government regulations, which makes it difficult to accept aid workers. The NS does accept financial assistance (e.g. DREFs, Appeals).

component_details.title: CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL, RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR (CBRN) EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS

component_responses.notes: This component was not assessed as MRCS does not fulfill this function.
This component was not assessed as the MRCS does not fulfill this role.

component_details.title: MANAGEMENT OF DEAD BODIES TO FACILITATE THEIR IDENTIFICATION

component_responses.notes: This component was not assessed as the MRCS does not fulfill this role.

It was noted that although MRCS has a focal point for RFL, the NS does not work in this area much during response. It was noted that RFL from the NS does occur during peacetime and they do have an MoU on RFL in detention centres, but no procedures are in place for disasters, in part as there has been no demand for such services.

The MRCS does not have the mandate for recovery under the Law and this is led by the government. Directive 20 includes a guidance for recovery and the NS follows this. When needed the NS develops recovery projects in coordination with the government but this is dependent on funding. As Malaysia is not a disaster-prone country there is no demand for setting up a recovery system but the NS does acknowledge the need to have staff trained in this specific area.

component_details.title: NS-specific areas of intervention
component_details.description: Sector-specific or services provided by the NS in case of emergencies, it is in line with the NS mandate and legislation in country. It includes Community Based DP/DRR, Evacuation, Health in Emergencies, Epidemic and Pandemic, First aid, WASH, Food security and Livelihoods, Search and rRescue, Shelter, Management of dead bodies, RFL, Transition to recovery, and CBRN preparedness.

component_responses.notes: The NS has the role to support evacuation in high-risk areas as part of its mandate and is considered under Directive 20 but it is not identified in different scenarios.

First aid was identified as one of the NS main sectors of intervention. It is part of the NS’s response strategy and identified in different scenarios. First Aid is a compulsory part of the components in the Village Adoption programme and is also part of the basic training for all members. It is noted that not all volunteers are trained in First Aid.

MRCS’s Strategy 2020 includes water and sanitation and is identified specifically in flood scenarios. At HQ the NS has response teams and appropriate equipment but at branch level it has only response teams. The NS has 3 staff members and 50 volunteers trained in WASH. The NS aims to increase its capacity in this area with WASH training planned in the near future. The NS has the required equipment to provide quality WASH services and knows how to obtain the equipment in-country as well as via IFRC although there are no clear SOPs for this process. The NS has 2 staff who can provide technical WASH support at HQ. MRCS coordinates with the government is part of the recently established NADMA WASH cluster.

The MRCS has community health volunteers who do basic health assessments in coordination with the local health department. These assessments do not happen on a regular basis. Not all volunteers are trained in basic first aid. All members are trained in first aid and receive a refresher every 3 years.

component_details.title: Coordination with External Agencies and NGOs
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and collaboration with Non-Governmental Organization (NGO), both local and international NGOs, civil society organizations (CSOs) and United Nations agencies in country.

component_responses.notes: The NS is part of the Humanitarian Country Team and attend meetings. The NS is aware of the IFRC’s role in shelter cluster coordination. The NS does not have agreements in place with non-movement partners such as UN agencies or NGOs, but states there is no need for them. Additionally, the NS acknowledges that there has not been a large enough disaster which necessitates a deeper understanding of a UN-lead cluster structure.

component_details.title: Civil Military Relations
component_details.description: Dialogue and interaction with military actors, essential to protect and promote humanitarian principles, avoid competition, minimize inconsistency and, when appropriate, pursue common goals.

component_responses.notes: NS recognises the need to adhere to the fundamental principles, IHL and CoD resolutions in its relationship with the military. It is noted that MRCS and partners (IFRC and ICRC) may have different approaches on how this is done in practice which may lead to concerns. NS uses military assets as a last resort and in times of extreme situations. There is no specific criteria/guidance/policy to decide within the NS when and how to liaise with the military. MRCS recognises the impact of liaising with military and thus tries to avoid it in most circumstances.

component_details.title: Coordination with Movement
component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_responses.notes: There is limited awareness of what the SMCC is by the NS, but when presented with a summary of its core purpose, the NS acknowledged its importance. MRCS has strong relationship with movement partners, but this is not formally documented through agreements (e.g. Movement Coordination Agreement) and coordination with partners is not formally articulated in NS plans or SOPs. NS does follow IFRC guidelines on DREF.

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_responses.notes: MRC’s role in the national humanitarian coordination system is established in NSC directives 18, 20 and 21. MRCS has an understanding of the general capacities of the government (e.g. Search and Rescue, Health, Epidemic, WASH). As noted in Component 1, the public authorities of NS role/mandate can be improved. NS has not been in a situation where authorities propose actions outside of the mandate of the NS.

component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_responses.notes: Some of the branches actively report yearly to HQ. This report includes disaster interventions manpower use and any other activities. There is a guideline in the DM SOPs and branches follow it when communicating and coordinating with CDRTs. Information is collected from the communities by the district and that will be sent to the branch. This information is taken into account for branch decision making in coordination with local authorities.

component_details.title: Cooperation with private sector
component_details.description: Mechanism that allows cooperation with private sector that often plays a strong role in response, particularly if there is impact on their staff and businesses. There is often a willingness to donate goods and services. Advance agreements help to expedite response actions.

component_responses.notes: NS does not have specific due diligence for screening prospective partners. On a case by case basis MRCS develops partnerships with organizations which follow the fundamental principles. Nonetheless, MRCS recognises the need to have a more detailed procedures and criteria for if and when to partner with another organization. In agreements which MRCS has with private sector companies, clauses are written to protect the use of the emblem. It is noted in Communication Policy (draft) that “the re-production of Emblem and MRCS logo must be verified by the Communications Department and approved by the Secretary General”, but there is a need for specific guidelines on the use of the MRCS emblem for donors. NS recognises the need to engage with private sector volunteers. There has been an attempt in the past to form partnership with large private sector companies in Malaysia.

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_responses.notes: MRCS has procedures to activate, deploy and manage response teams in their DM SOPs (but needs to be updated). A description of responders’ responsibilities is also in the DM SOPs. NS has first responders training and all responders are required to do specific training before deployment (e.g. basic first aid, education of RCRC and IHL). There are also internal trainings (e.g. health, disaster relief and rescue, home nursing, basic life support, advanced first aid). Specialised teams are trained in sphere standards and code of conduct. Responders have identification and visibility items. Responders are insured but are not regularly briefed on safety and security risks. This is not standardised or mandatory - depends on team leader. There is no consolidated database of volunteers and their skills. NS does not have procedures to speed up the recruitment of staff or volunteers. MRCS does however accept walk-in volunteers. No screening procedures for walk-in volunteers as they are used in low-risk tasks (not deployed). No psychosocial support available for staff and volunteers after emergencies. There are no trainings on self-care, violence and harassment in the workplace. Not all staff and volunteers sign code of conduct. MRCS in the process to make this mandatory.

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_responses.notes: The MRCS has not implemented the Safer Access Framework but some of the volunteers involved in ICRC projects have been orientated on the framework. Although there is no overarching safety and security policy and corresponding compliance and monitoring system MRCS has some actions in place to improve safety and security for staff and volunteers. These actions include insurance and PPE for all responders. Although there is no standardised safety and security procedures, it is noted that some volunteers (i.e. NDRT, SDRT) have been oriented in Stay safe and RDRT responders must complete the Stay Safe training. There is no NS focal point for security and the NS does not carry out context or risk analysis. The DM SOPs outline mechanisms for staff and volunteers to report safety and security risks and incidents.

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_responses.notes: MRCS has a communication focal point at HQ and branches. The official spokespersons are the Secretary General and Chairman at HQ level. At branch level the chairperson does the press releases. Press releases are the main communication method. Facebook, Instagram and the MRCS website are updated as well. MRCS uses social media for appeals and to draw attention to unmet needs from disaster. Rights of affected people are not communicated however. Standard communication temples are not utilised. There is no specific person in charge of tracking negative media, but if brought to NS attention they will react accordingly. In recent times there has not been large scale disasters to utilize joint communications (i.e. with IFRC, ICRC). There is no policy as such but there is understanding with volunteers and staff to only post appropriate material online.

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_responses.notes: The MRCS does not have a formal PMER system in place. The branches use standardised forms included in the DM SOPs for reporting.  The disaster officer consolidates these reports at HQ. DM HQ has ad hoc post-mortem meetings, but these meetings are not documented. It was however noted that branches do post-mortem meetings with local authorities and these documented learnings are sent to DM HQ. The NS has no standardised framework or plan of action for emergency operations but does identify operational results/objectives and indicators for DREF operations, as required by the DREF format. Information collected at the branch level is shared with local authorities.  IN the past the NS has revisited operational plans and used these as the situation warrants. The NS reports in a timely manner to different partners (e.g. IFRC, Australian Government, Shoken Fund) using the partners’ templates. It is noted that the MRCS does not have the resources for evaluation.

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_responses.notes: The MRCS has an automated accounting and financial system (MYOB) used at HQ level. Branches have their own accounting system (excel-based) but follow MRCS HQ financial procedures. All branches (except a few) uses templates for standardised accounting provided by HQ but due to the difference in accounting systems between HQ and branches there has been some delays in financial reporting. The NS has a focal point for finance in both peacetime and emergency response. NDRT and SDT teams are informed on financial procedures. During an emergency response the NS uses peacetime financial procedures, but this process offers limited options to expedite funds if needed. For example, requests only under 3000RM with justification does not need three quotations. The NS has procedures for transparency in place, but it acknowledges the need for these procedures to be strengthened. The NS uses the same procedures for control and oversight to prevent fraud and or corruption during peacetime and during emergencies. There is however a need for mitigating actions during emergencies. The MRCS has no MOU’s or agreements with vendors/suppliers during emergencies.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_responses.notes: MRCS has SOPs in place for mobile and radio communication, but they are outdated. When on response, staff and volunteers use their personal mobile phones and WhatsApp is used for emergency communication and updates. Team leaders have critical numbers saved on their phones. HQ and some of the branches have internet routers to provide data during responses. Key HQ staff and all branches have radio phones but there are limited resources for maintenance. At HQ all disaster vehicles have radio and at branch level only a few disaster vehicles are equipped with radios. The frequency licence for emergency radios have recently been renewed and all relevant personnel have been trained in radio communications. The NS has SOPs for radio and communication, but they are not updated. There is a portable generator at HQ and at some branches. The NS has no satellite phones. The NS has an IT focal point.

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_responses.notes: NS has a resource mobilisation policy but there is no specific strategy. At the moment there is no agreement or mechanism but NS is working on building partnerships with the private sector/donors for response capacity. NS does not have pre-disaster agreements. There is a need to strengthen the NS PMER capacity (quality proposal writing) for funding opportunities. A national emergency fund has not been formally established, however the NS has informal procedures to access limited resources upon request of SG, depending on the scale of disaster and capacity of branch. In kind donations are accepted based on needs subject to approval by SG. There are no formal procedures for accepting, rejecting donated goods.

The Logistics function is under the DM and Admin departments separately. Logistics under DM covers fleet, warehousing and stock management. Logistics under admin covers procurement. Supply chain for MRCS is not a function. There are procedures that exist for connecting the two logistics units. There is an administrative handbook that shows the route for procurement. Pre-positioned relief items are strategically located for some branches (Kuala Krai and Kota Bharu, Kelantan and Bukit Tadok and Kg Padang, Terengganu). These include a boat, buckets, Jerry Cans and cooking utensils and hygiene kits, emergency lights.  //Supply Chain Management appears not to be functioning within the NS. There is no documented expedited procedure. It is noted that they can request through WhatsApp but still has to request via an official letter. There are no formal procedures for accepting, rejecting donated goods. //NS has a designated person who gets on the job training on procurement.  This component is done by the admin department. Peace time financial procedures are used for procurement. There are no emergency procurement procedures. There is no database of suppliers. Additionally, the NS does not have pre-agreements in place with suppliers. //Fleet is managed under the DM department. All vehicles are insured and its usage is documented in logbooks. Maintenance records are not documented. HQ has sufficient vehicles and some branches have vehicles as well which appear sufficient. All drivers have valid licences, however there is no monitoring of expiration. All vehicles have seatbelts. Most do not have fire extinguishers and first aid kits. Drivers are trained in first aid. NS does not have emergency procedures to guide the hours for drivers including non-standard hours and compensation.// MRCS does not have a stock management manual but uses standard forms. Storage is insufficient and not secure to accept and store relief items during disasters. MRCS has storage in high risk areas of the country.

component_responses.notes: actualizar as politicas gestao, recrutamento e retencao do pessoal e voluntarios, Incorporar a componente do PGI, Formacao e Acesso Mais Seguro,garrantir medidas de seguranca, seguro de voluntarios e pessoal em emergencia

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_responses.notes: Existem políticas e procedimentos para garantir a sugurança do pessoal e voluntários, entrentanto, algumas não têm sido observadas.

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_responses.notes: A comunicação ainda não é a desejável, ainda precisamos de investir em formação e equipamento e adoptar a comunicação para a mudança.

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_responses.notes: A CVM nao tem procedimentos especificos de Administracao e Financas devidamente documentos para emergencias. Precisa de sistematiza-los e divulgar pelos gestores relevantes. Digitalizar os sistemas e procedimentos de autorizacao para acelerar assistencia humanitaria. Descentralizar a tomada de decisoes de acordo com a magnitude de emergencia.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_responses.notes: Foram criadas condições mínimas de funcionamento no entanto ainda precisa de um grande investimento de formação,

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_responses.notes: A CVM deve colocar a elaboracao de estrategia (Plano Director) de mobilizacao de recursos no topo de suas prioridades. Este plano deve ter em conta todas as referencias desta componente.

CVM tem um sector de logistica que atende assuntos globais da SN, o mesmo precisa de capacitação regular, tem manual de procedimentos gerais, precisa de procedimentos específicos de emergência. No sector e transportes precisa de renovar a frota e testar e induzir regularmente os motoristas e treina-los em Primeiros Socorros e Acesso Mais Seguro.  A CVM possui armazéns em locais estratégicos mas ese necessia de melhorar a localização dos mesmos para as comunidades mais vulneráveis e ceriar um padrão para gestão dos mesmos sobre tuido abrigo de emergêncuia. testar regularmente os

component_details.title: DRM Strategy
component_details.description: An outline of the overall goal that the NS seeks to achieve in its disaster and crisis response operations. The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

component_responses.notes: DRM is included in the PNGRCS Strategy from 2017 and in the updated draft Strategy 2021-2025 which will be presented to the General Assembly 2021. PNGRCS Strategy is reviewed annually with reports back to General Assembly every 2 years, and reflected in annual planning. Disseminated through the bi-annual GA. Gaps exist in reporting and monitoring against the strategy. PNGRCS DRM strategy is integrated and includes technical sectors, e.g. WASH, Health and First-aid. Support services engagement with DRM exists but is not specifically referenced. There is a need to strengthen technical support coordination from TWG at branch level. There will be specific reference to public health emergencies in the Strategy 2021.

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_responses.notes: PNGRCS DRM policy exists and an updated version is planned for adoption by GA in June 2021. IFRC policy was also acknowlegded and disseminated. PNGRCS DRM policy references the Fundamental Principles, is inclusive and integrates other sectors and services. DRM policy is reflected in trainings for staff and volunteers. The DRM policy will clarify the roles and responsibilities of DM and Health staff in epidemics.

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: No humanitarian diplomacy plan or actions in place yet based on IFRC's IDRL Checklist. Relevant legal facilities in national legislation have been identified. e.g. advocating for addressing gaps in the DM Act. PNGRC interest to compare existing Act with the Model Act. No staff trained in IDRL and IHL to be focal point, although some have attended conferences in this area. IDRL lessons learnt have been included in DREF reports or evaluations but not in a systematic manner. PNG RC participates in coordination meetings led by WHO.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_responses.notes: Affected communities are engaged through household assessments, including community elders. Tools used include VCA, CBFA, community-mapping, community profiling. All branches are trained on CEA. CEA has been integrated in the VCA with two-way communication with the community and quarterly reporting. Good practices exist for feedback and complaints - e.g. Branches have referral pathways established and there are complaint mechanisms referenced in various policies. A gap is identified to establish a mechanism for documentation, reporting and monitoring feedback and concerns. PSEA Policy has been adopted.  Training and adherence to protection policies could be strengthened. SPHERE standards exhibited in practice and there has been good support on adherence. A gap is identified to improve understanding and adherence of SPHERE standards, also at branch level. Policies are in place to minimize harm, e.g. Code of Conduct, but no specific plans in place to minimize specific, potential harmful impacts. PGI minimum standards are known by some in the NS but are yet to be more widely disseminated. PNGRCS is engaged in national cluster response, able to identify communication gaps and shares key life-saving messages, health promotions. Use of SADD  and PGI analysis is an area to be strengthened.

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_responses.notes: The PNGRCS Act establishes the National Society and its auxiliary role, with fundamental principles referenced in PNGRCS Act, policies and plans. While PNGRCS mandate is reflected in its constitution, policies, plans, and Fundamental Principles shared with those PNGRCS works with, more work is needed to disseminate and improve understanding among staff and volunteers. PNGRCS promotes IHL with the government and utilized humanitarian diplomacy to encourage government participation in the International Conference. Currently, PNGRCS has experience as auxiliary to health authorities on epidemic response, focused on community engagement, awareness and WASH; this is a focus area for 2021-2025.  PNGRCS is part of the country coordination mechanism and actively participated in the review of the DM Act 1984 (which includes Health).

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: Some, but not all branches have focal points for risk monitoring. There is an identified gap and finanical barriers to collecting primary and secondary data. NS is well accepted but gaps have not been identified. No early warning system exists currently, although branches work with partners and community to monitor for events. Another gap exiss in the HQ-Branch communications due to internet connectivity problems. A previous multi-hazard risk analysis existed but is not currently updated or shared further. IVCA is carried out at community level, this area could be strengthened. Disaggregated beneficiary data exists. No coordination of risk monitoring for cross-border areas currently. Cross-border coordination was done in the past. Some epidemic control training was done during Polio outbreak.

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_responses.notes: Existing scenario analyses are based on specific disasters. NS does not have own scenarios developed, relies on government-developed scenarios. NS response plans are aligned with public authorities' plans. Branches are involved in developing response strategy in partnership with local authorities. Contingency Plans do not really exist, or, like response plans, are developed on an ad hoc basis.

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_responses.notes: No specific trained staff for risk management at HQ. NS sometimes identifies, evaluates and mitigates potential risks through ground assessments, this is not systematic. While there is an integrated approach with WASH and First aid, there is room to improve holistic risk management. Key partner stakeholders are engaged. Fraud and corruption prevention systems are in place. Branches submit reports which end up with National Council or Governing Board. Crisis management discussions take place, but a specific unit does not exist. Protective equipment is available, trusted sources of information is disseminated.

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_responses.notes: Branch Coordinators are trained focal points for disaster preparedness. Lessons learnt sessions are carried out after responses. M&E identifies gaps and areas for improvement. NS relies on DREF and branches receive few financial resources. Preparedness actions are not updated, no NS policy or procedure exists to allocate budgets for strengthening preparedness capacity, NS refers to IFRC DREF policy/guidelines. Little to no epidemic preparedness.

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: NS does not have a BCP for major emergencies, except for COVID-19 (BCP not yet approved). Some BCP aspects are addressed in NS Strategic Plan. Communicating with donors to repurpose funds for unexpected needs is done on ad hoc basis, e.g. through DREF, communication links via RC/RC partners. No procedure in place.

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_responses.notes: No updated SOPs in place. SOPs from 2012 in use. For existing procedures, a gap is identified for more training and dissemination at branch and community levels. Procedures describe roles and responsibilities, incorporating some phases of response, procedures to scale alert levels up/down, but more training and dissemination is needed at branch and community levels. There is no decision-making flowchart or organogram. No branch level SOPs for disaster response.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_responses.notes: NS does not have an approved, multi-sectoral response plan for rapid deployment, response is ad hoc. Gender, age, disability and diversity is included on ad hoc basis, needs to be considered in planning. Commmunity members are involved in response plans. Plan adheres to principles and rules, fundamental principles, aligns with IFRC global standards. NS has experience in addressing secondary risks but more work is needed. NS plan includes response and recovery actions of other actors in its reports to Movement and other actors.   (NOTE: Interpretation of this Component is as a Response Plan triggered under a CP that is event specific.)

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes: Branch disaster response team have quarterly meetings, regular SMCC meetings. Key staff familiar with pre-disaster agreements but more training is needed. Coordination arrangements with local/national actors formalized for COVID-19 response. Movement partner capacity mapping is updated, movement coordination agreements are known, but needs to be further shared with branches. Some, not all, contractors have signed CoC. Pre-disaster agreements need strengthening. There are agreements with authorities for expedited import of humantarian goods, agreements with key suppliers of goods and services are formalized, no agreements with money transfer providers, no agreement with existing Social Protection systems.
Not applicable
Not applicable

5 out of 6 benchmarks acheived.  PNG RC uses a participatory approach including focus group discussions, inclusive of persons living with disabilities, different genders and from youth as well. IVCA is the main vehicle for community-based activities which has a "Member-led" approach where each community volunteer is trained. Through IVCA, the committees formed are from the communities themselves, enabling own response prior to other actors. Financial constraints means that only a limited number of IVCAs have been conducted.  NS supports communities to have in place an early warning system, but unclear if there is linkage to local early warning systems. There is emphasis on local knowledge for EWEA. Post-IVCA plans are developed, but no contingency planning besides DRR plan.

component_details.title: Mapping of NS capacities
component_details.description: A list of the NS capacities including HR (staff, response teams and volunteers) and equipment that are available for disaster/crisis response. Teams could include branch and national response teams. This should be defined by technical speciality where relevant.

component_responses.notes: 1 out of 6 benchmarks achieved.   Some pieces in place but not sufficient or consistent across branches.  PNG RC has a focal point for each specific area of intervention at HQ. Human resources needs are covered, however a gap was identified in DR personnel, available of sufficient equipment and training.  Currently no database to documents materials or equipment.  Sharing resources between branches is down ad hoc.   Area of strengthening: Making staff and volunteer training more systematic with assessments.

2 out of 6 relevant benchmarks achieved.   PNG RC receives technical support support from IFRC and ICRC for epidemics to ensure best practices. Many activities carried out ad hoc as no procedures in place, including methods to receive community feedback.   Areas of improvement: (1) SOPs and mechanisms for managing and responding to rumours (2) safety protocols and equipment for volunteers and staff.

component_details.title: Early Action Mechanisms
component_details.description: Designed to translate warnings into anticipatory actions to help reduce the impact of specific disaster or crisis events. They focus on consolidating available forecasting information and putting procedures in place to ensure that a NS can act ahead of any disaster/crisis. Forecast-based financing is included within the scope of this area.

component_responses.notes: 3 out of 6 benchmarks achieved.   PNG RC receives information from the national meteorological services on potential disaster but hasn’t established a clear process for actioning that information. In practice for information sharing, NS is part of the National Disaster Response Committee. At 2 branches, observatories monitor volcanic activity. Information is also passed down through branch networks and volunteers generally through mobile phones.  Area to strengthen: (1) creation of contingency plans and SOPs on who to alert when.

component_details.title: Cash Based Intervention (CBI)
component_details.description: An effective and flexible way, including all forms of cash and voucher-based assistance, to support people affected by emergencies, maintaining their dignity and choice, while fostering local economies. Cash should also be mainstreamed into other sectors (including Relief, shelter, livelihoods) and services (Logistics, Finance, etc.)

component_responses.notes: Not applicable

component_details.title: Emergency Needs Assessment
component_details.description: Assess the extent and impact of the damage caused by the disaster/crisis and the degree of vulnerability of the affected population. The first step in any emergency response, such an assessment will identify the needs that require external intervention and the gaps to be filled. It is a vital component of the programme-planning process.

component_responses.notes: 7 out of 7 benchmarks achieved.   Assessments are an area of strength for PNG RC. Assessments conducted include data on gender, age and other factors of vulnerability and also integrate local knowledge. The Needs assessments are quite comprehensive including secondary risks, coping mechanisms and early and self-recovery as well as gaps in existing capacities. Needs assessment are reflected in the EPoA with exception of DREF were there are constraints.  Volunteers and staff are trained and a standardized rapid assessment form.   Area to strengthen: (1) reviewing how age data is collected.

component_details.title: Affected population selection
component_details.description: Identification and selection of target Affected population for interventions, using a pre-defined set of criteria based on need and vulnerability. This includes consideration of specific vulnerabilities such as disability, age and gender.

component_responses.notes: 4 out of 5 benchmarks met.  Criteria identifying most vulnerable is used and well communicated with community. Branches have strong links to community leaders that support targeting of most vulnerable. Many volunteers receive on the job practice/training for data collection. Confidential data is protected, but assessment results are shared.   Area to Strengthen: (1) policy to better protect population data and transparency around how data is being used. (2) increase training for volunteers.

component_details.title: Emergency Operations Centre (EOC)
component_details.description: A central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions at a strategic level in an emergency situation. The common functions are to collect and analyze data; facilitate decision making that protects life and livelihoods; and disseminate those decisions to all concerned agencies and individuals. Generally located at the headquarter level of an organization.

component_responses.notes: PNG RC has an EOC at the HQ level and a few at branches or branches may be based out of provincial disaster management centres. At the HQ level the DM coordinator is the current focal point the EOC acts an information centre, rather than where strategic decisions are made. As an information centre, the EOC collects information then creates and disseminates sitreps. An EOC manual exists which includes SOPs but needs to be updated.   Areas to strengthen: (1) Update EOC SOPs in the manual and include integration of technical sectors and support services and clear levels of authority between the strategic and management levels of the EOC. (2) up to date contact list.

component_details.title: Information Management (IM)
component_details.description: Ability to manage information including requesting, receiving, analyzing and disseminating as per its procedures and partner requirements (IFRC and public authorities in particular). There should be a clear digital/paper trail that documents what, when and how the NS has acted and provides key information for the development of Emergency Plan of Actions. Includes IM between levels, between departments and Situational Reports, mapping, visualisation of data, GO platform (IFRC).

component_responses.notes: 3 out of 8 benchmarks achieved.   Key staff are not familiar with IM templates (from NS or IFRC), methodology and procedures with the exception of a standardized stirep. There’s limited and partial access to equipment to compile, visualize and share information. Meeting minutes are taken ad hoc to track decision making in the response. NS has access to data from local authorities at HQ and Branches.   Area for strengthening: (1) Establishing mechanisms to share information across levels, sectors and support services.

component_details.title: Testing and Learning
component_details.description: Drills and Simulations allow the organization to test, identify and learn from the results of these type of exercises and incorporate learning into future preparedness and response planning.

component_responses.notes: 0 out of 7 benchmarks acheived.  NS does not regularly conduct simulations and drills. Desktop simulations occur.

component_details.title: Activation of regional and international support
component_details.description: Procedures for requesting and accepting regional and international support in operations, including triggering coordination mechanisms for funding, materials and human resources deployments.

component_responses.notes: 4 out of 7 benchmarks achieved.  Key staff are familiar with support available from IFRC and ICRC, including funding mechanisms. SOPs aren’t in place but in practice very familiar with procedures like DREF. Close ties with IFRC country office who are informed regularly about potential needs but the context makes it difficult to relay information in the 24 hours timeframe. Emergency funding is received through the multi-lateral channel rather than bi-lateral ones

component_details.title: CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL, RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR (CBRN) EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS

component_responses.notes: Not applicable
Not applicable

3 out of 6 benchmarks achieved.   Stocks have been pre-positioned in areas of high risk but not based on an agreed upon scenario leading to concerns the numbers aren’t sufficient. Authorities are aware of these stocks. No pre-disaster agreements in place, supplies via IFRC. NS encourages communities to use locally available materials and communities have good knowledge on erecting tarpaulins.  Area to strengthen: Creation of SOPs on how to obtain stocks.

component_details.title: MANAGEMENT OF DEAD BODIES TO FACILITATE THEIR IDENTIFICATION

component_responses.notes: Not applicable - training provided in past
1 out of 2 benchmarks met.   PNG RC staff and volunteers have been trained and carry out RFL with the support of ICRC. Procedure and formal agreement not in place with ICRC.

5 out of 6 benchmarks achieved.  PNG RC role in recovery is informally acknowledged by authorities. Coordination with authorities is done through quarterly meetings and participation in JNAs, national recovery and reconstruction planning.  Key staff are familiar with the key recovery principles. Planning for transition from relief to recovery is challenging due to limited resources, however during assessments, gaps are identified for further support through partnerships. Areas to strengthen: Awareness of key recovery principles at the branch level.

component_details.title: NS-specific areas of intervention
component_details.description: Sector-specific or services provided by the NS in case of emergencies, it is in line with the NS mandate and legislation in country. It includes Community Based DP/DRR, Evacuation, Health in Emergencies, Epidemic and Pandemic, First aid, WASH, Food security and Livelihoods, Search and rRescue, Shelter, Management of dead bodies, RFL, Transition to recovery, and CBRN preparedness.

component_responses.notes: 3 out of 3 benchmarks achieved.   First aid is part of the integrated approach to (primarily) preparedness and disaster response. CBFA is part of DRR. The NS has trained and equipped volunteers. It’s noted that the NS isn’t always able to provide first aid kits.   Aare to strengthen: (1) exploring ways to prepare kits consistently across branches for volunteers in response.

4 out of 5 benchmarks achieved.   WASH is a part of PNG RC’s integrated response in practice and part of the draft DRM policy. WASH response is done in a coordinated way with partners through cluster participation and engagement with provincial partners. NS received technical support from IFRC and Australian RD.  Response teams have appropriate WASH training and skills. Not all branches have equipment in place.  Area to strengthen: SOPs for the branches to obtain WASH equipment.

3 out of 4 benchmarks achieved.   PNG NS has CBFA program and carry out community health and safety assessments as a part of that. Branches implementing CBFA consider planning with communities to conduct trainings which includes community mapping. Policy in place that states the need for volunteers to have first aid and annual refresher, however in practice, the limited resources means not all branches receive the refreshers. Health training for volunteers includes how to report suspect health events to staff or MoH.   Area to strengthen: (1) Ensure all branches have FA trainers.

component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_responses.notes: Area of strength for PNG with 3 out of 4 benchmarks reached.   Mechanisms exist at branch level to exchange information with communities and vice versa including executive committees who exchange information with communities and forward to HQ, branch focal points that liaise with NDRTs.  This information is considered in decision making through communications networks that link communities to HQ. Branches support community level response systems through collaboration with local partners, particularly local DR office.
