Gap identified that no communication procedures or SOPs in place that state when and with who to share information.

component_details.title: Cooperation with private sector
component_details.description: Mechanism that allows cooperation with private sector that often plays a strong role in response, particularly if there is impact on their staff and businesses. There is often a willingness to donate goods and services. Advance agreements help to expedite response actions.

component_responses.notes: PNG RC needs a screening tool in order to consistently do due diligence when selecting partners. Intermediary partners have systems in place to conduct assessments for accepting goods. NS has tools in place to support appropriate use of the emblem including their constitution and CoC with partners.   PNG RC has a corporate giving program that includes financial contributions and volunteer time that would leveraged to engage volunteers from corporate partners  Area to strengthen: A formal policy for corporate screening to increase awareness among staff and volunteers and avoid reputational risks.

component_details.title: Coordination with External Agencies and NGOs
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and collaboration with Non-Governmental Organization (NGO), both local and international NGOs, civil society organizations (CSOs) and United Nations agencies in country.

component_responses.notes: Area of strength for PNG RC. 4 out of 5 benchmarks met.   PNG RC is an active member of the humanitarian community. The established DMT for NS work together with UN and other NGOs in responses. NS provides information to the humanitarian coordination system. PASSA in place implemented in branch. PNG RC has recent experience UN-led appeals  for the COVID-19 pandemic.   Gap identified in partnership agreements. There was a previous project agreement with UN but none known of for response coordination. Agreements need to formalized and shared with the branches.

component_details.title: Civil Military Relations
component_details.description: Dialogue and interaction with military actors, essential to protect and promote humanitarian principles, avoid competition, minimize inconsistency and, when appropriate, pursue common goals.

component_responses.notes: Area of strength with PNG RC. 5 out of 5 benchmarks met.   PNG RC has coordination arrangement with military through ICRC IHL committee and works to promote the Fundamental Principles and use of emblem.  Military has assisted with the distribution of NFIs in coordination with local authorities. When coordinating with military forces, PNG RC is guided by the fundamental principles and the Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocols.   Context: PNG is currently in peacetime and it’s noted that this needs to be regularly reviewed and adjustments made should the military become involved in a conflict.    It's been announced that the military will be taking over the country's disaster response making this more relevant

component_details.title: Coordination with Movement
component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_responses.notes: Component of strength for PNG RC. 3 out of 4 benchmarks achieved. PNG RC has strong ties with IFRC and ICRC reflected through regular meetings, technical and financial assistance. Framework to receive, coordinate and report on assistance from IFRC well established. Have increased their coordination with neigbouring NS during the COVID-19 pandemic.  Areas to strengthen around (1) framework to receive, coordinate and report collaborations with PNS and (2) bi-lateral activities with neighbouring NS.

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_responses.notes: An area of strength for PNG RC with 4 out of 4 benchmarks reached. There are mechanisms in place to facilitate coordination with local and national authorities, through the RC Act and UN cluster meetings. Authorities are aware of their ability to provide technical support particularly around NFIs. PNG RC has always participated in government response planning and is currently inputting into the DM law review.    Areas to strengthen around (1)   coordination with local/provincial authorities and branches through update of RC Act and (2) mechanisms of control over assets, particularly donated goods.

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_responses.notes: 1 out of 12 benchmarks achieved. PNG RC does not have a documented strategy for resource mobilization but income generating activities including membership fees, first aid training and property lease. A portion of the this peace time revenue is set aside for future responses. NS has not yet carried out resource mobilization specific to disasters. Progress is expected on this as there are incoming funds that will enable the creation of an RM position. Practical mechanisms such as SOPs for activation, coordination and reporting, MOB tables and donation tracking system are identified gaps.  Area to strengthen: (1) Developing a resource mobilization plan that is tied to the response strategy including pre -disaster agreements with partners and donors, (2) Leverage existing Corporate Partnership program to mobilize resources in emergencies. (3) having a dedicated platform for donations that can be activated in 48 hours and SOPs for it.

In an emergency, PNG RC relays information in an ad hoc manner using social media and mobile phones. Branches and HQ have radios but devices and networks not regularly maintained. More common to rely on mobile phones and some branches have satellite phones as the secondary communication method. To support operational continuity in an emergency, HQ has generator and internet router and pockets WiFis are available at all levels but internet connectivity is a challenge in PNG due to infrastructure and cost.   Areas to strengthen: (1) consistent secondary communication system (2) establish a centralized server that would increase information sharing. (3) appointing a focal point and providing trainings to staff (4) creation of an IT policy. //4 out of 7 benchmarks met. Ad hoc logistics unit/function is in place, but coordination is not systematic as the software is not yet in place. Key staff at HQ are familiar with IFRC logistics services as they use the IFRC Logistics hand book regularly. There’s no pre-existing supplier agreements as this is conducted through IFRC. Prepositioned stock meet SPHERE standards.   Areas for strengthening: (1) Tools to facilitate regular reporting twice a year (2) creation of logistics policy outlining procedures for operations (3) Review strategic location of prepositioned stocks in disaster prone and locations with good transportation links (4) increased training of staff at the branch level on roles in distribution, supply chain management, stock receipt and management.//Component of strength as 3 out of 4 benchmarks met.   Area for Strengthening: establishment of SOPs for managemtn of in-kind donations.//0 out of 5 benchmarks met. No procurement focal person in place and lack of procedures and systems established. IFRC provides support on this component.//2 out of 10 benchmarks met.  No manual in place yet that would document many procedures to meet more benchmarks. Physical fleet well maintained through licensed mechanics and maintenance records. //Area of strength: 3 out of 4 benchmarks met. Manual in place and staff and volunteers are trained on procedure through on the job training. Branches have storage available 24/7. Branches organize transport after or during (usually) working hours to receive or dispatch supplies.

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_responses.notes: 6 out of 14 benchmarks acheived.  TORs for volunteers occur under DREFs but not other operations as there’s no HR person. Responders receive training that include behavioral standards including CoC and Child protection policy and all staff and volunteers have signed the CoC. Personnel have visibility items but IDs are not appropriate for the context. In the absence of a policy safety and security managed ad hoc but done well in practice. Volunteers have accident insurance and there’s a per diem policy in place. Difficult to maintain a formal database due to volunteer turn over but branches know who to contact in emergencies.   Area to strengthen: (1) Standardizing progressive training plan that fully incorporates gender and post-training assessments. (2) establishment of ERT SOPs. (3) Establish procedures to incorporate spontaneous volunteers during emergencies. (4) Trainings on self-care, violence, and harassment in the workplace for volunteers and staff at all levels.

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_responses.notes: An area for improvement for PNG RC as 0 out of 7 benchmarks met as some aspects happening in practice but no formal policy or system in place. In practice, branches have strong knowledge of safety & security practices and networks for information. Branch focal points share information and ensure teams have appropriate equipment.

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_responses.notes: 5 out of 10 benchmarks acheived.   PNG RC has some structure around their communication. There’s a designated focal point at HQ and available templates through IFRC as well as a designated spokesperson. When needed there’s joint coordination with IFRC and ICRC on communication and key messages messages in an emergency are developed and shared with staff regularly.  Area to strengthen: (1) training of communication focal points at the branch level. (2) tracking of negative media and process to respond. (2) finalize communications and social media policy (currently in draft)

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_responses.notes: 3 out of 8 benchmarks reached for this component. PMER capacity exists but no specific focal point or framework exists for response. IVCA and DREF have  M&E components that are used. Incorporation of lesson learnt into future operations done ad hoc.   Areas to strengthen: (1) Creation of a standardized monitoring and reporting tools (2) ensuring a unified system/framework between branch, HQ and IFRC (3) increase resources to conduct evaluations and integrate lessons learnt

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_responses.notes: Financial procedures are in place but no specific procedures related to emergencies. No specific focal point for emergency finance and admin but some staff have been trained. An internal auditor is on staff and procedures are in place such as the Finance and Admin manual, fraud policy and Code of Conduct facilitate transparency.   Areas to strengthen: (1) finance procedures don’t specify in-kind donations. (2) training for branch staff on details of agreements (3)  increase ability for operations/programs manager to have oversight on monitoring and compliance of budgets.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_responses.notes: In an emergency, PNG RC relays information in an ad hoc manner using social media and mobile phones. Branches and HQ have radios but devices and networks not regularly maintained. More common to rely on mobile phones and some branches have satellite phones as the secondary communication method. To support operational continuity in an emergency, HQ has generator and internet router and pockets WiFis are available at all levels but internet connectivity is a challenge in PNG due to infrastructure and cost.   Areas to strengthen: (1) consistent secondary communication system (2) establish a centralized server that would increase information sharing. (3) appointing a focal point and providing trainings to staff (4) creation of an IT policy.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_responses.notes:
• Monitoring and Early Warning is very strong for PRC as related to hydrometrical emergencies (e.g. typhoons, flooding) as PRC is linked to the national weather forecasting organizations (i.e. PAGASA) that provide “Climate Outlooks” for the year.
• Early warning messaging is distributed through the Hazard App and through other means (WhatsApp, Viber, Phone).
• Hazard App is an excellent example within the RCM of risk messaging and preparedness actions that can be taken.
• PRC recently started a forecast-based financing project.
• DMS uses various (e.g. INFORM, government census data) and has used innovative forms of data collection (e.g. 510) to identify multidimensional risks.
• PRC completes VCAs and working to digitize them to make it more useable.
• Man-made risks/incidents are collected however noted that there is limited analysis, and this information is not centralized with other national risk data.
• It was consistently noted that there is limited time and technical capacity to conduct analysis of hazard/risk data within PRC.
• Does not appear to have centralized and accessible database/mapping of previous disasters or have completed analysis of trends.
• Unclear how hazard, risk and context analysis informs through evidence-based process the selection of priority areas for preparedness actions (e.g. high-risk chapter)
• Appears hazard data is not made widely accessible and shared with chapters or other departments.

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_responses.notes:
• An earthquake contingency plan is in draft. The document is strong CP example and expected to be tested/revised following simulated exercise.
• The document contains relevant information. The scenario defined aligns with the government scenario. The draft is a strong example, on which other contingency plans can be developed.
• A Contingency Planning development process exists with support of a Contingency Planning TWG, which is multi-departmental.
• DMS Response Unit to determine next CP to develop, but unclear how this is linked with hazard/risk/context analysis conducted or rating of impact/likelihood.
• To-date, other contingency plans do not appear to exist.
• Noted other departments (e.g. Health Department) has developed CP for public health emergencies (e.g. Ebola, influenza).

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_responses.notes:
• Does not appear there is a formal structure to systematically monitor, evaluate, report, and mitigate organizational, financial, and/or reputational risks.
• Organizationally sensitive incidents reported and managed by the SG (and subsequently delegated to legal) without a feedback mechanism to track how risks were managed.
• Apart from the SG, there is not a dedicated staff person assigned to manage risk, although Internal Audit department is in place. Risk Management functions exist partially through different departments/focal points such as IHL and Communications, but not centralized through focal point or committee, for instance.
• Strategic plan contains areas to develop include increasing accountability and transparency. Tendering process exists to mitigate procurement risks.
• Tight financial controls (i.e. signing authorities) and layers of administrative processes acts to reduce financial risks, however increases operational risks (i.e. delays).

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_responses.notes:
• PRC has many institutional preparedness and response capacity projects (predominantly in DMS) but also within other departments.
• No NS-wide (i.e. cross-departmental) and accessible mapping of preparedness activities. Noted that IRSPO contains excel workbook of partner project information.
• PRC has not completed a systematic and holistic assessment of its institutional preparedness and response capacity, however DRCE is meant to support this.
• PRC acknowledged need for a general baseline of its response capacity to support preparedness activities in a systematic and holistic manner.
• It does not appear that PRC allocates a certain % of response funding for capacity-building although noted that often capacity building activities are included in response budgets.
• There is more recent effort for hazard/context analysis to inform the selection of priority areas for preparedness actions, however this is not consistently applied as partners or PRC leadership often pre-identify areas/locations.

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes:
• Blood Services mandated to have business continuity plans in place by law.
• Out-of-date Business Continuity plan exists for PRC, but appears not well known or accessible.
• Business continuity plan referenced in the DMS Manual.
• Business Continuity Plans are identified as necessary documents for both NHQ and Chapter Disaster Preparedness that appear to have cross departmental function (i.e. volunteers, logistics, information).
• In the draft DMS Manual, at the Chapter level, it is noted that a localized version of a Business Continuity Plan should exist, of which HQ would provide the template/guidance.

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_responses.notes:
• PRC acknowledges this is an area that requires urgent attention.
• PRC has draft of written guidelines, roles and responsibilities, command structures, coordination mechanisms among departments.
• Response procedures/checklists exist within different departments, but does not appear to be consolidated.
• Communication and information requests from HQ can be overburdening for chapters, with different HQ departments contacting chapters often requesting similar information.
• Draft SOPs contains information on activation of regional and global RCM tools.
• There is a need to increase sensitization of the response procedures at all levels (i.e. governance, management at HQ, and at Chapter-level) with PRC and across department.
• PRC in discussions to adopt Incident Command Structure (ICS), which is an excellent initiative and will create clear roles and responsibility and command structures.
• PRC DR SOP identifies the phases of response and actions at different organizational levels. Procedures could be better aligned with flowchart.
• Chapter Administrators are knowledgeable of their roles and responsibilities during a response, however not documented; often based more on past experience and trainings. Risk of Chapter nonfunctional during a response if CA is unavailable.
• Decision-making authority and budget approvals often significantly affects the quality and timeliness of service delivery.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_responses.notes:
• PRC leverages barangay recovery committees (BaReCom) to aid in the identification of those affected.
• Results are presented back to communities at assemblies.
• In general operational objectives appear to be appropriately defined
• In general, it was noted that PRC does not always consistently consult, and consultation methods are not always consistent. The general trend is that during response, there is less consultation, however longer-term recovery involves greater consultation.
• IFRC Appeal developed before finalization of PRC Plan of Action, but noted this is not common practice.

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes:
• Although they can vary, pre-disaster meetings among departments and with RCM partners do occur annually, but typically before typhoon season.
• A Movement Coordination Agreement (MCA) between PRC-IFRC-ICRC currently in draft form.
• PRC has agreement with Finnish RC for Camp Management ERU, and expected that IFRC to support ERU and FACT.
• To facilitate the import of humanitarian aid and to expedite visas for incoming personnel, the Government of the Philippines has the  Philippine International Humanitarian Assistance (PIHA) guidelines, of which PRC provides input.
• PRC has pre-agreements with companies to support Cash Transfer since 2012.
• PRC has no framework agreements with suppliers.

component_details.title: Cash Based Intervention (CBI)
component_details.description: An effective and flexible way, including all forms of cash and voucher-based assistance, to support people affected by emergencies, maintaining their dignity and choice, while fostering local economies. Cash should also be mainstreamed into other sectors (including Relief, shelter, livelihoods) and services (Logistics, Finance, etc.)

component_responses.notes:
• PRC has been using CTP since 2009 during Typhoon Ketsana (Ondoy), Tropical Storm Bopha (Pablo) in 2012, during Typhoon Yolanda, and more recently during the Mayon Response.
• PRC has agreements with financial service providers; LBC can cater 200 beneficiaries per day while Globe and PhilPost can cater 3000 beneficiaries in 3 hours. PRC has had agreements since 2012, which have been renewed until today.
• Draft SOP and Guidelines for Cash Transfer Programming have existed since Oct 2013. It was noted that previous CTP guidance documents existed in 2008, however document could not be located. In 2012, PRC developed Cash for Work Guidelines. These documents likely need to be updated based on recently learnings.
• CTP self-assessment indicates there is apprehension in using CTP at leadership levels.
• “Red Rose” platform has been tested during Mayon response in transferring 2800 cash grants.
• PRC has launched a CTP project (Nov 2017), with ambitious targets: “to be able to reach over 100,000 households in large-scale cash interventions”.
• There are concerns that scaling-up CTP for large emergencies would be challenging due to financial, administrative, logistics and IT bottlenecks, as well as not having procedures to mitigate security risk.

component_details.title: Emergency Needs Assessment
component_details.description: Assess the extent and impact of the damage caused by the disaster/crisis and the degree of vulnerability of the affected population. The first step in any emergency response, such an assessment will identify the needs that require external intervention and the gaps to be filled. It is a vital component of the programme-planning process.

component_responses.notes:
• PRC collects information on impact, effects to basic lifelines, and problems by sector, and Chapter capacities in rapid assessment (RDANA) form.
• Information gathered includes gender, disability, protection issues.
• Detailed assessment form collects information on social/market capital impact, and damage to natural resources that would inform the affect to market capital/livelihoods.
• Form has "gap identification" section highlighting types of assistance already being provided and which organization and sector and specific assistance provided.
• PRC ENA self-assessment considered that Primary Data Collection is strong.
• PRC ENA self-assessment identified that Primary Data Analysis, Reporting/Dissemination, and Secondary Data Collection were gaps.
• PRC ENA SWOT Analysis showed gaps include: Absence of Data privacy and use policy;  Insufficient trained volunteers, No unified/composite standardized assessment template. NHQ
requests for different templates from different services to be filled up (health, social, DM); No analytical framework (nothing clear on how to do analysis);  Absence of Data privacy and use policy; No structured assessment guidelines
• Noted that a plan to address the SWOT analysis gaps have beendeveloped.
• As related to the SWOT analysis findings, the government of Philippines enacted data privacy law recently, by which all organizations must comply, but doesn’t appear PRC developed method to ensure compliance with law as of yet.

component_details.title: Affected population selection
component_details.description: Identification and selection of target Affected population for interventions, using a pre-defined set of criteria based on need and vulnerability. This includes consideration of specific vulnerabilities such as disability, age and gender.

component_responses.notes:
• PRC has primary/secondary criteria which include damaged or partially damaged housing, those affected who did not receive assistance from government or other organizations.
• Selected beneficiary listings from local governments are verified by RC143 volunteers. Those displaced by disasters are provided hot meals and NFIs.
• DMS has within their DM Operation Manual, general guidance on beneficiary selection.
• PRC uses barangay recovery committees (BaReCom) to aid in the identification of those affected. Results are presented back to communities at assemblies.
• Likely varying between chapters, responders use standardized forms for data collection. Limited use of mobile data collection.
• Beneficiaries that do not receive assistance are prioritized by PRC.

component_details.title: Emergency Operations Centre (EOC)
component_details.description: A central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions at a strategic level in an emergency situation. The common functions are to collect and analyze data; facilitate decision making that protects life and livelihoods; and disseminate those decisions to all concerned agencies and individuals. Generally located at the headquarter level of an organization.

component_responses.notes:
• PRC’s EOC, once activated, is strong RCM example of a crossdepartmental central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions. The EOC is in part related to the physical space, but its strength reflects the team coordination and collaboration.
• There is dedicated space for operational management to convene.
• There are assigned staff for ensuring EOC functionality on a 24/7 basis.
• There are system backups and redundancies, and specific procedures for the EOC activation.
• There is an identified need for clearer roles and responsibilities in the EOC SOPs.

component_details.title: Information Management (IM)
component_details.description: Ability to manage information including requesting, receiving, analyzing and disseminating as per its procedures and partner requirements (IFRC and public authorities in particular). There should be a clear digital/paper trail that documents what, when and how the NS has acted and provides key information for the development of Emergency Plan of Actions. Includes IM between levels, between departments and Situational Reports, mapping, visualisation of data, GO platform (IFRC).

component_responses.notes:
• Information Management is a cross-organizational component, and encapsulates all manners of information, knowledge, data and its supporting policies, structures and procedures that should help inform evidence-based operational decision-making.
• There are good examples of good practices of IM within PRC (e.g. DMS) but in general IM is a gap for the NS.
• Departments have their own databases of information (e.g. volunteer, staff, trainings, deployments) which is collecting information in different manners, some incomplete, and updated without predictable frequency.
• Timely access to information and data sharing from OpCen to other departments has been identified as a challenge.
• IM identified as a key area with strategy, “volunteers + logistics + information technology”, however general observation is there are misunderstandings between IM, IT/MIS and ICT.
• There is no centralized place to collect and view PRC documents (e.g. NS Policies, Procedures, Operational Documents, evaluations, reports, etc.), which makes understanding and adherence to new policies and procedures difficult.
• It is often cited that capacity and time to conduct analysis is limited, which is in part related to inconsistent IM structures procedures.
• Noted in ENA Workshop that there is “No Information Management guidelines”.

component_details.title: Testing and Learning
component_details.description: Drills and Simulations allow the organization to test, identify and learn from the results of these type of exercises and incorporate learning into future preparedness and response planning.

component_responses.notes:
• PRC leadership appears to have a very strong desire to conduct regular drills, simulations, and tabletop exercises.
• PRC has done earthquake tabletop exercises (large and small scale), and some departments conduct their own regular exercises (e.g. ERU)
• Learnings from the earthquake tabletop exercise were captured, and expected to feed into planning.
• Latest draft of EQ Contingency Plan expected to be tested using simulation/tabletop exercise, and revised accordingly.
• Not clear whether all Chapters have simulations and drills, however it is common that chapters regularly participate in LGU-led drills.
• Does not appear that evidence-based hazard/risk and context analysis is driving which type of emergency simulations should be prioritized; this appears this is directed by PRC leadership.
• PRC involved in national-level drill exercises with public authorities.
• There appears to be no formal testing schedule.
• Noted that RFL and Safety Services integrate scenarios which may include security risks, into their training.

component_details.title: Activation of regional and international support
component_details.description: Procedures for requesting and accepting regional and international support in operations, including triggering coordination mechanisms for funding, materials and human resources deployments.

component_responses.notes:
• Significant experience from past emergencies of available IFRC/ICRC supports
• Good communication/collaboration with IFRC during response phase reduces the need for PRC to be intimately familiar with various IFRC response processes.
• PRC has International Relations for Strategic Partnership Office (IRSPO) exists, to assist regional/international responders.
• Following Haiyan Response, government formed Philippines International Humanitarian Assistance Cluster (PIHAC) as a "one-stop shop/welcome center" to facilitate international assistance.

component_details.title: CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL, RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR (CBRN) EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS
MANAGEMENT OF DEAD BODIES TO FACILITATE THEIR IDENTIFICATION
NS-specific areas of intervention
component_details.description: Sector-specific or services provided by the NS in case of emergencies, it is in line with the NS mandate and legislation in country. It includes Community Based DP/DRR, Evacuation, Health in Emergencies, Epidemic and Pandemic, First aid, WASH, Food security and Livelihoods, Search and rRescue, Shelter, Management of dead bodies, RFL, Transition to recovery, and CBRN preparedness.

component_details.title: Mapping of NS capacities
component_details.description: A list of the NS capacities including HR (staff, response teams and volunteers) and equipment that are available for disaster/crisis response. Teams could include branch and national response teams. This should be defined by technical speciality where relevant.

component_responses.notes:
• Services keep information on trained volunteers/staff, but no consolidated database.
• Service have list of staff and volunteers trained. Some volunteers trained on multiple areas of intervention; different services often competing for these volunteers.
• OpCen has up-to-date mapping of response assets (e.g. fleet), which has controls/restrictions on access to this information based on user profile.
• HR resources typically made available for the initial response. Noted that for longer term responses and recovery, PRC has difficulty finding adequate manpower. This often leads to overstretched staff.
• Among chapters, HR resources are often shared. No formal mechanisms exist for the sharing of resources across chapters. Examples were noted of HQ directing some resources inefficiency.
• PRC uses Chapter Classification based on income generation (e.g. A-E), and does not necessarily capture response capacity. Often a chapter with a low classification may be very capable responders, and viceversa. The chapter classification provides the number assets, number of people trained, and also identify the number of families it is expected to provide support.
• A tool referred to as Performance Quality Accountability (PQA), used in 20% of chapters has been piloted and has been mentioned to be able to measure Chapter capacity but not shared with all response units (i.e. DMS) as of yet.
• PRC HQ also has chapter profiles, and has good informal sense of the “strong responding” chapters, but not agreed PRC-wide method and assessment tool developed.

component_details.title: Early Action Mechanisms
component_details.description: Designed to translate warnings into anticipatory actions to help reduce the impact of specific disaster or crisis events. They focus on consolidating available forecasting information and putting procedures in place to ensure that a NS can act ahead of any disaster/crisis. Forecast-based financing is included within the scope of this area.

component_responses.notes:
• PRC linked to the national weather forecasting organizations (PAGASA) and information is collected, translated and relayed
• PRC has the Hazard App which is used to send alerts and early warning messages to users.
• Also the OpCen uses text messages and PRC is active on twitter, Viber, Facebook and WhatsApp.
• PRC maintains at 24/7 OpCen to send out messages and they include a call-back number to contact them.
• Through RC143 community volunteer network, PRC is able to communicate with community members for alerts and response actions (e.g. evacuation).
• Alerts and early actions exist structured through a trigger-based system with pre-defined criteria.
• Forecast-based financing is being explored through new project.

component_details.title: Coordination with External Agencies and NGOs
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and collaboration with Non-Governmental Organization (NGO), both local and international NGOs, civil society organizations (CSOs) and United Nations agencies in country.

component_responses.notes:
• PRC attends and sometimes hosts Humanitarian Country Team (HCT) meetings.
• Typically IRSPO represents on behalf of the PRC/SG.
• PRC share operational updates, and coordinate with external partners.
• IFRC is part of the UN cluster system and involves PRC in various meetings for different thematic areas (e.g. food security, emergency shelter, protection, early recovery, camp management, cash, gender)
• Identified need for greater information sharing among PRC departments on engagement with external agencies.

component_details.title: Civil Military Relations
component_details.description: Dialogue and interaction with military actors, essential to protect and promote humanitarian principles, avoid competition, minimize inconsistency and, when appropriate, pursue common goals.

component_responses.notes:
• Although PRC has developed relationships with the military, engaging through meetings and military exercises, it is acknowledged that the CRM function still needs to be formally established within PRC.
• There is a need to increase PRC awareness of its role and engagement with the military.
• PRC recently identified a dedicated focal person on Civil-Military Relations.
• PRC is the representative for Southeast Asia in the Asia Pacific CivilMilitary Working Group.
• In Mindanao, PRC does coordinate with military before entering insecure areas.
• PRC has invested in assets which has allowed them to remain less dependent on military assets for response.
• With PRC's experience in conflict in the south, there is an understanding of having precaution when using military assets.
• There is understanding the risks with close engagement with Military.
• IHL department has relationship with other civ-mil organizations.

component_details.title: Coordination with Movement
component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_responses.notes:
• Philippines is a laboratory context for the Strengthening Movement Coordination and Cooperation (SMCC) process.
• Draft Movement Coordination Agreement (MCA) developed.
• For partners in-country, PRC has bilateral agreements with 11 PNS which are project-based (currently working on developing MoU with Turkish RC).
• A security map to facilitate RCRC operations in the south of the country, which was previously off limits to PNS and IFRC, indicates an openness of other partners to participate in the response.
• During an emergency, it is standard practice for PRC-ICRC-IFRC to meet (i.e. mini-summits around emergencies) to define the response roles and responsibilities per organization.
• Acknowledged that there is a need for a 4W (who, what, where, when) for coordination of preparedness actions, and more structured/regularly partner meetings.
• In principles, coordination meetings planned for 3rd week of every month, but are less predictable.
• PRC has some capacity to receive international assistance, mediumscale disasters. In the event of a large scale disaster, would likely request support from IFRC for response tools to manage the coordination.
• Noted for Vinta, IFRC prematurely launched an appeal prior to PRC completing its PoA. The IFRC appeal was not fully contextualized/appropriate for the Vinta response. Acknowledged that this is not common practice.
• It was noted from PNS that IFRC should increase its support to facilitate Movement Coordination, but acknowledged this requires shared vision from all parties of what this means.

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_responses.notes:
• PRC is officially part of the national and local humanitarian coordination systems through the NDRRMC, RDRRMC, PDRRMC, and MDRRMC.
• PRC role is well articulated in the Republic Act 10072 (i.e. Red Cross Law) as well as the Republic Act 10121 (Philippines DRRM Act of 2010).
• PRC has been one of the original members of the NDRRMC (and is also the only non-government member) since 1972.
• Since Haiyan, PRC is part of the PIHAC.
• NS has established good coordination and communication lines with authorities at different levels, which would enable PRC to better understand government capacities to respond, and where PRC is best positioned to support as an auxiliary.
• In general, good connections at local levels, often with local authorities being volunteers.
• PRC involved in many simulation and drill exercises with public authorities at NHQ and chapters.
• PRC is the only identified permanent non-governmental member of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC), formerly the National Disaster Coordinating Council (NDCC) as defined by Presidential Decree No. 1566 “Strengthening the Philippine Disaster Control, Capability and Establishing the National Program on Community Disaster Preparedness”.

component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_responses.notes:
• As identified in the draft Playbook, there are connections between the community, chapter and HQ.
• Although at times informal, information sharing from communities to chapters is effective in practice.
• Information is collected from communities to support decision-making at chapter and HQ levels, with regard to response actions.
• Chapters have established communication lines with RCAT143 team leads, to collect information, share early warning messages, and mobilize resources.
• RCATs form the community response structure, and are often part of the local authorities.
• Good connections with Barangay Recovery Committees and other local response groups.

component_details.title: Cooperation with private sector
component_details.description: Mechanism that allows cooperation with private sector that often plays a strong role in response, particularly if there is impact on their staff and businesses. There is often a willingness to donate goods and services. Advance agreements help to expedite response actions.

component_responses.notes:
• PRC’s Fund Generation Policy Annex H identifies a list of blacklisted partners based on criteria from “RCM Guidelines for Corporate Partnership (2003)”. The document also identifies characteristics of desirable partnerships.
• General practice that PRC does not accept funding from tobacco companies (not in policy).
• Any requests to use PRC emblem/logo for fund activities are vetted by IHL and Legal reviews agreements.
• If fund generation received a request from corporation to volunteer it would be directed to VS or DMS.
• Appears no formal process to engage with corporations for the use of staff as volunteers.
• Some examples of cooperation with private sector (e.g. Globe, Shell, Del Monte, Cebu Pacific).

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_responses.notes:
• HR appears to have identified the key areas to improving their response contribution, as outlined the PRC Strategy 2017-2020.
• HR identified key priorities including: HRIS (HR Information System), IPMS (Integrated Performance Management System), study on compensation and benefits.
• Appears there are no approved expedited recruitment procedures in emergency, including rapid scaling-up (i.e. fast lane).
• Formally approved expedited procedures do not appear to exist for accepting spontaneous volunteers.
• No consolidate and accessible database exists showing HR/VR information, trainings, capacities, etc. Exists in many different locations among different departments.
• HR has a roster of all staff, containing general information (contact details, name, gender, religion), but database is incomplete, and only updated on an ad hoc basis upon request of management.
• HR recently developed checklist for emergency response, however not tested or formalized.
• Previous evaluation findings indicate long delays in issuing contracts, often leading to delays in staff getting paid.
• Currently Performance Evaluation Development Framework (PEDF) is a compliance tool, used twice a year. Some examples observed of managers investing in professional development HR/VR.
• Volunteers need to pay their own insurance which may discourage volunteer engagement.
• Volunteer engagement is ad hoc, typically dependent on management/leadership of chapters and resources available.
• No HR retention strategies in place, but looking to complete study on retention.
• No systematic on boarding process of staff/volunteers exist, however HR piloted "New Employee Orientation (NEO)" in July 2017.
• Noted that Volunteer Policy needs to be updated, as drafted in 1970s.
• Noted that there is no consistent rates for per diems for volunteers from chapter to chapter.

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_responses.notes:
• PRC does not have a dedicated focal point to manage safety and security issues, including monitoring, collection of information on incidents, and procedures for remedial actions. The Safety and Security function is spread among different roles and departments under the Health, Safety and Security Committee (e.g. Health and Safety Officer, Safer Access Officer, IHL).
• PRC is reliant on ICRC security structures (e.g. 24 radio room) and security focal point for advice prior to deployment.
• Although it was noted that since 2012 PRC collected incident information from social media and the news, there is no robust safety and security analysis completed.
• Expected that larger security incidents are reported, however no formal mechanism/thresholds for when to report, what information to provide, and to whom to report.
• Noted that some chapters in the field have a strong relationship with ICRC in coordinating deployment to conflict-affected areas.
• A safety and security memo was sent in 2016 (Memo 61-2016).
• This is a corporate risk to the organization, and there is a need for developing and ensure compliance with safety and security protocols.
• Safer Access training is not mandatory of staff and volunteers.
• It was noted that analysis of data is limited, and that there is no consistent monitoring of staff.

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_responses.notes:
• Communications in emergencies appear to be working well in terms of a strong presence on social media, clear directives on who can be a spokesperson, high quality press releases.
• Communications department has good relationships with media contacts, to correct misinformation.
• Strong relationship among PRC-ICRC-IFRC. Officially meet monthly to ensure good coordination as it relates with Communications.
• Identified communications focal points at chapters. Acknowledged that many individuals receiving basic trainings have since left.
• The NS uses Social Media (e.g. Facebook, Twitter) for fund development and to draw attention to response needs.
• Does not appear communication material translated into local language.

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_responses.notes:
• MEAL Unit within DMS responsible for coordinating, producing and sharing operational bulletins.
• PRC has a standard Plan of Action template used for operations that contain specific operational objectives and indicators.
• 3W (who, what, where) established is an excellent RCM example of information sharing within the RCM.
• Unit has GIS/mapping capacity, able to display information visually.
• Operation Sheet is used to monitor all response actions and includes damage and needs, 3W, deployments, situational updates, and other operational data. The data is contained in a single source (i.e. excel) and accessible on Google Drive by all HQ DMS Staff.
• Operational plans are updated with more accurate figures from the damage and needs assessments.
• Noted that learnings coming out of the EQ tabletop exercise were incorporated in to response procedures.
• Noted that there has generally been no application of lessons learned from previous responses, although there have been lessons captured from recovery programming.
• MEAL provides monthly reports to ASG office on projects and special funding, but acknowledgement this communication and information sharing with PMER department is needed.

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_responses.notes:
• Draft Finance Manual contains emergency procedures. PRC has internal financial controls that are followed, but there is a need for a ‘fast-lane’ to expedite procedures during emergencies.
• Funds can be released with electronic approval from SG, and documentation is regularized the following day.
• Signing authorities are very low and centralized; typically all approvals go to the SG which prevents timely operational response.
• Noted there is a bureaucratic and paperwork-intense approval process.
• Noted that fear of signing off without previous senior management approval, which creates “reverse approval” process (i.e. if the SG signs first, everyone down the line will easily sign).
• There is an over-reliance on memos/directives to facilitate decisionmaking from leadership, and few agreed-upon policies to follow as an alternative.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_responses.notes:
• PRC has post-paid phones for all managers • PRC has Viber group and Facebook chat with all key staff number accessible for a response.
• Chapters interviewed appeared to have access to radios. Additionally, some chapters noted the range was not very sufficient for the radios.
• Headquarters OpCen has functioning radio room.
• Fleet vehicles are not consistently equipped with radios, although DMS vehicles do.
• PRC has dedicated frequency cleared by national authorities.
• Sat Phones are not centralized. DMS, OpCen, SG, ASG have their own.
• OpCen has access to generator and UPS (battery). Recommended from HQ that all chapters have this, but not all do.
• OpCen also has dedicated internet connection.
• PRC IT department negotiating with Microsoft to get access to Office 360. Plans exist to eventually migrate to Office 360.
• Data is not backed-up across all departments. Accounting digitally backup data. Plan to have information eventually on the cloud.

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_responses.notes:
• During an emergency, Fund Generation (FG) is part of the EOC. DMS defines targets and FG support in reaching this target.
• PRC has Fund Generation Policy which defines its roles and responsibilities (including for chapters), guiding principles, and procedures.
• PRC does collaborate with private sector and signs MoAs with corporations when approached, but appears not to strategically seek partnerships through FG.
• PRC does not have an online platform for accepting donations although they are working towards this. Current online platform only provides banking information so donors can deposit funds. Previously PRC had SMS donation, but no longer exists.
• FG is aware of general practices for accepting in-kind goods and is documented in the FG policy.
• It was identified that PRC needs to have a better understanding of how the organization is perceived by external stakeholders (e.g. public, authorities, private sector, etc.) vis-à-vis its role, mandate, and function to help support fund generation.
• In general, PRC has no pre-set percentage of annual budgets for Preparedness activities, although Blood Services has annual targets.
• PRC has corporate strategy which includes annual income targets.
• It was noted that more compelling images, stories could be collected to support fund generation.

• PRC Logistics identified as key strategic area, and completed a thorough logistics assessment with support from IFRC and Finnish RC.
• A clear logistics function exists within PRC, managing procurement, warehousing, transportation, and fleet. However it is noted that many of the PRC service departments (e.g. DMS, Health, WASH) have their own parallel logistic functions.
• Procurement is partially centralized by the Procurement unit (40%) of the NS spend, the rest is managed by the units directly (60%).
• Process lead time appears long, up to 2 months as per some user experience, however no procurement follow up, data base or dashboard exist, therefore no information on the procurement follow up is provided along the process to the requester.
• Procurement Process has multiple and heavy approval process and the signatory rights are centralized to higher management.
• The financial procurement thresholds do not meet up with the current nominal value of Philippine peso, creating congestion to procurement department on processing large number of purchase orders with small financial values, creating essentially an administrative workload.
• There are no contracts/framework agreements in place for frequent or cyclic procurement.
• There is no formal filing and archiving procedure or system set up regarding procurement.
• While PRC does have vehicles physically available, they have not been used efficiently
• The Fleet unit manages only 30% percent of the vehicles in use at the NHQ level. The rest have been allocated and managed by other departments.
• There is no formal system of sharing the vehicle pool which causes inefficiency in utilization.
• The process of dispatching a vehicle for transporting cargo takes minimum of three days due to excessive approval process for any planned expenditure over PHP 3000.
• 10 Warehouses located throughout the country. Within Metro Manila, two warehouse located along water bodies to allow transport of goods in the event roads are not accessible. In Mindanao, pre-positioned stocks are made available, as well as 6 WASH hubs.

component_details.title: DRM Strategy
component_details.description: An outline of the overall goal that the NS seeks to achieve in its disaster and crisis response operations. The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

component_responses.notes:
• PRC 2017-2020 Strategy takes an organization-wide approach to strengthening institutional response across different departments.
• The document clearly articulates outcomes, outputs it aims to achieve, as it relates to strengthening its ability to respond effectively and efficiently to emergencies.
• It is expected that the strategy will translated into yearly operational plans.

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_responses.notes:
• Currently PRC does not have an organization-wide Response Policy in place, although it can be argued the DMS Manual currently acts as the organization’s de facto response policy and reference.
• DMS Manual (2003) contains out-of-date information (e.g. "Cash assistance is not extended to families affected“). Additionally it makes reference to out-of-date laws.
• Draft DMS Manual appears to be a very comprehensive operational document for DMS covering all aspects of the DM Cycle.
• As document is still in draft form, it is not disseminated/shared within the organization.
• Draft DMS Manual appears to have sub-functions of DMS related to Logistics, Finance/Admin, and HR.

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.notes:
• PRC provided technical support to executive review of national Philippine 2016 DRM Law.
• As member of DRM council, PRC and IFRC provided input on PIHA Guidelines.
• PRC had provided direct technical support in the legal drafting of the National DRR Management Council executive review in 2016.
• According to technical advisors, the Philippines' Disaster Law is considered one of the most comprehensive in the world.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_responses.notes:
• Response documents (e.g. DMS Manual) make reference to Sphere Standards, and PRC provided examples of how this is used in practice.
• CEA focal point exist, however noted there is a need to invest in development of CEA policy as still in draft. Noted that PMER Learning Framework includes CEA and defines methods for managing feedback mechanisms and complaints.
• Learnings from previous emergencies (e.g. Nock Ten) indicated that “CEA was not integrated in the planning of the project”.
• ENA aims to collect information on marginalized groups, to enable more appropriate response.

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_responses.notes:
• PRC operates within a very strong legal base.
• Mandates and roles of the NS are clearly articulated in the Republic Act No. 10072 - Philippine Red Cross Act of 2009.
• The legal basis and government acts are referenced in different response documents (e.g. draft SOP, draft DMS Manual).
• The law makes reference to the NS adherence to the RCRC Fundamental Principles.
• There is acknowledgement for a need to understand how PRC is perceived outside the organization, and to gauge the public’s understanding of PRC’s mandate, role and services it provides

▫ A clear logistics function exists within PRC, managing procurement, warehousing, transportation and fleet. However, it is noted that many of the PRC service departments (e.g. DMS, Health, WASH) have their own parallel logistic functions. ▫ Procurement lacks uniformity in the procedural management, each department appears to have its own way of doing procurement. E.g. WASH unit has a focal person for all WASH related procurement and logistics, who centralizes and processes documents to ensure coherence with the organization’s procedural uniformity. ▫ Procurement team suggested regular orientation/training of new staff on procedures and timelines as well as the broad logistics functions at the chapter level. ▫ As per the desk review, there seem to be clear SOPs and procedures in place, with specific reporting lines and action point e.g. PRC‐PROC 03‐02 Procurement of Goods and Services Procedure which includes a flow for emergency procurement need. However, most procedures reviewed refer to "normal times/business as usual situation”. ▫ Logistics manual developed and well circulated NS wide. However, needs improvement in warehouse management, fleet maintenance and suppliers’ identification with established agreements for bulk purchase during disasters. There are no contracts/framework agreements in place for frequent or cyclic procurement. Survey results indicate there are still some gapsto be addressed in terms of long lead time and centralized and heavy approval processes. ▫ Logistics capacity varies from chapter to chapter. ▫ It was noted that delivery of supplies from NHQ to Chapters has been timely during the past disasters. However, electronics (laptop/projector) essential in reporting and dissemination purposes could take 2‐3 months to be delivered. Survey responses also indicated facing some supply chain difficulties due to geographical landscape.

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_responses.notes: ▫ PRC has developed Volunteer Services manual (still in draft form but on its final printing stage for circulation nationwide. Soft copies will be uploaded in PMER dashboard regarding Knowledge Management Module. It is undergoing copyright registration.). ▫ Draft Volunteer Services manual stipulates that a database of skilled/specialized volunteers will be maintained and updated regularly. It outlines proceduresfor mobilization and retention of volunteers as well as the Code of Conduct to be signed by all NS volunteers. ▫ PRC takes measures to protect staff and volunteers during epidemics by limiting their risk of exposure. ▫ NS has expedited procedures to incorporate spontaneous volunteers during emergencies which meet minimum screening procedures and comply with its volunteer in emergency policy. ▫ Survey findings indicate that no consolidated and accessible database exists showing HR/VR information, trainings, capacities, etc. Databases exist in many different locations among different departments. NHQ confirms that the OVD exists and is available under the PMER dashboard. ▫ Some chapters have their own system in which every response unit can recruit, train and manage its own volunteers independent of other units. ▫ HR has a roster of all staff, containing general information (contact details, name, gender, religion) but this database is incomplete, and only updated on an ad hoc basis upon request of management. ▫ The importance to revaluate recruitment and retention strategies due to high turnover of staff and volunteers was highlighted in multiple survey responses. ▫ Volunteers need to pay their own insurance which may discourage volunteer engagement

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_responses.notes: ▫ PRC NHQ has an internal Safety Security TWG and a focal point (FP) for Safety and Security matters. Chapters do not have dedicated staff to oversee this however, the responsibility is with the Chapter Administrators. ▫ PRC implements Safer Access and has appropriate security systems in place to protect staff and volunteers. Safer Access and security protocols are integrated in volunteers’ trainings. ▫ PRC managers completed Security management training. ▫ At chapter level, PRC is actively disseminating Safer Access among its responders and reminds them of Code of Conduct during deployments. ▫ Volunteer services manual contains a section mentioning Safer Access: 6.4.5 Volunteers shall observe the policies and guideline concerning “Safer Access” particularly in areas affected by armed conflict. Refer to ICRC Safer Access Manual  ‐ this indicates that there is a Safer Access policy in place. ▫ Safety and Security FP keeps tracks of security issues in the field. However, there are still gaps in regular reporting of security concerns as these are only submitted on as‐needed basis. In addition, there is no clear collection of data related to safety and security incidents

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_responses.notes: ▫ PRC's Chairman and Secretary General are the official designated spokespersons in an emergency – based on desk review. ▫ Survey findings indicate that external communication is strong. In times of emergencies,social media is used widely and efficiently to disseminate information to public. In addition, high quality press releases are issued. ▫ Communications department has good relationships with media contacts to correct misinformation when it occurs. ▫ Public awareness messages are also shared with staff during emergencies. ▫ Reliance on technology can be a barrier, especially if there is internet/phone disruption during an emergency. ▫ PRC has a limited number of VSATs available to install during disasters to restore communication links in the most damaged areas. ▫ PRC has in‐house Tower Public Announcement System which is not implemented due to limited funds.

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_responses.notes: ▫ PRC has designated MEAL staff at NHQ and reporting focal persons are deployed in field during operations, as needed.  Some templates, forms, and guidelines are in place. ▫ NS operates an M&E system at the field level to collect, manage and report on data to branches, NHQ and IFRC against the set objectives of the operation. ▫ Operation Sheet is used to monitor all response actions and includes damage and needs, 3W, deployments, situational updates, and other operational data. The data is contained in a single source (i.e. excel) and accessible on Google Drive by all NHQ DMS Staff. ▫ Operational plans are updated with more accurate figures from the damage and needs assessments. ▫ The Learning component seems to be missing i.e. learnings from the past operations are not widely shared or incorporated in applicable policies and/or plans. ▫ Reporting flow during a disaster response can be unclear at times with staff reporting the need to respect lines of management and chain of command ▫ Data collection seemsto remain an issue. Lack of a specific template leads to duplication of data and burdensome reporting on the same topic.

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_responses.notes: ▫ There is an identified need to improve Finance in Emergencies procedures i.e., a ‘fast‐lane’ to expedite procedures during emergencies. ▫ The desk review identified only one SOP related to finances and logistics (not specifically related to emergencies). Existing procedures and SOPs for "normal" situations are the same as for emergency, leading to delays during an emergency. ▫ NS has trained personnel in Finance and Admin emergency support procedures. Deployment of finance people should be contained at some degree since most chapters are trained on finance procedures. The finance team is continuously conducting finance technical training to services and chapters to strengthen their capacity during operations in terms of the organization’s accounting and finance procedures. ▫ The survey clearly indicates that delays are always prevalent, even in emergencies, due to the very burdensome and centralized procedures. Approvals are required at a very high level ‐ up to Chairman office ‐ which slows down the process. ▫ The WASH Unit has a sector focusing on WASH‐related emergency operations, in order to monitor and expedite the procedure to respond effectively in the affected area. Parallel to other offices or services which have a team focusing on emergencies, establishment of a WASH response team who will prioritize the response will contribute to effective operations.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_responses.notes: ▫ NS has trained IT support focal points able to support with technical issues and equipment (e.g. computers, software, phones, cameras, GPS) and provide maintenance. ▫ Volunteers should be properly equipped (with mobile phone or walkie talkie) according to the draft Volunteer Services manual. ▫ The survey results indicate that all staff and volunteers are not equally equipped, and that stock is limited. For example, radios are only with DMS. Note that the issuance of assets is based on the functions of the services. Since PRC only have limited stocks and items, and equipment is allocated to services who usually use them. ▫ Not all chapters have stable Internet connection and appropriate equipment (e.g. satellite phone, radio) functioning or belonging. Satellite phones are particularly needed in times of emergencies when all services are disrupted. ▫ Some challenges were noted with approving phone bills during times of emergencies. The approval of the excess phone bill needs to be done by ASG and SG. ▫ IT needs improvement in digital back up of the accounting system. ▫ Availability of knowledge, training and capacity differs from one chapter to another.

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_responses.notes: ▫ PRC fund generation webpage Ways to donate is launched and provides easy access to donate funds through several means. For example, online (PayPal, Lazada, Shopee), Mobile Wallet (Gcash, Paymaya JUSTPAY.TO and Grabrewards) and through the listed banks. ▫ PRC has Fund Generation Policy which defines its roles and responsibilities (including for chapters), guiding principles, and procedures. ▫ PRC relevant staff is aware of general practices for accepting in‐kind goods and this is documented in the Fund Generation Policy. ▫ Although document strategy and new fundraising channels (for example GCash) exist, several findings mention a need for improvements and greater accountability of funds received by donors: private or governmental. ▫ Survey results indicate a strong mobilization of donors in times of major calamities as opposed to other type of emergencies i.e. pandemic. ▫ Some indication that chapters seem to be in favour of having access to fundslocally, by having the ability to fundraise and collectsupport locally.

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.notes:
▫ PRC provided technical support to the executive review of national Philippine 2016 DRM Law and in the legal drafting of the National DRRMC executive review in 2016. As member of DRRMC, PRC and IFRC provided input on Philippines International Humanitarian Assistance (PIHA) Guidelines.  
▫ Pursuant to Republic Act 10121 the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Plan (NDRRMP) 2020‐2030 was established with the support of PRC ‐ therefore indicating an ongoing dedicated support from PRC to the drafting of national DRM law.  
▫ PRC is a member of National DRRMC, and Local DRRMCs (Province, Municipal and City). PRC is a part of any ongoing reviews of DRRM policy at National level.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action.
