• Capacity & Advocacy: PRCS does not have trained staff to serve as IDRL/IHL focal points during emergencies. Advocacy with government on IDRL is situational rather than based on a structured, long-term agenda, and there has been no systematic push to enact legislation in line with the Model Act.
• Learning & Application: While lessons learned are captured after major disaster responses, these do not specifically focus on IDRL and are not used to systematically inform humanitarian diplomacy work.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_responses.notes:
• Community Engagement: PRCS ensures participation of affected populations through CEA & PGI mechanisms, though these are project-based and not permanent. Communities influence decision-making to some extent via hotline 1030, area selection, and assessments. For example, flood recovery assessments showed preference for multipurpose cash, shaping NS decisions.
• Focal Points & Capacity: CEA/PGI focal points are in place at HQ and key provincial branches, supported by more than 20 trained volunteers at HQ and additional volunteers at branch level.
• CEA Planning & SOPs: A CEA plan is included in the Unified Plan with IFRC. A dedicated CEA SOP (2023) exists, supported mainly by project-linked funding from NorCross and ICRC.
• Feedback & Complaints: The 1030 hotline is the main feedback mechanism, but with inconsistent documentation and feedback loop, supplemented by community volunteers. Whistleblower and anti-harassment policies are under development.
• Protection Standards & Policies: PRCS adheres to Sphere Standards, Core Humanitarian Standards, and Minimum Standards for PGI in Emergencies. PSEA policy adoption remains to be confirmed. Protection services include psychosocial support, restoring family links, and safe spaces.
• Do No Harm Principle: Incorporated in HR Code of Conduct, signed by all staff, ensuring minimal negative impacts of assistance.
• Overall: Although there have been efforts to integrate PGI/CEA for projects due to donor requirements, there is no ownership of NS on CEA.

component_details.title: Business continuity
component_details.description: A strategy to counter any potential or anticipated obstacles to effective functioning of the NS, with an eye to ensuring that personnel and assets are protected and able to function in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes:
• Business Continuity Plan: PRCS does not have a separate business continuity plan. In practice, after the initial days of a response, some staff remain engaged in response while others resume regular duties, but this is not guided by a formal plan.
• Donor Communication Procedures: No formal SoPs exist for repurposing donor funds. PRCS requests repurposing on a case-by-case basis, depending on needs, the situation, and donor flexibility.

component_details.title: Emergency Response Procedures (SOPs)
component_details.description: Written guidelines that describe duties and rights of personnel, command structures, coordination with other organizations, and reporting requirements, etc. Includes detailed organogram, decision-making flow chart, and defined roles and responsibilities.

component_responses.notes:
• Existence of SOPs: PRCS has Disaster Response SOPs, but they are outdated, shelved, and last updated in 2016 despite commitments for annual revision. They are not institutionalized or used during operations, and no approved SOPs exist at branch level.
• Dissemination & Use: SOPs have not been disseminated and are not known by staff or volunteers. In practice, PRCS relies on broader RCRC guidelines and best practices to manage emergency operations.
• Roles & Coverage: While roles and responsibilities are documented, the SOPs are overly focused on the IFRC Country Delegation, with little on PRCS branches or communities. The 2016 version does not comprehensively cover all phases of response and lacks procedures for scaling alert levels up or down.
• Decision-Making & Structure: The SOPs do not contain a decision-making flowchart, although a response organogram exists at KP branch. An organogram is included but without contact details.

component_details.title: Response and recovery planning
component_details.description: A documented set of procedures for the disaster/crisis response and recovery process. Including use of local capacities, transition to recovery, type of activities and serivices provided during response and recovery activities and exit strategies, procedures for DREF & EA, and templates for planning, budgeting and accessing funds.

component_responses.notes:
• Multi-Sectoral Response Plan: PRCS does not maintain a pre-approved multi-sectoral response plan for rapid deployment of resources. Instead, emergency response plans are developed post-disaster, integrating gender, age, disability, and diversity considerations.
• Participation & Principles: Formal consultation with communities, governance, and partners is limited by the absence of a standing plan. However, emergency plans that are developed adhere to PRCS DM policy, Fundamental Principles, and IFRC standards, including EPoA templates.
• Recovery & Adaptation: Plans routinely account for secondary risks and incorporate recovery interventions after detailed needs assessments. Self-recovery of affected populations is promoted through participatory approaches. PRCS adapts response plans to evolving contexts and integrates lessons learned from previous operations.
• Transition & Coordination: PRCS has demonstrated capacity to transition from relief to medium-term recovery in large-scale responses. Plans acknowledge other actors’ roles and are shared with Movement and external stakeholders.
• Resource Mobilization: PRCS communicates priority needs through situation updates and donor engagement, facilitating both domestic and international support.

component_details.title: Pre-disaster meetings and agreements
component_details.description: A commitment to arrange meetings and agreements with Movement stakeholders and external actors to identify, plan for and address gaps for any upcoming disaster season (e.g. monsoon, floods or cyclones, or for any generic disaster/crisis event (e.g Epidemic, pandemic, confilict situations). Pre-disaster agreements should set out each partner's role in the event of a disaster/crisis.

component_responses.notes:
• Pre-Disaster Meetings: PRCS conducts pre-disaster meetings with key stakeholders, particularly around the Monsoon Contingency Plan, to confirm commitments and contributions. While these engagements are functional, they are not underpinned by formal pre-disaster agreements.
• Agreements & Coordination: Broader MoUs and LoUs exist with selected actors such as NDMA and PMD, but there are no formalized pre-disaster agreements with public authorities, NGOs, or INGOs. Similarly, coordination with national and local actors lacks structured arrangements. Movement coordination agreements are in place and known across partners, ensuring some consistency within the RCRC framework.
• Capacity Mapping & Standards: PRCS does not have updated capacity mapping of Movement partners and has not institutionalized contractor compliance with the Code of Conduct. Existing agreements, such as with FSPs, transporters, media, and social protection systems (NSER, BISP), provide operational entry points but remain fragmented. No agreements exist to facilitate expedited imports or visas for personnel, and SOP alignment with Quality and Accountability standards is missing.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_responses.notes:
• Risk Monitoring & Early Warning: PRCS does not yet have a formal risk monitoring system, though it uses PMD advisories and NDMA dashboards. A PRCS-owned dashboard linking monitoring to preparedness and early action is being developed. An early warning system exists through the Riverine Flood sEAP for Kabul River, but it has not been activated in the past two years. A revised five-year EAP, covering KP, Punjab, and Sindh along the Indus River, has been submitted and validated, pending final budget approval.
• Data & Risk Analysis: HQ and branches can collect and analyse primary and secondary data, with information presented in Movement coordination forums. There is no established mechanism for data consolidation at NHQ level. Security and access challenges are acknowledged in high-risk areas, with reliance on government authorities. National multi-hazard risk mapping is not produced or shared with branches.
• Community Engagement: EVCA is incorporated into CDRT, DDRT, and some BDRT trainings, with provincial managers linking updates from community members. Risk assessments also consider community sensitivities and dynamics. Data on vulnerabilities and capacities is disaggregated by age, gender, disability, income, and cultural factors.
• Cross-Border Coordination: There is no mechanism in place for risk monitoring or information sharing with neighbouring National Societies in cross-border high-risk areas.
• Overall: PMD & NDMA are doing risk monitoring and PRCS do not need to duplicate the technical capacities, but utilize its community presence and use different data sources effectively to complement decision making.

component_details.title: Scenario planning
component_details.description: A set of practical operation plans that closely mirror the generic disaster or crisis response plan but are tailored to a specific hazard type (e.g. earthquake, dengue epidemic, floods, cyclone) and a specific scenario (i.e. number of people affected, their locations and other important factors).

component_responses.notes:
• Scenario Analysis: PRCS has a Monsoon Contingency Plan with a multi-sectoral response strategy, integrating health, livelihoods, and protection. Climate change is acknowledged as a key driver that intensifies disaster risks (e.g., KP cloudburst, 2022 floods).
• Contingency Planning: Current planning is limited to the monsoon season, aligned with NDMA forecasts and advisories. While this plan is shared with authorities and partners, there is no broader multi-hazard contingency plan. However, funding has been secured from ICRC to develop a national multi-hazard disaster response plan in 2026.
• Branch Involvement & Response Strategies: Branches are fully engaged in developing the Monsoon Contingency Plan, contributing stock and HR capacity assessments. Response strategies are tailored to branch capacities and vulnerabilities.
• Security & Triggers: The plan includes staff safety and security considerations, relying on government support in restricted areas. Triggers for activation exist for monsoon hazards, while simplified EAPs for heatwave, dengue, and drought are planned.
• Regional Coordination: Limited cross-border engagement exists; regional coordination for epidemics/pandemics remains weak despite discussions in national dialogue forums.
• Overall: Contingency plan for one hazard only and need to consider for other hazards. Challenges with implementation and application of contingency plan.

component_details.title: Risk management
component_details.description: A mapping of the potential risks in every area, along with its related mitigation measures. Including financial, reputational, organizational risks etc.

component_responses.notes:
• Risk Management Framework: PRCS does not have a dedicated, systematic risk management function. The last risk analysis was conducted in 2019 and the last security audit in 2014. A newly appointed DD Security is managing safety and security, but broader institutional systems are lacking.
• Operational & Reputational Risks: Security situation analyses are carried out in practice but are not comprehensive and do not formally cover reputational risks. Risk management is not holistic across sectors, and mitigation measures are not consistently applied.
• Stakeholder Engagement: PRCS identifies key stakeholders and develops engagement strategies to enhance acceptance, though these require further strengthening.
• Systems & Oversight: Systems and procedures for fraud prevention and reputational risk management are unclear, with verification needed from senior management and finance. Reputational and integrity risk is not consistently addressed at the Governing Board level.
• Crisis Management: No formal crisis management unit exists; critical incidents are managed ad hoc as situations arise.
• Overall: There is a need for this component to be well understood and risk management to be carried out at various levels.

component_details.title: Preparedness plans and budgets
component_details.description: Plans identifying organisational resources, determining roles and responsibilities, and developing policies, procedures and activities in order to reach a level of preparedness to be able to respond effectively to a disaster or crisis. Budgets ensure that the necessary financial support is secured to allow capacities to be built and readiness maintained.

component_responses.notes:
• Disaster Preparedness Focal Point: PRCS does not have a dedicated focal person. Responsibilities are covered by JD Ops and AD DM. DM team structure needs to be revisited, and the right staff to be given this responsibility.
• Preparedness Gaps: There is no systematic process to identify gaps. Priorities include strengthening human resources and modernizing outdated systems. Manual procurement, the absence of a real-time database, and depleted warehouse stocks after the 2022 floods highlight significant weaknesses.
• Remedial Actions: Preparedness gaps have been repeatedly identified but no concrete actions have been implemented.
• Financial Resources & Policies: PRCS lacks a resource mobilization strategy, policies, and procedures for preparedness. Budgets rely on project-based partner discussions. While Unified Planning with IFRC includes preparedness activities, funding is not confirmed. Limited support has come from British Red Cross and ICRC, and some trainings (NDRT, EVCA, CVA) were conducted, but overall mechanisms remain ad hoc and insufficient.

• Participation & Inclusion: PRCS applies a participatory and inclusive approach in community programming, ensuring local needs and strengths, including marginalized groups, are considered in preparedness planning and activities.
• Awareness & Education: Disaster risk reduction awareness sessions are regularly conducted through youth and volunteer activities in schools and communities, with increased visibility during international disaster and RCRC days.
• Early Warning & Action: While PRCS has an early warning framework, it is not currently active nor linked with local early warning systems, limiting community-based early action capacity.
• CDRT Capacity: Community Disaster Response Teams are trained and equipped to support local response in areas where DRR projects have been implemented. However, they lack formal response and contingency plans aligned with local resources and systems.
• Inclusiveness in Planning: DRR programming integrates inclusive, gender-sensitive, and conflict-sensitive practices during assessment, planning, and response at community level.

• Role & Planning: PRCS has not systematically identified multi-sectoral response needs for epidemics. Planning is limited to monsoon floods and an sEAP for the Kabul River Basin, with a dengue sEAP planned. Health in Emergencies activities remain largely partner-driven. PRCS’s role in epidemics, quarantine/isolation, and management of dead bodies is not clearly defined, with some support linked to donor projects in KP and merged areas.
• Capacity & Resources: Training includes a ToT on Epidemic Control for Volunteers (25 participants cascaded to 170–200 volunteers) and a One Health training under an IFRC project. Core areas are PFA, MHPSS, ECV, and RCCE. PPE stocks are maintained, though shortages of gloves and masks occur. MHU doctors train staff, orientations are conducted before deployment, and safety protocols cover basic items. Rumour management is included in training but remains limited and inconsistently applied.
• Partnerships & Coordination: Community engagement is supported by provincial data staff/volunteers and a feedback tool developed by PGI/CEA. No structured coordination role established at national or regional levels, and technical support remains limited and project-linked.

• First Aid Strategy & Integration: First Aid is a flagship program of PRCS and is clearly reflected in the PRCS Strategy 2030. It is also included as part of ongoing CBDRR activities and projects, though its reflection in the CBDRR manual and DRR strategy remains to be clarified.
• Capacity & Deployment: All provinces maintain dedicated First Aid teams, training around 600 first aiders annually. Training includes search and rescue and dead body management. Trained responders are regularly deployed, most recently in Buner, Bajaur, and Swabi.

• WASH Strategy & Integration: WASH is a core sector in PRCS response, particularly in floods, and is reflected in the NS response strategy. Coordination with other sectors is recognized as important.
• Capacity & Equipment: PRCS has 23 mobile water treatment plants pre-positioned in 3 warehouses, 350 temporary latrines, and 82 trained volunteers, including female responders. Training includes hygiene promotion and PHAST sessions. Recent deployments, such as Buner (Aug 2025), provided safe water for 1,500 households. However, no capacity at branch level. Staff in the past were project-based, and trained volunteers limited to basic WASH. Existing equipment need refurbishment, and 1 technical person is responsible for all 23 plants so there is limited deployment capacity to multiple areas at the same time. 
• Technical Support & Coordination: Dedicated WASH teams exist at NHQ, with support from IFRC and Movement partners. PRCS participates in the national WASH Cluster and shares information on gaps and response activities.

• Monitoring & Analysis: PRCS uses Pakistan Bureau of Statistics data for long-term food security monitoring and conducts rapid and detailed needs assessments during emergencies. Coordination with the Food Security & Livelihoods (FSL) Cluster ensures alignment and prevents duplication.
• Technical Capacity: Food security and assistance are led by the DM Department and CVA team, with cash and livelihoods officers at branch level. While technical expertise exists, staff retention remains a challenge due to limited salary competitiveness.
• Coordination: PRCS actively engages with NDMA, DDMA, and humanitarian coordination forums such as the Pakistan Humanitarian Forum, alongside cluster-level collaboration with WFP, ICRC, and others.
• Integration into Response: Food distribution is integrated into response strategies, with adherence to Sphere standards for dry rations. Assistance includes both cooked food and dry rations depending on community needs.
• Operational Planning: A specific action plan exists for food aid procurement and distribution, covering SOPs, beneficiary selection, ration calculations, and distribution systems. Packages are tailored to provincial preferences and designed to prioritize vulnerable groups such as elderly, PLW, and child-headed households.

• Strategic Integration: Livelihoods are not incorporated into PRCS DRM strategy or plans, as no such strategy exists. The DRM policy also does not prioritize livelihoods.
• Policies & Focal Points: PRCS has not identified national safety nets or employment policies related to livelihoods. There is no dedicated livelihoods focal point, and the function is currently managed under DM. Staff capacity is limited, with key positions vacant since December 2024. Upcoming projects supported by British RC and King Salman Humanitarian Aid are expected to re-establish technical capacity.
• Livelihoods Systems & Risk Identification: PRCS has not documented livelihoods zones, systems, or market baselines, nor developed plans for protecting community and household productive assets in disaster-prone areas.
• Emergency Tools & Coordination: Livelihoods are included in post-disaster recovery plans (e.g., 2022 flood recovery with livestock distribution and cash for work). PRCS coordinates with WFP and other networks through the Pakistan Humanitarian Forum.
• Staff & Volunteer Capacity: Training in livelihoods data collection is conducted during projects, but volunteer retention remains a challenge, requiring frequent retraining.

• Community Consultation: PRCS conducts rapid and detailed needs assessments, engaging Union Counsellors and communities to identify vulnerable households and appropriate shelter solutions.
• Prepositioned Stocks: Shelter supplies, including over 7,000 shelter toolkits, are being procured after depletion during the 2022 floods.
• NFI Kits & SOPs: Standard NFI kits, aligned with Sphere standards, are prepositioned with clear SOPs, jointly procured with IFRC.
• Supplier Agreements: There are no pre-disaster and framework agreements with suppliers.
• Shelter Designs: Standard emergency and temporary designs exist, adapted through community consultation (e.g., winterized shelters in the North, lighter designs in Sindh). Permanent shelters are supported during recovery.
• Volunteer Capacity: Shelter kit trainings were previously conducted, but volunteer capacity has since diminished, with no active trained pool currently available.

component_details.title: MANAGEMENT OF DEAD BODIES TO FACILITATE THEIR IDENTIFICATION

component_responses.notes:
• RFL Services Capacity: PRCS has dedicated staff and professional volunteers in place to deliver quality RFL services. Ten staff (with ongoing training support for new members) and ten specialized volunteers provide expertise in detention and emergencies. Teams are actively deployed in the field, including the KP cloudburst response, to assess needs and support affected communities. RFL activities extend to detention centres in Punjab and Sindh, with services such as free phone calls in development, as well as migration support at border points with Afghanistan.
• Partnership & Procedures with ICRC: Since 2021, RFL files have been handed to PRCS, with ICRC continuing to focus on conflict-affected areas. PRCS follows the global RFL Strategy and maintains procedures and agreements with ICRC. The program has shown strong progress, improving its monitoring and evaluation score from 2.8/4 in 2020 to 3.3/4 in 2024.

• Recovery Principles & Capacity: PRCS key staff are trained in recovery planning, emphasizing detailed assessment, community participation, cross-cutting issues, and resilience-building. However, capacities are uneven across branches, requiring harmonization.
• Mandate & Coordination: There is no formal mandate on recovery agreed with public authorities. While PRCS coordinates at local levels, structured national-level recovery collaboration remains weak. Participation in joint planning with authorities and humanitarian actors is limited, though occasional joint assessments occur.
• Systems & Transition: PRCS has enabling systems that support a smooth transition from relief to longer-term recovery, including HR, support services, and early recovery planning.
• Integrated Programming & Partnerships: Recovery interventions consider integration across sectors to maximize community impact. External partnerships are pursued, more frequently in relief operations, but increasingly considered for recovery to fill strategic gaps.

component_details.title: CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL, RADIOLOGICAL AND NUCLEAR (CBRN) EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS

component_responses.notes:
• Role & Planning: PRCS does not have a defined role in national, regional, or local emergency plans for technological and biological hazards, as such government plans appear not to be available or accessible. Consequently, there is no action plan or SOPs with safety protocols in place.
• Capacity & Resources: There is no dedicated focal point, trained staff/volunteers, or protective equipment for technological/biological response. RASB messages may cover limited aspects, but there are no comprehensive public messages, which is linked to the unclear role of PRCS in this area.
• Partnerships & Coordination: No network of expertise or engagement with neighbouring NSs. Participation in forums is minimal, with only one event attended in Austria and no follow-up actions. PRCS has not identified or communicated needs for international assistance, also connected to the unclear role of PRCS in this area.

• Health Contingency Planning: PRCS delivers health projects via provincial teams under NHQ guidance, including immunization, infectious disease preparedness (until Nov 2025), and primary health care in KP and merged areas. MHTs collect stock data, but there is no annual community-level health contingency planning; health is only covered under the broader Monsoon Contingency Plan.
• First Aid Training: Regular refresher training stopped after ICRC funding cuts. Some volunteers are trained, but the main focus now is on commercial first aid training.
• Reporting of Health Events: Volunteers supporting immunization also report suspected health events to the Ministry of Health, integrated with zero-dose child reporting.
• Community Engagement & Simulation: Engagement occurs through village health committees in KP, merged areas, and Balochistan (with challenges), supported by religious leaders and social mobilizers. Lady Health Visitors link communities with health facilities. Punjab and Sindh branches manage their own health activities, while NHQ deploys MHTs to GB, NorCross supports in conflict areas and ICRC in merged areas and AJK (during the recent conflict). Although MoH promotes an integrated approach through coordination meetings, PRCS participation in these structures remains inconsistent.

component_details.title: Mapping of NS capacities
component_details.description: A list of the NS capacities including HR (staff, response teams and volunteers) and equipment that are available for disaster/crisis response. Teams could include branch and national response teams. This should be defined by technical speciality where relevant.

component_responses.notes:
• Focal Points & Technical Support: PRCS has designated focal points for all intervention areas at NHQ, though many hold additional responsibilities alongside their technical roles. This varies at branch-level; even some branches lack core staff (e.g., Secretary or RFL Manager at AJK branch). No centralized HR system that include capacities at branches.
• Training & Capacity Building: Regular sectoral trainings are organized for staff and volunteers, ensuring technical knowledge remains updated (e.g., during last 2-3 years, 2 NDRTs, 8 BDRTs and 35 CDRTs).
• Response Materials & Equipment: Databases (lists; not a formal database) for stocks, medical equipment, fleet, and water treatment units are updated. However, data is not centralized, and addressing gaps is difficult under resource constraints. Movement partners and local donors are approached to fill gaps, especially during monsoon contingency planning.
• Resource Availability: PRCS maintains adequate resources to cover initial response requirements.
• Capacity Mapping: There is no system to map capacities against different levels of response (Green–Yellow–Red).
• Resource Sharing: Mechanisms exist to share resources between HQ, branches, and with sister National Societies.

component_details.title: Early Action Mechanisms
component_details.description: Designed to translate warnings into anticipatory actions to help reduce the impact of specific disaster or crisis events. They focus on consolidating available forecasting information and putting procedures in place to ensure that a NS can act ahead of any disaster/crisis. Forecast-based financing is included within the scope of this area.

component_responses.notes:
• Integration with National Systems: PRCS is an active member of the National Coordination Forum on Anticipatory Action (NCF-AA) led by NDMA and co-chairs the thematic sub-committee on “Learning and Evidence.” Its Early Action Protocol (EAP) for riverine flooding along the Indus and major tributaries is well accepted and integrated into the national anticipatory action system.
• Methodology and Triggers: PRCS applies the EAP methodology, with clearly defined thresholds, targeted areas, and justified early actions based on vulnerability and exposure analysis.
• Coordination Mechanisms: A broader MoU with the Pakistan Meteorological Department ensures regular forecasts. The EAP is implemented in close coordination with PMD, Flood Forecasting Division, and PDMAs for major hazards.
• Use of Technology: PRCS has piloted SMS-based early warning dissemination through the “What Now” project in KP, and contracted a cellular provider for flood alerts under the sEAP. However, scaling of technologies across all hazard contexts remains limited.
• Communication Procedures: Dedicated AA/FbF focal persons at NHQ and relevant branches are in place to communicate alerts and initiate early actions.
• Branch and Community Networks: Trained volunteers under sEAP disseminate flood warnings in Kabul River communities, with readiness mechanisms extending to the Indus basin. MoUs with authorities for message dissemination are also part of the preparedness system.

component_details.title: Cash Based Intervention (CBI)
component_details.description: An effective and flexible way, including all forms of cash and voucher-based assistance, to support people affected by emergencies, maintaining their dignity and choice, while fostering local economies. Cash should also be mainstreamed into other sectors (including Relief, shelter, livelihoods) and services (Logistics, Finance, etc.)

component_responses.notes:
• Cash Preparedness Planning: PRCS does not have a standalone, budgeted cash preparedness plan, though priorities are included in the IFRC Unified Plan and the Riverine Flood sEAP. 
• Capacity & Tools: More than 50 CVA trained NDRTs and volunteers are in place, with additional CVA Level 2 trainings completed in 2024.  SOPs and toolkits exist but remain outdated (last revised 2016), requiring urgent updating to strengthen readiness.
• Systems & Partnerships: PRCS has framework agreements with FSPs (Telenor, HBL) and is finalizing arrangements with GPO, including addendums to support anticipatory action. An API platform enables flexible cash disbursement. Market assessments are done through the Cash Working Group, with alignment to the Minimum Expenditure Basket.
• Coordination: PRCS participates actively in national cash coordination. Internal cash technical working groups exist but need stronger strategic direction.

component_details.title: Emergency Needs Assessment
component_details.description: Assess the extent and impact of the damage caused by the disaster/crisis and the degree of vulnerability of the affected population. The first step in any emergency response, such an assessment will identify the needs that require external intervention and the gaps to be filled. It is a vital component of the programme-planning process.

component_responses.notes:
• Tools & Teams: Templates for data collection are available but not standard, though branches often adapt them and partner-driven templates are sometimes used. A trained multi-sectoral emergency assessment team is lacking, with insufficient technical staff at PHQ and branch levels.
• Needs Assessment Practices: Emergency plans of action are based on assessment findings, using both primary and secondary data. Assessments generally cover accessibility, availability, quality, and use of goods and services, as seen in recent flood responses. Partners highlighted some gaps in timely sharing of needs assessment reports. 
• Data Quality & Gaps: Disaggregation by gender, age, disability, and other diversity factors is not systematically applied. Assessments also lack analysis of national and international capacities, as well as consideration of secondary risks, coping mechanisms, or pathways for early and self-recovery.
• Overall: While basic tools and practices exist, strengthening multi-sector assessment capacity, systematic disaggregation, and inclusion of secondary risks and resilience factors is critical for a comprehensive approach.

component_details.title: Affected population selection
component_details.description: Identification and selection of target Affected population for interventions, using a pre-defined set of criteria based on need and vulnerability. This includes consideration of specific vulnerabilities such as disability, age and gender.

component_responses.notes:
• Selection Criteria: Beneficiary selection criteria are defined in the PRCS Monsoon Contingency Plan and applied during operational planning. Criteria are communicated to affected populations primarily for tangible interventions such as livelihoods, shelter, and cash assistance. The criteria include considerations of gender, age, diversity, and disability, ensuring an inclusive approach.
• Data Protection & Training: PRCS protects collected data to the best of its ability, with use restricted to internal purposes. Responders are trained in data collection, including the use of standardized templates. In practice, data collection is not conducted during the initial response phase but is introduced once concrete interventions such as cash or shelter support begin.
• Verification & Cross-Checking: Population lists are cross-checked with community leaders, authorities, and other agencies to address inclusion and exclusion concerns. While this process was not initiated during the early stage of the ongoing flood response, it is consistently practiced during later phases of implementation.

component_details.title: Emergency Operations Centre (EOC)
component_details.description: A central command and control facility responsible for carrying out disaster/crisis management functions at a strategic level in an emergency situation. The common functions are to collect and analyze data; facilitate decision making that protects life and livelihoods; and disseminate those decisions to all concerned agencies and individuals. Generally located at the headquarter level of an organization.

component_responses.notes:
• EOC Focal Point & SOPs: PRCS does not maintain a regular focal point for the EOC, except in Sindh branch. No EOC SOPs exist at HQ or KP, and staff and volunteers are not trained on defined roles. Without SOPs, sectoral and support services lack integration, and no formal thresholds guide EOC activation.
• Facilities & Systems: The Disaster Management and Logistics Center (DMLC), supported by Turkish Red Crescent, serves as the EOC with adequate meeting space and equipment. It has backup for electricity and communication, though limited, and no alternate site if inaccessible. Contact details are maintained through coordination mechanisms, and PRCS uses HF/VHF radios, though coverage is restricted to Islamabad and not linked with other stakeholders.
• Operations & Decision-Making: The EOC was non-functional during the recent floods, limiting information management. However, PRCS issues situation reports from collected data. Strategic decisions are made through coordination meetings, authority levels are defined in the Monsoon Contingency Plan, and a control room operates 24/7, though not the full EOC.

component_details.title: Information Management (IM)
component_details.description: Ability to manage information including requesting, receiving, analyzing and disseminating as per its procedures and partner requirements (IFRC and public authorities in particular). There should be a clear digital/paper trail that documents what, when and how the NS has acted and provides key information for the development of Emergency Plan of Actions. Includes IM between levels, between departments and Situational Reports, mapping, visualisation of data, GO platform (IFRC).

component_responses.notes:
• IM Systems & Templates: PRCS lacks standardized IM templates and relies on manual tools for disaster response. Databases are being developed for specific projects (e.g., IFRC-supported immunization, NorCross-supported health, and PRCS blood bank). Standard situation report formats exist and are used, though provinces have adapted them, creating a need for greater uniformity. Ongoing discussion with British RC for a centralized IMS. 
• Equipment & Data Access: PRCS has adequate infrastructure and equipment (printers, scanners, projectors) to support information management. It also has access to updated demographic and risk data from national and provincial DMAs.
• Storage & Information Sharing: There is no shared drive or system for storing and managing files; data is shared mainly through email. Informal mechanisms exist for communication across levels and sectors, but stronger branch ownership and commitment to IM are required.
• Use of Information: Decisions are documented, and situation reports are used to inform and adapt response plans, though improvements in record-keeping are needed.

component_details.title: Testing and Learning
component_details.description: Drills and Simulations allow the organization to test, identify and learn from the results of these type of exercises and incorporate learning into future preparedness and response planning.

component_responses.notes:
• Testing Systems: PRCS conducts simulations with NDRT, DDRT, BDRT, and CDRT, including early warning dissemination and rescue under the sEAP for riverine floods. Branches in high-risk areas also run drills through BDRTs.
• Learning & Adaptation: While simulations are practiced, lesson learning is weak. Reports are not systematically generated or disseminated to inform revisions of emergency procedures.
• Access & Principles: Training covers acceptance, security, and the Fundamental Principles, but these are not consistently integrated into drills. Safe access issues (perception and security) are not explicitly tested.
• Partnerships: PRCS engages in joint drills with NDMA, PDMA, and other partners. In 2024, Pakistan Scouts participated in a BDRT simulation in Sindh.
• Cross-Border Testing: No cross-border simulations are conducted, leaving a preparedness gap in regional contexts.

component_details.title: Activation of regional and international support
component_details.description: Procedures for requesting and accepting regional and international support in operations, including triggering coordination mechanisms for funding, materials and human resources deployments.

component_responses.notes:
• Familiarity with IFRC/ICRC Support: Key PRCS staff at NHQ and PHQ, through NDRT training and regular practice, are familiar with IFRC/ICRC tools and capacities. PRCS routinely updates IFRC (Go) within 24 hours of major emergencies. The Society is also well acquainted with IFRC funding mechanisms, such as DREF, Emergency Appeals, and Forecast-based Financing, and has practical experience in their use.
• SOPs & Procedures: While coordination with IFRC is referenced in the Monsoon Contingency Plan, there are no updated SOPs detailing coordination procedures or processes to request and integrate regional or global support teams. Existing Response SOPs remain outdated.
• Coordination & Focal Point: PRCS requests bilateral assistance in practice, though without a formal framework, and effectively coordinates with PNSs, embassies, and corporates. The Director of Operations serves as the assigned focal point for international responders, ensuring consistent coordination despite procedural gaps.

component_details.title: Cooperation with private sector
component_details.description: Mechanism that allows cooperation with private sector that often plays a strong role in response, particularly if there is impact on their staff and businesses. There is often a willingness to donate goods and services. Advance agreements help to expedite response actions.

component_responses.notes:
• Due Diligence: No standardized process exists for partner selection or donation acceptance. Decisions are handled case by case, often driven by partner requirements (e.g., The Bank of Punjab), with the finance department involved.
• Emblem & Visual Identity: PRCS has visual identity guidelines, though the 1970s governing law is outdated with only a minimal fine for emblem misuse.
• Corporate Volunteer Engagement: No formal mechanism is in place. An Associate Membership Guide, previously used for schools and academic institutions, could be adapted for corporate partners. Some corporate engagement exists through commercial first aid training.
• Roundtable with private sectors conducted recently and engagements exist with several corporations (MOU with Nestle) to support response, and plan to scale up efforts on private sector. 
• Branches (KP, Sindh) are actively engaged with corporate sectors on CSRs.

component_details.title: Coordination with Movement
component_details.description: Mechanisms that facilitate the coordination with ICRC, IFRC, and PNS in-country.

component_responses.notes:
• Adherence to SMCC Principles: PRCS adheres to the SMCC framework, with signed cooperation agreements in place with IFRC, ICRC, GRC, NorCross, and TRC, valid until December 2025. Expansion to include Chinese RC and British RC is planned.
• Coordination Mechanisms: While formal three-tier coordination structures exist (L1 strategic, L2 management, L3 technical committees), meetings have not been held regularly in the last two years especially for L1 & L2 meetings, limiting consistent information exchange. Multiple L3 coordination meetings (e.g., OD, PMER, CEA, health, etc.) technical committees are active and meet regularly (e.g., quarterly). There is a clear need to reinvigorate these structures to ensure systematic coordination with Movement partners.
• Cross-Border & International Assistance: Engagement with neighbouring NSs (e.g., Iran, Bangladesh) is limited, mainly on migrant transfers. When international assistance is accepted, PRCS establishes frameworks with IFRC for coordination, accountability, and reporting, as seen in DREF/Emergency Appeals and bilateral agreements such as with the Chinese RC.

component_details.title: Coordination with authorities
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and cooperation with local and national authorities. It is connected to the NS auxiliary role for humanitarian assistance.

component_responses.notes:
• National Coordination: PRCS is formally part of the national humanitarian coordination system and engages regularly with NDMA, PDMA, and other government authorities. While it does not consistently participate in provincial-level cluster meetings, it ensures representation and coordination with relevant public structures during emergencies. On migration, there is coordination with authorities together with UNHCR and IOM.
• Auxiliary Role & Caseload: PRCS understands national authorities’ capacities and aligns its support accordingly. In practice, the Society assumes a defined percentage of the caseload during operations, reflecting its auxiliary role and operational capacity.
• Independence & Use of Assets: PRCS maintains control over its assets, resources, and emblem when working with public authorities. While there are occasional challenges in regular operations, the National Society has been able to safeguard its independence, including in the current response.
• Local-Level Coordination: At the operational level, PRCS establishes coordination mechanisms with district authorities from the onset, as seen in the ongoing response in Buner, KP.

component_details.title: Coordination with External Agencies and NGOs
component_details.description: Mechanism that facilitates coordination and collaboration with Non-Governmental Organization (NGO), both local and international NGOs, civil society organizations (CSOs) and United Nations agencies in country.

component_responses.notes:
• Humanitarian Coordination: PRCS participates in UN and NGO coordination mechanisms, but engagement remains limited and not systematically focused on response efficiency. Information sharing through situation reports with NDMA, UNOCHA, and other forums provides some level of visibility, though active participation in cluster systems is weak.
• Cluster Role & Appeals: The National Society does not have a pre-agreed cluster role and does not consistently attend cluster meetings. Awareness of UN-led appeals and strategic processes is minimal, limiting opportunities for alignment and advocacy.
• Partnerships & Agreements: While situational coordination with UN and NGOs occurs during emergencies, no formal partnership agreements are in place. This reduces predictability and continuity of collaboration across branches and headquarters.

component_details.title: Civil Military Relations
component_details.description: Dialogue and interaction with military actors, essential to protect and promote humanitarian principles, avoid competition, minimize inconsistency and, when appropriate, pursue common goals.

component_responses.notes:
• Military Coordination: PRCS does not have formalized arrangements with the military but engages situationally when required, primarily through NDMA. In conflict areas, a no-objection certificate from the military is a prerequisite to operate, and PRCS generally receives a more positive response compared to other organizations.
• Guidance & Principles: The Movement’s 2005 guidance on relations with military bodies has not been disseminated or applied within PRCS. Nonetheless, the Society ensures that engagement with the military is limited and aligned with the Fundamental Principles and IHL.
• Use of Assets & Security Considerations: Military assets are used only as a last resort, with coordination through local authorities and IFRC informed when necessary. PRCS avoids armed protection or armed military transport and carefully considers the potential impact of such coordination on affected communities.
• Promotion of Principles & Emblem: PRCS continues to promote the Fundamental Principles and ensure appropriate use of the Movement’s emblems.
• ICRC full mandate on IHL does not apply in Pakistan as there is no active conflict declaration, but there is some limited work on dissemination and promotion of IHL, and capacity building for PRCS as needed – NS has a lead role in civil military coordination.

component_details.title: Coordination with local community level responders
component_details.description: Engagement with Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), through training, coordination, and the development of community disaster preparedness and response plans.

component_responses.notes:
• Information Flow: PRCS lacks formalized procedures to manage information between communities, branches, and headquarters. However, in districts with branches, coordination is maintained through ongoing contact with community response teams.
• Community Input in Decision-Making: Information from communities informs branch-level decision-making and is shared with headquarters, but this practice is mostly limited to districts where community-based DRR projects are active.
• Branch–CDRT Coordination: Branches maintain communication and coordination with CDRTs, again primarily within project-supported districts.
• Support to Community Systems: PRCS strengthens local response systems by establishing CDRTs, equipping them, and supporting contingency and evacuation planning in community-based DRR project areas.

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_responses.notes:
• Systems & Policies: PRCS has compound safety measures (guards, cameras, radio/control room) and security monitoring of vehicle movements, but no comprehensive Safer Access implementation or formal safety and security policy. KP branch has developed its own framework.
• Staff & Training: Security roles at PHQs are usually additional responsibilities, with no dedicated personnel. Few responders have completed basic safety/security training; broader awareness of Safer Access and Stay Safe remains limited.
• Risk Analysis & Communication: No formal context or risk analysis mechanism exists, though NHQ monitors media reports. Communication mechanisms for incident reporting (phones, radio room, WhatsApp groups) are in place and widely used.
• ICRC can provide comprehensive safety and security assessment for PRCS including field level operational security to identify gaps, and provide further capacity building on this area.

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_responses.notes:
• PMER Structure & Resources: PRCS maintains a dedicated PMER function at the portfolio level with three staff (1 DD, 2 AD). While branches no longer have dedicated PMER focal points since 2017, responsibilities are covered by CEA/IM focal points. Resources are sufficient, but decentralised PMER capacity remains limited.
• Learning & Adaptation: Lessons learned workshops and after-action reviews inform response planning. For example, lessons from the 2022 floods were applied in current DREF planning. Implementation of recommendations is weak. Operational plans are updated based on needs.
• Frameworks & Systems: Standardized IFRC-aligned operational plans and ITT tables are developed for emergency operations. Field-level M&E systems are in place, though reliance on individuals highlights the need for stronger knowledge management and digitalization to support systematic information sharing and evidence-based decision-making.
• Evaluations & Reporting: Evaluations are conducted for longer-term projects, while short-term responses rely on lessons learned exercises. Reporting uses standardized templates (finalized 2014, revised 2019), with monthly submissions and annual reports. PRCS also contributes to Movement-wide PMER processes through FDRS and ICRC cooperation.

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_responses.notes:
• Systems & Procedures: PRCS operates an automated ERP-based financial system with segregation of duties. In-kind donations are processed and tracked, though approval workflows remain paper-based. Finance and Admin have adapted emergency procedures, approved by the board and compliant with NDMA guidance and IFRC practices. Finance is fully engaged in operations, but EOC SOPs are lacking.
• Capacity & Training: Six finance staff are trained in emergency support procedures, supported by a finance working group with IFRC and partners. Admin functions remain a separate department.
• Transparency & Oversight: Internal audit is an independent unit reporting to the chairperson. Annual external audits are conducted, with the latest in June 2024. Two new audit officers are being recruited, and branch audits are planned under the 3-year operational plan. Oversight tools include reconciliations, documentation review, and interviews, supported by NorCross.
• Fraud Prevention & Compliance: An anti-fraud policy is drafted but not yet in place. Complaints can be referred via the 1030 hotline or website, though none have been recorded. Staff require further awareness of emergency-related MoUs and updated financial procedures, as current policies date back to 2008 and are under revision.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_responses.notes:
• Mobile & Internet Connectivity: PRCS provides mobile phones and SIMs for NHQ staff, but provincial branches running independent programs are not equally supported. Limited IT resources exist, with 300 Microsoft nonprofit accounts but no regular IT budget or comprehensive firewall. Contact lists are standardized, and internet routers and pocket WiFi are available for field personnel.
• Notification & Social Media: There is no approved emergency notification protocol or SOPs. Instead, WhatsApp groups are used by the DM team, including one permanent group linking NHQ and branches. PRCS also operates official social media pages for emergency communications and messaging.
• Radio & Satellite Communication: Radio systems for HQ and branch staff are not available due to funding gaps. Only a few vehicles are equipped with handheld radios, and emergency frequencies have been tested but not cleared. Staff have not received radio training, no SOPs exist, and satellite phones are not assigned.
• Power & IT Support: NHQ has a fixed generator but no portable units. IT support focal points are available at NHQ and in some branches, such as Sindh, to provide technical support and equipment maintenance.

LOGISTICS MANAGEMENT:
• Logistics Unit & Capacity: PRCS has a dedicated logistics function with staff covering procurement, warehousing, and fleet, but capacity is insufficient for the workload. Roles are clearly defined, and staff are trained, with close coordination maintained with IFRC during emergencies.
• Supply Chain & Prepositioning: Pre-qualified supplier lists exist and are being expanded to include IFRC and PNS suppliers, with framework agreements under development. Relief items such as hygiene kits and tents meet standards and follow FIFO principles. Warehouses are strategically located at Karachi (39k families), Haripur (30k), and Islamabad (300), with a new warehouse planned in Islamabad. A Sukkur warehouse is needed to strengthen coverage for northern Sindh and southern Punjab. Pre-positioned stocks were depleted during 2022 monsoon floods response.
• Volunteers & Coordination: Around 50–60 volunteers are trained in logistics, though records are not centralized. PRCS coordinates with Movement partners and adheres to the Emergency Items Catalogue.
• Procedures & Gaps: There is no documented expedited request procedure for branches, and no updated SOPs for in-kind donations.
SUPPLY CHAIN MANAGEMENT:
• Status Agreements & Exemptions: No agreement exists between IFRC and the government for import duty or tax exemptions. IFRC has no legal status in the country, but PRCS may rely on NDMA exemptions during emergencies for certain goods.
• Coordination & Standards: PRCS maintains its own stocks and those of in-country Movement partners, ensuring coordination with stakeholders and adherence to Movement standards, including the Emergency Items Catalogue.
• Branch Requests & Procedures: No documented expedited procedure exists for branches to request relief items. Branches can informally request supplies from NHQ stocks in the three warehouses, but local branch-level stocks are not formally recorded.
• In-kind Donations & Import Procedures: SOPs for managing in-kind donations are outdated, with the last warehouse manual issued in 2016. No formal import procedures exist, and PRCS typically relies on clearing agents. No international procurements have taken place in the past two years.
PROCUREMENT:
• Procurement Capacity: PRCS has one procurement officer and two assistants in place. While staff are trained and functional, overall capacity remains limited in relation to workload. Few partners raised concerns on transparency (isolated incidences).
• Procedures & Framework: There is no updated, approved emergency procurement manual. The existing finance policy includes one chapter on emergency procurement, but this is outdated, and procurement continues to be managed case by case. A TOR has been drafted for a new Procurement Manual & Policy, which is pending approval.
• Supplier Management: PRCS maintains a database of pre-qualified suppliers and is expanding the list to include IFRC and PNS suppliers while developing framework agreements. The system includes provisions to blacklist suppliers for non-compliance or underperformance, with decisions taken by a Procurement Committee. A tent supplier was blacklisted due to delivery delays.
• Pre-Agreements: PRCS has established pre-agreements with suppliers, including for blood donation services and a transporters framework, ensuring access to key services during emergency response.
FLEET AND TRANSPORTATION MANAGEMENT:
• Fleet Manual & Documentation: PRCS has an approved fleet manual covering vehicle management, safety, and insurance. Vehicle insurance is being finalized for models post-2015. Use of vehicles is documented through logbooks, maintenance records, and fuel checks, with incident reports filed for accidents.
• Fleet Capacity & Standards: PRCS maintains its own fleet, including two trucks for relief transportation, with the option to rent additional vehicles. New vehicles are equipped with seatbelts and first aid kits, but no fire extinguishers. A no-weapons policy is enforced. All maintenance is conducted through licensed workshops. However, existing fleet is quite old. 
• Drivers & Procedures: PRCS maintains a list of vendors for rentals, while branches manage their own local lists. Drivers are licensed and regularly tested, and new drivers undergo formal induction and approval through the fleet department. While some drivers are trained in first aid, training is not universal.
• Emergency Procedures: No formal procedures exist for regulating driver hours during emergencies. In practice, drivers work extended shifts, with per diem and overtime provided for additional hours.
WAREHOUSE AND STOCK MANAGEMENT:
• Manuals & Procedures: PRCS does not have an approved warehouse and stock management manual. Stocks are released through DM approvals but lack standardized guidance, forms, or templates. Staff and volunteers require further training on warehouse procedures.
• Systems & Tracking: The warehouse IT database is outdated (from 2005), not online, and not integrated across locations, creating challenges for stock tracking. Separate tracking mechanisms are required for medicines and NFIs. An integrated logistics tracking system connecting the three warehouses is needed to improve efficiency and accuracy.
• Warehousing Capacity: PRCS maintains three rented warehouses in Karachi, Haripur, and Islamabad, with adequate security in place (e.g., 10 guards in Haripur). These warehouses provide secure space to receive, store, and dispatch relief supplies as per response needs. Most warehouses are rented and not sustainable. Provincial branches warehouses to be included as part of the overall capacity.
• Strategic Location: Warehouses are positioned near high-risk communities to ensure accessibility during disasters. A new PRCS-owned warehouse is planned in Islamabad to strengthen long-term capacity.

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_responses.notes:
• Deployment & Skills: PRCS deploys trained CDRT, DDRT, NDRT, and RDRT teams based on needs, though safety equipment gaps remain. Response teams were not deployed in 2022 floods. While some specialized trainings are offered, there is no structured learning path or competency framework. A shift toward open, competency-based nominations under new leadership has created a more empowering environment.
• Standards & Protection: Some responders are trained on CEA, PGI, and accountability standards, with access to IFRC’s Learning Platform. Orientation sessions are organized but vary across branches. Staff and volunteers sign the Code of Conduct, while policies on child protection, anti-harassment, and whistleblowing are still under development.
• Identification & Insurance: Volunteer ID cards and visibility items are available, though IDs are issued selectively due to past misuse. Staff and 500 volunteers are insured annually, with a volunteer solidarity mechanism under development. Safety briefings occur before deployment.
• Volunteer Management: A database of 6,200 active volunteers supports response, alongside specialized sectoral lists. Spontaneous volunteers are guided by the revised 2025 Youth and Volunteering Policy, though rapid screening remains a challenge. Scaling mechanisms exist, with short-term contracts possible, but formal recognition of volunteers is limited. Retention is weak, with no formal rotation strategy, though youth mentorship and engagement initiatives exist.
• Wellbeing & Support: Safer Access analyses are not conducted, and psychosocial support and self-care training are absent. Responders’ expenses are covered through advances and per diems.

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_responses.notes:
• Focal Points & Training: PRCS has identified communications focal points across NHQ and branches, with a core team of seven at NHQ and designated officers at some branches. Training for focal points was conducted in 2024 with 27 participants, though sustained capacity building remains a priority.
• Spokespersons & External Messaging: Official spokespersons are designated with SG and Chairperson approval, and branches engage media locally. PRCS provides public information within 24 hours of emergencies through key messages, donation appeals, radio campaigns, and promotion of services such as psychosocial support and RFL.
• Media & Advocacy: PRCS uses six social media channels and public platforms to highlight unmet needs and rights of affected populations, supported by standardized templates and ongoing development of a Communications Strategy (communications in emergencies is a component), which includes updated Visual Identity Guidelines, and new Social Media Guidelines.
• Internal & Crisis Communications: Key messages are regularly shared with staff and integrated into NDRT training. Reactive lines are shared with branches during emergencies, and crisis communication capacity is embedded into staff practice.
• Monitoring & Coordination: Negative media and social media are tracked by a dedicated officer, with complaints, including harassment cases, referred to relevant departments. Coordination with IFRC and ICRC ensures alignment under SMCC.
• Evidence & Advocacy: Communications staff produce monthly reports on engagements and advocacy, linking closely with the Resource Mobilization department to generate evidence-based messages targeting decision-makers and communities.

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_responses.notes:
• Resource Mobilization Practices: PRCS mobilizes resources through domestic campaigns, donor engagement, and targeted replenishment of stocks. It has benefited from the National Society Investment Alliance (NSIA) support and plans to expand sustainable income streams (e.g., blood donation and diagnostic labs). Preparedness activities are supported, but earmarked funding limits flexibility. 
• Strategy & Branch Capacity: A long-term Resource Mobilization (RM) Strategy (zero draft) exists but requires wider consultation and endorsement. Branch sustainability remains weak, with no branch-level RM plans in highly vulnerable areas. A Calamity Fund is maintained at NHQ and some branches. During the PER workshop, participants raised the question: are we properly managing existing resources and partners?
• Partnerships & Agreements: Collaboration with the private sector is ad hoc, with limited systematic fundraising or pre-disaster agreements. A stronger RM department is needed to structure efforts.
• Systems & Procedures: A focal point supports emergency operations, and reporting is coordinated across departments. Donation platforms exist but lack online/mobile options. In-kind donation lists exist, but no formal donation tracking system is in place.

component_details.title: RC auxiliary role, Mandate and Law
component_details.description: A constitutional reference to the role of the NS in responding to disasters and crises, which may be legislated or included/ recognized in the National Response System.

component_responses.notes:
- Posibilidad de incidir para que se reconozca el rol auxiliar de la CRC en temas como Salud, Migración, entre otras.
- Hacer un inventario de las participaciones formales de la CRC.
- Incidencia para generar convenios en DIH con la Defensoría del Pueblo, las Fuerzas Militares, y las partes interesadas.
- Recuperación de Espacios en capacitación a Entidades Públicas.

component_details.title: DRM Strategy
component_details.description: An outline of the overall goal that the NS seeks to achieve in its disaster and crisis response operations. The goal considers: context analysis, ongoing/regular all-hazards risk assessments: it may define the target proportion of affected population that will be reached, and a definition of the areas/sectors where a NS will usually respond during an emergency.

component_responses.notes: - Fortalecer en la estructura de los tres componentes de Conocimiento y Reducción del Riesgo de Desastres, y Manejo de Desastres, el personal técnico permanente  que de una alcance a los programas.

component_details.title: DRM Policy
component_details.description: Reflects the NS mission, RCRC principles and mandate. It acknowledges other relevant NS policies, and aligns with the government policy (where applicable), incorporating the general rules that the NS will obey in order to achieve something (i.e mandate, strategy, etc.)

component_details.title: DRM Laws, Advocacy and Dissemination
component_details.description: Designed to support the NS in improving legal preparedness for disasters and crisis and to promote the use of the IDRL Guidelines in order to reduce human vulnerability.

component_responses.notes: La CRC realiza la evaluación de lecciones aprendidas de IDRL en las operaciones de respuesta; sin embargo, se identifica como una oportunidad de mejora en la diplomacia humanitaria.

component_details.title: Quality and accountability
component_details.description: Describes the essential elements of principled, accountable, and high-quality humanitarian action. The RCRC Movement provides support to the most vulnerable people in line with the Sphere and CHS standards, Code of Conduct for the RCRC Movement and NGOS in Disaster Relief and the Code for Good Partnership of the RCRC Movement, Gender & Diversity, inclusion and protection, BPI/ Do no harm, context-sensitive analysis, violence prevention, accountability to affected population and disability considerations, Community engagement and accountability (CEA).

component_responses.notes:
- Se están estableciendo los puntos focales para canalizar el Sistema de Protección contra la explotación y los abusos sexuales.
- Establecer la Estrategia Nacional de CEA.

component_details.title: Safety and security management
component_details.description: Addresses policy and procedures to ensure the safety of staff and volunteers. This include awareness, effective recruitment, training and management processes in place to ensure that personnel are capable of undertaking the roles demanded of them (from NS operational, management and leaders) according to the Stay Safe (IFRC) and Safer Access (ICRC). Based on safer access framework, including concepts of access, perception, identification and acceptance, and protection and violence prevention.

component_responses.notes: Se cuenta a nivel de Cruz Roja Colombiana con la Política Nacional de Seguridad, la cual aborda un sistema de seguridad operacional y de acceso más seguro en terreno. Esta se complementa con el "Manual de Seguridad Operacional – Serie 1000 (2024 – 2028)", de los cuales constantemente se realizan actualizaciones y capacitaciones. A su vez, para actualización de contextos se cuenta con las Salas de Crisis y para el reporte y monitoreo se cuenta con la CITEL de Sociedad Nacional y de las Seccionales. Para concluir, se cuenta con un sistema robusto de seguridad anclado con la línea de Acceso Más Seguro financiado por el CICR, en el que igualmente faltaría reforzar las capacidades y herramientas de las Seccionales con menores capacidades. Finalmente, el curso de Manténgase a Salvo debería ampliarse a todo el personal y voluntarios en todo momento.

component_details.title: Operations Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Learning
component_details.description: The PMERL is designed to implement a results-based planning, monitoring and evaluation system that provides an evidence base of NS performance, including relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact. A reliable and trusted organization is accountable, providing transparent and timely information and building systems to strengthen data collection and reporting. It is data-driven, analytical and results-based.

component_responses.notes: La Sociedad Nacional cuenta con un sistema de Monitoreo, Evaluación, Presentación de Informes y Aprendizaje de las Operaciones a nivel administrativo, financiero, operacional y de proyectos en el cual se evalúan las operaciones a nivel gerencial que impactan a las específicas. Igualmente, se deja la recomendación de hacer más visible estas evaluaciones a todos los colaboradores de la organización y de implementar planes de acción de las lecciones aprendidas por proyectos. Específicamente, se debe ampliar la socialización de la Guía PMER a todos los colaboradores y que incluya procesos de monitoreo a nivel administrativo, financiero y operacional y no solo de Proyectos.

component_details.title: Finance and Admin policy and emergency procedures
component_details.description: Overall budgeting, accounting, treasury, assets, financial reporting and financial services operations. it also includes the efficient delivery , cost effective and timely services to the NS. Pre-approved, auditable, expedited procedures that allow for flexibility during a disaster/crisis. These must meet transparency, oversight and accountability standards. Procedures may include faster approval processes, fewer signatures, different authority levels. The Emergency Procedures are activated for a specific period of time.

component_responses.notes: Se cuentan con herramientas en los procesos de administración y finanzas para responder a las emergencias, se tiene la experiencia de situaciones anteriores y, por tanto, las diferentes áreas conocen los mecanismos. No obstante, resaltamos la importancia de contar con un procedimiento generalizado para todas las áreas que sea específico para emergencias o lineamientos para que estas políticas y procedimientos ya existentes se implementen en situaciones de emergencia. De esta forma poder clasificar a los proyectos según el nivel de respuesta que deban tener.

component_details.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)
component_details.description: Refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications. This includes the Internet, wireless networks, mobile phones, radios and other communication mediums.

component_responses.notes: La Cruz Roja Colombiana cuenta con equipo robusto de TI y de Telecomunicaciones, se cuenta con 7 Seccionales que corresponde al 21% con servicio de CITEL 24 horas y otras 3 Seccionales cuentan con mínimo 6 horas de funcionamiento, sin embargo, se asegura que todas cuenten con al menos un radio base VHF-HF. Adicional a esto, cuando ocurre una emergencia, se tiene la capacidad para activar el servicio de CITEL en cualquier Seccional, enviando a personal capacitado desde el mismo territorio u otros territorios si la emergencia supera la capacidad de respuesta. Por otro lado, se evidencia una oportunidad de mejora para la atención de emergencias desde las Seccionales, con la adquisición de antenas portables satelitales para el suministro del servicio de internet y la capacitación a todo el personal en manejo básico de radios. Finalmente, se evidencia la oportunidad de mejora en la actualización del Manual de Telecomunicaciones.

La Cruz Roja Colombiana cuenta con un sistema de logística, compras y cadena de suministros robusto en el país, que permite la respuesta efectiva y eficaz ante emergencias en territorio Nacional. Igualmente, se deja la recomendación de implementar evaluaciones de necesidades previas a las emergencias en corto tiempo, para una respuesta rápida cumpliendo con las necesidades de las comunidades. Adicionalmente, se recomiendo estandarizar los procesos de gestión de almacén y compras a nivel de Seccionales y Sede Nacional, dado que no se cuenta con un proceso único que aplique a toda la Cruz Roja Colombiana, esta funciona dependiendo de los procesos de cada Seccional.

component_details.title: Staff and volunteer management
component_details.description: Well-functioning staff and volunteer management systems and practices allow for effective recruitment, supervision, support and encouragement of staff and volunteers.

component_responses.notes: El buen funcionamiento de los sistemas y prácticas de gestión del voluntariado y del personal permiten la contratación, la supervisión, el apoyo y el reconocimiento eficaz de personal y voluntarios en la Sociedad Nacional de la Cruz Roja Colombiana. Sin embargo, el código de ética y conducta únicamente se socializa para los voluntarios pero no se establece ningún documento que mencione su obligatorio cumplimiento, por tanto, se ve una acción de mejora en este punto.

component_details.title: Communication in emergencies
component_details.description: Incorporates a system of public messaging to enable the NS to share timely, accurate information before, during, and after a disaster or crisis.

component_responses.notes: La Sociedad Nacional incorpora un sistema de mensajería pública que permite compartir información correcta y oportuna antes, durante y después de un desastre o crisis. No obstante, se evidencian acciones de mejora como un medio de comunicación oficial entre la Sede Nacional y las Seccionales en momentos de emergencia que no sea Whatsapp. Por su parte, no se tiene un procedimiento específico que establezca un tiempo mínimo para las comunicaciones oficiales en emergencias. Finalmente, las comunicaciones negativas en redes sociales no cuentan con un monitoreo sistematizado.

component_details.title: Resource Mobilisation
component_details.description: A documented strategy for raising domestic funds from the government, private sector, general public and other in-country actors to support the national society’s response. This would include allocation of responsibilities, practical mechanisms for accepting funds and for being accountable on funds.

component_responses.notes: La Sociedad Nacional cuenta con una estrategia documentada para recaudar fondos nacionales del gobierno, el sector privado, el público en general y otros actores dentro del país para apoyar la respuesta. Esto incluye la asignación de responsabilidades, mecanismos prácticos para aceptar fondos y rendición de cuentas sobre los fondos. Sin embargo, evidenciamos como acciones de mejora, ampliar el conocimiento interno del proceso de MDR y la socialización de otras plataformas de servicios para operaciones conjuntas por parte de la FICR o del Movimiento.

component_details.title: Hazard, Context and Risk Analysis, Monitoring and Early Warning
component_details.description: Describes how the NS monitors and maps past, present and potential hazards, disasters and crises (e.g. hazard, vulnerability assessments, gathering information from communities and government authorities) and systematically evaluates the damage that could be caused by a potential disaster/crisis, the frequency, severity of the impact, and the alert the relevant areas to scale the preparedness actions to reduce population vulnerability.

component_responses.notes:
La SN tiene un sistema formal de monitoreo de riesgos, con puntos focales en Dirección Nacional y Seccionales. Se recopilan y analizan datos primarios (formatos, levantamiento de datos comunitarios con metodologías como AVCA) y secundarios sobre tendencias emergentes, generando reportes semanales de Situación, Pronósticos y Alertas, que se comparten en reuniones regulares con Seccionales. Se han identificado brechas y riesgos en la seguridad y acceso, abordados mediante comités de seguridad y el uso del Marco de Acceso Más Seguro. Además, se monitorean los umbrales definidos a través de los sistemas propios del gobierno para desastres y se implementa un sistema de alerta temprana.
